ilaten_requirement: All future architectural, engineering, security, operational, and product decisions must remain consistent with this document.
The document shall evolve without changing previously accepted architectural decisions unless a formal Architecture Decision Record (ADR) explicitly supersedes them.
The system shall not be redesigned unless explicitly authorized through the applicable governance process.
Consistency shall be preserved across the entire document.

Upon formal approval and publication as Version 1.0, this document shall become the official public engineering standard of ILATEN. Until that approval, it remains the single controlled working source from which the canonical standard is produced.
Required enterprise-grade content shall not be replaced with outline-only text, abbreviated placeholders, or unsupported assertions.
Substantive reasoning, controls, obligations, boundaries, and decision context shall be preserved while unnecessary repetition is removed.
The Executive Summary may summarize the document’s purpose and architecture. All other sections shall use the level of detail required by their subject and intended audience.
Every section shall be written as enterprise-grade documentation.

Subsection and section page allocations are descriptive planning ranges derived from the current accepted content and standard reference rendering. When accepted content changes materially, the Index shall be updated to reflect the resulting page range rather than forcing arbitrary compression, expansion, omission, or repetition.
Duplicate information shall be avoided.
Formal technical English and enterprise terminology shall be used throughout.
Every section shall be self-contained while remaining consistent with the rest of the document.
The content shall be suitable for chief technology officers, software architects, enterprise customers, investors, auditors, and research and development grant evaluations.
The document shall remain implementation-independent whenever possible.
The architecture shall remain technology-agnostic except where an explicit product or canonical architecture decision requires otherwise.
Conversational language, development-session history, named development assistants, model-provider references, and implementation-chat references are prohibited.
The handbook shall describe ILATEN as a product and engineering system, not as a development conversation or a collection of tools.

ILATEN is an Enterprise AI Operating System designed to make AI-assisted decisions and actions secure, verifiable, policy-governed, and auditable. It provides the institutional control layer required for organizations to use artificial intelligence within business-critical environments without surrendering security authority, operational accountability, or human responsibility. ILATEN is not positioned as a general-purpose conversational interface or an isolated automation product. It is a governed operating environment through which AI-assisted work can be requested, evaluated, authorized, executed, validated, continuously evidenced, and reviewed under enterprise-defined controls.

The strategic need for ILATEN arises from a fundamental gap in enterprise AI adoption. Generative systems can produce plans, recommendations, code, content, and operational instructions at significant speed, but their outputs are probabilistic and cannot be treated as inherently authorized, correct, safe, or compliant. Traditional application controls are insufficient when a system can dynamically propose actions, invoke tools, interact with sensitive environments, or influence material business decisions. Enterprises therefore require more than model access. They require a durable trust architecture that separates reasoning from authority, constrains execution, enforces organizational policy, preserves evidence, and ensures that accountable individuals retain control over consequential outcomes.

The platform is organized around complementary architectural planes. The experience layer provides controlled interfaces for operators, reviewers, and authorized users. The secure access layer validates identity, tenant boundaries, request integrity, rate limits, correlation, and replay protection. The control plane manages task orchestration, policy enforcement, capability assignment, risk evaluation, approval requirements, model access, tool access, cancellation, timeout, retry, and compensation behavior. The execution plane performs approved work inside restricted environments with narrowly scoped access to required resources. The Trust and Evidence Plane records material events, binds outputs to their provenance, verifies integrity, and provides an independently reviewable history of what occurred. Together, these planes create a coherent operating model in which trust is established through controls and evidence rather than assumed from a component, user, or output.

At summary level, the canonical operational lifecycle proceeds through request intake; identity, tenant, and request-integrity verification; creation of the Immutable Context and authority scope; preparation of a plan or action proposal; policy and capability evaluation; risk classification; explicit human approval where required; issuance of time-bound and constrained execution authority; isolated execution through the Tool Gateway; independent assessment through the Validation Pipeline; acceptance or rejection; and controlled delivery, closure, and review. Detailed behavior, failure paths, and state transitions are defined in the System Architecture section.

Security is treated as a product property rather than an external compliance activity. ILATEN applies Zero Trust, least privilege, secure-by-default behavior, explicit authorization, isolated execution, defense in depth, and continuous verification. No user, model, device, integration, or execution component is trusted solely because it exists inside the platform boundary. Capabilities are task-specific, time-bound, scope-limited, observable, and revocable. Sensitive actions—including production deployment, destructive data operations, financial transactions, external communications, privilege changes, access to protected information, and security-policy modifications—require defined authorization and, where applicable, explicit human approval. The system is prohibited from expanding its own privileges, weakening controls, bypassing failed validations, disabling required tests, or modifying audit history.

Human accountability remains central to the operating model. ILATEN is intended to amplify institutional capability, not replace accountable decision-making. Risk-sensitive actions remain attributable to identified owners and approvers. The platform supplies the context, controls, validation results, and evidence required for informed authorization, while the organization defines which decisions may be automated, which require review, and which remain exclusively human. This approach enables enterprises to increase operational speed without creating an accountability vacuum or allowing convenience to supersede governance.

The initial commercial focus is secure AI-assisted software development and controlled enterprise digital operations. In the primary adoption scenario, an authorized user requests analysis or a controlled change within a version-controlled software repository. ILATEN validates the request, determines the applicable scope and policy, classifies risk, obtains approval when required, executes permitted work in an isolated environment, runs the defined validation process, and produces a traceable evidence package. The verified result can then be delivered through a controlled change mechanism. This initial focus aligns the product with measurable enterprise needs: reducing unsafe changes, increasing review quality, improving traceability, enforcing engineering standards, and accelerating delivery without weakening security or accountability.

The product is designed for modular expansion beyond the initial use case. Its control, execution, validation, and evidence foundations can support additional enterprise workflows where AI-assisted actions must operate under policy and produce defensible records. Expansion shall remain dependency-driven and governed by explicit product scope, architecture decisions, security review, and measurable customer value. New capabilities shall not be introduced merely because a technology is available or fashionable. Every material addition must have a defined purpose, ownership model, risk treatment, acceptance criteria, operational boundary, and evidence requirement.

ILATEN therefore establishes a clear category position: an Enterprise AI Operating System that governs how AI-assisted work enters, moves through, and exits an organization’s operational environment. Its purpose is to make enterprise AI usable under real institutional constraints by combining policy-governed control, human accountability, restricted execution, independent validation, cryptographic evidence, and continuous auditability. The long-term objective is to become the global trust layer for enterprise AI while preserving the principle that trust must be earned through verifiable behavior and evidence.

ILATEN envisions a future in which artificial intelligence can participate in consequential enterprise work without weakening institutional control. In this future, organizations will not be required to choose between innovation and assurance, operational speed and accountability, or advanced intelligence and responsible governance. AI-assisted capabilities will operate within explicit boundaries, under enforceable policy, with evidence sufficient to establish what was requested, what was authorized, what occurred, why the result was accepted, and who remained accountable for the outcome.

The vision is founded on the principle that enterprise trust cannot be derived from confidence in a model, vendor, interface, or individual output. Trust must be established continuously through identity, authorization, policy enforcement, controlled execution, validation, traceability, and evidence. ILATEN seeks to make these controls a standard operating foundation for enterprise AI, allowing organizations to adopt changing intelligence technologies without rebuilding their governance and assurance architecture for every provider, model generation, business unit, or use case.

ILATEN aims to make trustworthy AI operations practical at institutional scale. Security and governance must not remain fragmented across isolated applications, manually enforced procedures, or provider-specific controls. They must become reusable platform capabilities that apply consistently across departments, workflows, infrastructure environments, and deployment models. The platform vision therefore extends beyond securing individual requests. It establishes a common control language for identity, capability, policy, risk, approval, execution, evidence, audit, and accountability across the enterprise.

The vision also defines a clear standard for responsible autonomy. Increased automation is acceptable only when it remains bounded by policy, least privilege, defined risk tolerance, revocable authority, validation, and audit. Greater capability shall not imply unrestricted control. Human accountability shall not be removed from consequential decisions. System evolution shall increase the quality, consistency, and efficiency of controlled execution while preserving the organization’s ability to intervene, deny, revoke, investigate, recover, and learn.

Global relevance requires the architecture to accommodate different industries, regulatory environments, deployment constraints, organizational structures, and risk profiles without weakening its foundational principles. ILATEN must support adaptable policies and operating models while maintaining consistent expectations for security, evidence, accountability, and verification. The platform should be capable of serving organizations with differing maturity levels, from controlled initial adoption to complex multi-entity operations, without fragmenting the canonical trust model.

The mission of ILATEN is to convert enterprise AI governance from an abstract policy objective into an enforceable operating capability. The platform exists to ensure that AI-assisted work is not merely generated, but is controlled throughout its complete lifecycle. Every material task must enter through an authorized channel, be evaluated against organizational policy, receive the required level of approval, execute within a bounded environment, undergo defined validation, and produce evidence sufficient for accountability and review. ILATEN fulfils its mission when enterprises can use advanced intelligence while retaining effective control over authority, risk, data, infrastructure, and outcomes.

ILATEN shall provide a consistent governance boundary between probabilistic reasoning and enterprise operations. Intelligence components may analyze information, formulate recommendations, or prepare proposed actions, but operational authority remains external to those components. The platform translates organizational intent into explicit controls governing who may request an action, which resources may be accessed, what conditions must be satisfied, when human approval is required, how execution is constrained, and what constitutes an acceptable result. This boundary enables useful intelligence to participate in real work without becoming a source of unbounded authority.

Policy enforcement is a primary mission obligation. ILATEN must allow organizational requirements to be expressed as actionable rules and evaluated at the relevant stages of a task. Policy shall govern identity, capability, data access, execution scope, environmental constraints, risk thresholds, approval requirements, validation criteria, retention, and evidence obligations. A policy decision must be attributable, reproducible where applicable, and associated with the task to which it applies. Failed or unsatisfied controls shall prevent acceptance or execution rather than being treated as advisory warnings.

Human approval is retained wherever organizational accountability, legal obligation, material risk, or ethical responsibility requires it. ILATEN shall provide decision-makers with sufficient context to understand the requested action, affected resources, identified risks, applicable policies, expected consequences, validation plan, and available recovery options. Approval must be explicit, scoped, attributable, time-bound where appropriate, and inseparable from the task that received it. The platform shall support efficient review without reducing approval to a ceremonial step or transferring responsibility to the system.

Controlled and isolated execution is essential to limiting operational exposure. ILATEN shall ensure that approved work is performed with the minimum capabilities necessary for the specific task and within an environment appropriate to its risk. Access must be limited by resource, operation, duration, identity, and context. Execution boundaries must prevent a permitted action from becoming unrestricted access to adjacent systems or data. The platform must support interruption, revocation, timeout, failure handling, and recovery so that organizations can remain in control when execution deviates from expected behavior.

Verification is required before results are treated as trustworthy. ILATEN shall apply defined validation procedures to outputs, artifacts, state changes, and execution outcomes according to the nature and risk of the task. Validation may include structural checks, policy checks, tests, integrity verification, security controls, quality gates, and business acceptance conditions. A completed execution is not automatically a successful execution, and a successful execution is not automatically an accepted result. Acceptance depends on evidence that the applicable requirements have been satisfied.

Evidence generation is a continuous lifecycle obligation and a mandatory product output. ILATEN shall preserve a traceable record of the material facts produced from request intake through closure and review, including task origin, context creation, authorization basis, planning, policy decisions, risk classification, approvals, execution context, significant actions, validation results, artifacts, integrity information, exceptions, and final disposition. Evidence must be protected against unauthorized alteration and organized so that authorized reviewers can determine what occurred without relying on memory, informal explanation, or unverifiable system claims. Cryptographic integrity and append-only audit behavior support this obligation without replacing governance, access control, or operational oversight.

Independent review must remain possible. The mission is not satisfied when a platform evaluates its own actions through opaque mechanisms and presents only a final assertion of success. ILATEN shall expose sufficient structured evidence for authorized technical, security, risk, compliance, and audit functions to assess whether controls operated as intended. Verification mechanisms should remain separable from the reasoning process that proposed the action, and critical acceptance criteria should be deterministic wherever practicable.

The mission includes preserving enterprise choice. Models, infrastructure components, interfaces, and execution technologies will evolve, and organizations must be able to adopt improved capabilities without abandoning their governance foundation. ILATEN shall therefore maintain implementation independence where possible, define stable control boundaries, and treat intelligence providers as replaceable components rather than sources of institutional authority. Product decisions that intentionally constrain technology must be explicit, justified, and governed through the canonical architecture process.

ILATEN shall advance adoption through disciplined, measurable expansion. Initial capabilities focus on secure AI-assisted software development and controlled digital operations because these domains provide concrete validation, audit, and evidence requirements. Future expansion must preserve the same control model and proceed only where customer value, operational ownership, security treatment, and acceptance criteria are clear. The mission does not include pursuing unrestricted autonomy, bypassing human responsibility, or expanding functionality without a defensible enterprise purpose.

This mission establishes a permanent product obligation: every ILATEN capability must strengthen the organization’s ability to govern, constrain, verify, evidence, and account for AI-assisted work. Features that increase execution power while weakening policy enforcement, human authority, isolation, validation, evidence, or auditability are inconsistent with the product mission. Product progress shall be measured by the quality of trusted outcomes and responsible adoption, not by the volume of automated activity alone.

ILATEN’s Product Values define the enduring beliefs that guide product strategy, architecture, engineering, security, operations, customer relationships, and organizational conduct. They establish how decisions shall be made when requirements compete, information is incomplete, or short-term opportunity conflicts with long-term trust. These values are not promotional statements. They are decision criteria that apply to product capabilities, internal practices, commercial commitments, and the conduct expected of every party responsible for designing, operating, reviewing, or representing ILATEN.

The values operate as a coherent system. Security without transparency can become opaque control. Evidence without human accountability can become administrative recordkeeping. Determinism without continuous verification can preserve incorrect behavior. Enterprise quality without trust by design can produce a polished but unreliable product. Decisions shall therefore consider the complete value set and resolve trade-offs in a manner consistent with ILATEN’s mission and canonical architecture.

Security takes precedence over convenience, speed, feature volume, and short-term commercial pressure. Product capabilities shall be designed with explicit consideration of identity, authorization, data exposure, execution boundaries, misuse, failure, recovery, and auditability. A release, integration, or customer commitment shall not proceed when a material security risk is unowned, inadequately controlled, or deliberately obscured. Security First does not require the elimination of all risk; it requires that risk be identified, evaluated, controlled, accepted by the appropriate authority, and supported by evidence.

This value also requires secure defaults. Customers and operators should not need exceptional expertise to avoid unsafe baseline behavior. Capabilities that can affect sensitive information, infrastructure, production systems, financial interests, or external parties must begin from denial or minimum authority and expand only through explicit, governed decisions.

Trust is an architectural outcome, not a claim added after implementation. ILATEN shall embed identity, policy, approval, isolation, validation, evidence, and accountability into the normal lifecycle of a task. These controls shall not depend solely on optional configuration, manual discipline, or retrospective review. Product design must make trustworthy behavior the expected path and make deviations visible, attributable, and governable.

Trust by Design also applies to customer relationships. Product documentation, security representations, service commitments, and commercial claims must accurately reflect verified capabilities and known limitations. ILATEN shall not create confidence through ambiguity or imply assurance that cannot be demonstrated.

Operational control must remain predictable even when intelligence outputs are probabilistic. ILATEN values deterministic rules for authorization, policy evaluation, capability boundaries, validation gates, evidence generation, and final acceptance wherever practicable. The same relevant inputs and governing conditions should produce consistent control decisions, and material exceptions must be explicit and reviewable.

ILATEN gives priority to verifiable facts over expectation, reputation, confidence, or informal explanation. Decisions about task completion, security, quality, compliance, and release readiness must be supported by appropriate evidence. An assertion that a control operated, a validation passed, or an action succeeded is insufficient when the platform can produce objective records.

Evidence must be relevant, attributable, integrity-protected, and understandable to its authorized audience. The quantity of records does not substitute for evidentiary quality. ILATEN shall capture the material facts required to evaluate an outcome while avoiding unnecessary collection that increases privacy, security, or operational risk.

AI-assisted capability does not remove human or institutional responsibility. Every consequential product decision, risk acceptance, policy definition, privileged authorization, and material customer commitment must have an identifiable accountable owner. ILATEN shall support informed human judgment with context, risk information, validation results, and evidence, while preserving the authority to approve, deny, interrupt, revoke, investigate, and remediate.

Human Accountability rejects both uncontrolled automation and symbolic oversight. Review must occur at the level required by risk and must be designed so that the responsible person can make a meaningful decision. Accountability shall remain clear across product ownership, engineering, security, operations, customers, and authorized third parties.

ILATEN shall be engineered and operated to standards appropriate for business-critical use. Enterprise Quality includes correctness, security, reliability, maintainability, resilience, performance, accessibility, supportability, interoperability, and professional documentation. A capability is not complete merely because it functions under ideal conditions. It must behave predictably under expected load, failure, misuse, change, and recovery scenarios relevant to its approved scope.

This value requires disciplined lifecycle practices, explicit acceptance criteria, quality gates, controlled releases, and ownership after deployment. Technical debt, defects, and limitations must be visible and governed. Quality shall not be simulated through presentation or substituted with feature breadth.

ILATEN shall make material system behavior, control decisions, limitations, and responsibilities understandable to authorized stakeholders. Users and reviewers should be able to determine why an action was permitted or denied, which policies applied, what evidence exists, what uncertainties remain, and what remedial options are available. Documentation shall distinguish verified capability from planned capability and product fact from assumption.

Transparency does not require unrestricted disclosure. Sensitive data, security controls, customer information, and protected intellectual property must remain appropriately safeguarded. The value requires purposeful visibility to authorized audiences, accurate communication, and the absence of deceptive or materially incomplete representations.

Trust and quality must be re-established as systems, policies, dependencies, environments, and risks change. A control that operated correctly in the past cannot be assumed to remain effective indefinitely. ILATEN shall promote ongoing validation of software, configuration, access, policy behavior, evidence integrity, resilience, and operational readiness throughout the product lifecycle.

Continuous Verification includes detecting drift, reassessing risk, testing recovery, reviewing access, monitoring control performance, and learning from defects and incidents. Improvement must be controlled and evidence-based; it shall not silently redefine accepted architecture, weaken safeguards, or bypass formal decision processes.

Collectively, these values define the character of ILATEN. When a decision presents a conflict between rapid expansion and governed reliability, ILATEN shall preserve security, trust, evidence, accountability, and enterprise quality. When uncertainty exists, the organization shall seek verification rather than rely on assumption. When capability increases, control and transparency must increase with it. Product decisions that cannot be reconciled with these values require explicit review and shall not be normalized through precedent or convenience.

Product Foundations define the essential capabilities and qualities on which ILATEN depends. They establish what the product must preserve as technologies, deployment models, markets, and customer requirements evolve.

These foundations are mandatory. They apply to every material capability, integration, release, and architecture decision. A proposed change that conflicts with them must not be accepted through informal exception, implementation convenience, or commercial urgency. Any legitimate supersession requires documented justification, impact analysis, formal review, and an approved Architecture Decision Record.

ILATEN is founded on demonstrable trust. Trust is established through identity, explicit authority, policy enforcement, bounded execution, validation, evidence, and accountability. No component, user, integration, or output receives unconditional trust based on location, reputation, provider, or prior success. Trust must be appropriate to the specific action and continuously supported by observable behavior.

Security protects the confidentiality, integrity, availability, and authorized use of enterprise resources. It must exist across the complete product lifecycle and task lifecycle, including design, development, deployment, access, execution, validation, monitoring, recovery, and retirement. Security controls shall be proportional to risk while preserving mandatory protections that cannot be waived for convenience.

Organizations must retain effective authority over what ILATEN may do, under which conditions, within which boundaries, and on whose approval. Control includes policy, capability, risk classification, approval, interruption, revocation, timeout, recovery, and final acceptance. Increased intelligence or automation shall never eliminate the organization’s ability to constrain or stop consequential activity.

Material decisions and actions must produce sufficient evidence to support verification, accountability, audit, investigation, and learning. Evidence shall be attributable, relevant, integrity-protected, and accessible to authorized reviewers. The evidentiary model must connect requests, decisions, approvals, execution events, validation results, artifacts, exceptions, and final outcomes without relying on informal reconstruction.

ILATEN must be suitable for governed use in real organizations. Enterprise Readiness includes identity integration, tenant and data boundaries, policy administration, reliability, resilience, observability, supportability, change control, documentation, compliance operations, and accountable ownership. Product maturity shall be evaluated against operational obligations, not demonstration quality alone.

The product must scale across workloads, teams, business units, customers, policies, evidence volumes, deployment environments, and organizational complexity without fragmenting the trust model. Scalability includes technical capacity, operational manageability, governance consistency, and economic sustainability. Scale shall not be achieved by weakening isolation, reducing evidence, bypassing review, or obscuring responsibility.

Product Principles convert the Product Foundations into binding product decisions. They define permanent requirements that govern product strategy, architecture, engineering, security, operations, and acceptance.

Every material AI-assisted action must be evaluated under an applicable policy before execution. Absence of policy does not imply permission. The organization defines the authority, conditions, resources, risk limits, approvals, and acceptance requirements associated with each class of action. Policy enforcement is a core product capability rather than an optional external safeguard.

Evidence is required for every material task and control decision. A task cannot be considered complete when its outcome cannot be traced to authorized inputs, governed execution, and verified results. Evidence requirements may vary according to risk and data classification, but they shall never be reduced to unsupported assertions of success.

Material activity must be recorded with sufficient context to support authorized review. Auditability includes the ability to determine who or what initiated an action, which controls applied, what was approved, what occurred, what changed, which validations ran, and how the task concluded. Audit records must remain protected against unauthorized modification and governed by defined access and retention rules.

Intelligence models are interchangeable implementation components, not sources of architectural authority. Core governance, security, execution, validation, evidence, and audit behavior must remain independent of any single model or provider wherever practicable. Replacement must be possible through defined interfaces, controlled evaluation, and compatibility requirements without redesigning the Trust Core.

When convenience conflicts with a material security requirement, security prevails. Product design should minimize unnecessary friction, but it shall not remove meaningful controls merely to accelerate adoption or simplify operation. Exceptions require explicit risk ownership, documented scope, compensating controls, expiration where appropriate, and formal authorization.

ILATEN prioritizes predictable, testable, policy-bound behavior over unrestricted autonomy. Reasoning may remain probabilistic, but authorization, capability boundaries, required approvals, validation gates, evidence obligations, and acceptance decisions shall be deterministic wherever practicable. Greater autonomy may be introduced only inside explicit limits and must remain observable, revocable, and accountable.
Design Principles govern how the Product Foundations and Product Principles shall be expressed across architecture, user experience, security, data, operations, and future capabilities.

Default configurations and normal workflows must select the safer permissible behavior. Access begins denied or minimally scoped, sensitive operations require explicit authorization, and protective controls are active without depending on optional user action. Unsafe expansion must be deliberate, visible, and governed.

Every identity, service, integration, and execution context receives only the capabilities required for an approved task, for the minimum necessary duration and scope. Authority must be revocable and must not silently propagate to adjacent resources, environments, or future tasks.

Personal, confidential, regulated, and customer-controlled data must be protected through purposeful collection, classification, minimization, access control, encryption, retention, deletion, and evidence practices. The product shall avoid collecting or exposing information that is not necessary for an authorized purpose. Privacy requirements must influence architecture before implementation and remain enforceable throughout operations.

Design decisions must define how correctness, authorization, control operation, and outcomes will be demonstrated. Evidence requirements are established before a capability is accepted, not reconstructed after release. Observability and audit data must be designed to support meaningful verification while respecting security, privacy, retention, and proportionality.

Human review is mandatory where risk, law, organizational policy, ethics, financial impact, external consequence, or irreversible change requires accountable judgment. The review experience must provide enough information for a meaningful decision and must preserve the ability to approve, deny, request modification, interrupt, or revoke. Human involvement shall be risk-based and substantive rather than universal, arbitrary, or ceremonial.

The foundations establish what ILATEN must preserve; the Product Principles define what the product must always require; the Design Principles determine how capabilities must be shaped. When principles appear to compete, the interpretation that best preserves security, human accountability, policy control, evidence integrity, and enterprise operability shall take precedence. Conflicts that cannot be resolved through this hierarchy require formal architectural governance.

Every product proposal and material engineering decision must demonstrate alignment with these principles through its requirements, threat assessment, acceptance criteria, validation plan, evidence plan, and operational ownership. Compliance shall be evaluated by observable product behavior. Naming a principle in documentation without implementing its required control is not sufficient.

This Constitution is binding across product management, architecture, engineering, security, operations, governance, customer delivery, and executive decision-making. Compliance requires observable alignment in product behavior and operational practice. Statements of intent, documentation language, or internal approval cannot compensate for a capability that violates a constitutional obligation.

Every ILATEN capability shall be designed, implemented, deployed, and operated according to enterprise security requirements appropriate to its scope and risk. Material security controls shall not be disabled, bypassed, weakened, or deferred solely to accelerate delivery, simplify adoption, reduce cost, or satisfy a commercial deadline. Residual risk must be documented, assigned to an accountable owner, and formally accepted by the authority entitled to accept it.

No material AI-assisted action shall execute without an applicable authorization and policy decision. Policy defines the permitted purpose, identity, capabilities, resources, conditions, risk limits, approvals, validation requirements, and evidence obligations. Missing, ambiguous, failed, or expired authorization shall result in denial or suspension rather than implied permission. Operational authority shall never be inferred from the persuasiveness, confidence, or apparent quality of generated output.

ILATEN shall not remove human or institutional responsibility from consequential decisions. Actions involving material security, legal, financial, operational, privacy, ethical, or external impact require the degree of accountable human authority defined by organizational policy. Approval must be informed, attributable, scoped, and reviewable. Automation may reduce manual effort, but it shall not create an accountability gap or obscure the owner of a decision.

Every material task shall produce evidence sufficient to establish its origin, authorization basis, applicable controls, execution history, validation results, artifacts, exceptions, and final disposition. Material events must be auditable, integrity-protected, and governed by defined access and retention rules. A task cannot be treated as trustworthy merely because it completed without a visible error. Trust requires evidence that the right action occurred under the right authority and satisfied the right acceptance conditions.

ilaten_requirement: The Product Constitution may evolve only when a material change is necessary, justified, and formally governed. Amendments require a documented proposal, rationale, affected provisions, architecture and security impact analysis, operational and customer implications, migration requirements, and approval through the applicable Architecture Decision Record process. An amendment must identify whether it clarifies an existing obligation or supersedes a previous decision. Historical decisions and evidence shall remain preserved.

No roadmap item, release plan, customer request, internal instruction, or implementation choice automatically overrides this Constitution. When ambiguity exists, interpretation shall favor security, policy governance, human accountability, evidence integrity, architectural continuity, and responsible enterprise use. This hierarchy ensures that ILATEN can evolve substantially while preserving the trust commitments that define the product.

The ILATEN Product Philosophy defines the role that artificial intelligence should occupy within enterprise operations. Intelligence is a capability that can expand human and organizational effectiveness, but it is not an independent source of legitimacy, responsibility, or trust. The product shall therefore be designed around four enduring philosophical commitments.

Organizations and accountable individuals remain responsible for consequential decisions and outcomes. ILATEN may provide analysis, recommendations, controlled execution, and evidence, but it shall not be used to transfer ownership of risk or ethical judgment to a probabilistic system. Human authority must remain meaningful wherever consequences require informed responsibility.

ilaten_requirement: Trust shall result from verified behavior, not reputation, confidence, fluency, or assertion. Evidence must show that identity was established, policy was applied, authority was valid, execution remained within scope, validation was completed, and the outcome met its acceptance conditions. Trust is therefore provisional, contextual, and continuously renewable rather than permanent or assumed.

The product is positioned for enterprises that want to move beyond isolated AI experimentation but cannot permit probabilistic systems to exercise unbounded operational authority. These organizations require a common foundation for policy enforcement, human accountability, constrained execution, independent validation, continuous audit, and cryptographically protected evidence. ILATEN addresses that requirement by converting governance from an external policy exercise into enforceable product behavior across the complete lifecycle of AI-assisted work.

For organizations adopting AI in consequential software and digital operations, ILATEN is an Enterprise AI Operating System that transforms proposed actions into policy-governed, risk-aware, independently validated, and continuously auditable outcomes. It separates planning from permission, authority from intelligence, and execution from acceptance. Unlike products focused primarily on interaction, generation, orchestration, or retrospective monitoring, ILATEN provides the institutional control architecture required to authorize, constrain, verify, evidence, and account for AI-assisted activity.

The operating-system designation reflects the product’s role as a shared foundation. ILATEN coordinates the lifecycle and control responsibilities required by multiple enterprise workflows rather than solving only one task. It establishes durable boundaries for identity, policy, capability, approval, execution, validation, evidence, audit, and recovery. Business applications and specialized capabilities may operate above or through this foundation while remaining subject to the same canonical trust model.

ILATEN is also not tied conceptually to one model provider, one infrastructure environment, one user interface, or one deployment pattern. Product decisions may intentionally adopt specific technologies where required, but the market position depends on stable control and trust capabilities rather than a transient implementation choice. This independence protects the customer’s governance investment as underlying intelligence technologies evolve.

The initial commercial position is secure AI-assisted software development and controlled enterprise digital operations. This entry point offers clear enterprise value and objectively verifiable outcomes. An authorized request can be associated with a defined repository or digital environment, a proposed plan, explicit policy and capability limits, a measurable risk classification, required approval, restricted execution, deterministic quality gates, controlled delivery, and a complete evidence history.

This focus enables ILATEN to demonstrate its core promise through practical measures such as reduction in unsafe changes, policy compliance, validation success, evidence coverage, review efficiency, recovery performance, and traceable delivery. It also aligns with existing enterprise governance concerns around source integrity, access control, change management, software quality, supply-chain risk, and audit readiness. Expansion into additional enterprise workflows shall build on this proven trust foundation rather than dilute the product into a broad, ungoverned automation offering.

ILATEN differentiates through governance before execution. Planning and recommendation occur before and separately from authorization. Policy, capability, and risk controls determine whether execution may proceed. Human approval remains explicit where required. Time-bound and scope-limited authority is issued only after the relevant conditions are satisfied.

The value proposition is therefore shared but not generic: ILATEN enables faster use of AI where speed is valuable, stronger control where consequences are material, and better evidence where trust must be demonstrated. It reduces the organizational gap between what advanced intelligence can propose and what an enterprise can responsibly permit.

All product, sales, partner, investor, and public communications shall remain consistent with the canonical position. ILATEN must not be represented as capable of unrestricted autonomous operation, guaranteed correctness, universal regulatory compliance, or functionality that has not been verified. Product maturity, deployment readiness, and supported use cases must be stated accurately. Commercial messaging may adapt to an audience, but it shall not redefine the product category or weaken the constitutional boundaries.

The North Star provides a single enduring direction for product strategy, architecture, engineering, security, operations, commercialization, and organizational prioritization. It is the standard against which ILATEN evaluates whether an initiative advances the product’s defining purpose or merely increases activity. Roadmaps, investments, partnerships, releases, and customer commitments shall contribute to the creation of a trusted enterprise operating foundation for AI-assisted work.

“Most trusted” is not a promotional superlative or a claim that can be established through market visibility alone. It describes a measurable product condition in which organizations can rely on ILATEN to preserve policy authority, constrain execution, maintain human accountability, validate outcomes independently, generate continuous evidence, protect audit integrity, and recover from failure. Trust must be demonstrated through observable control performance, reliable operations, transparent limitations, and evidence that can withstand authorized technical, security, risk, compliance, and customer review.

“Enterprise AI Operating System” defines the scope of the ambition. ILATEN is intended to provide a shared control and trust foundation across multiple AI-assisted workflows rather than optimize a single interaction or task. The operating-system role requires stable architectural boundaries for identity, Immutable Context, policy, capability, risk, approval, time-bound authority, controlled tool access, isolated execution, validation, acceptance, delivery, audit, evidence, and recovery. These responsibilities must remain coherent as intelligence components, interfaces, infrastructure, customers, and use cases evolve.

The North Star establishes a clear priority order. Capability growth is valuable only when accompanied by proportional control, evidence, security, and operational maturity. Adoption is valuable only when customers can use the product responsibly and achieve verifiable outcomes. Automation is valuable only when it remains policy-bound, observable, revocable, and accountable. Speed is valuable only when it does not weaken quality gates or conceal risk. When these objectives conflict, the interpretation that preserves durable enterprise trust shall prevail.
1. **Does it increase trustworthy enterprise capability?** The proposal must solve a legitimate organizational problem and improve the ability to perform useful work under defined controls.

2. **Does it strengthen or preserve the canonical trust model?** The proposal must maintain policy governance, least privilege, human accountability, independent validation, continuous audit, and evidence integrity.
3. **Can its value and control performance be verified?** The proposal must have measurable outcomes, explicit acceptance criteria, an evidence plan, and accountable ownership.

4. **Can it scale without fragmenting governance?** The proposal must remain operable across relevant customers, teams, environments, and workloads without creating inconsistent or provider-dependent trust boundaries.

Progress toward the North Star will be assessed through the Success Metrics defined in Section 1.12. No single metric represents trust. The evaluation must combine control effectiveness, evidence completeness, policy compliance, validated task outcomes, security performance, recovery capability, enterprise adoption, and customer confidence. Growth that is accompanied by declining assurance does not represent North Star progress, while strong controls without useful adoption do not fulfil the product purpose.

The North Star is intentionally durable. Product strategy and implementation priorities may change as markets, risks, regulations, and technologies evolve, but the objective remains constant: ILATEN shall enable organizations to use AI-assisted capability with verifiable trust and retained institutional authority. Any proposal to replace or materially reinterpret the North Star requires formal governance and must demonstrate that the change preserves the Product Constitution, architectural intent, and long-term enterprise mandate.

The ideal customer has a meaningful need for control rather than a purely experimental interest in AI. It operates version-controlled software or structured digital environments, maintains defined ownership for systems and data, and has existing expectations for access control, change management, testing, security review, incident response, or audit. The customer may be at an early stage of governed AI adoption, but it must be willing to define authority, risk tolerance, approval boundaries, validation requirements, and measurable success criteria.

The executive sponsor requires a defensible balance between innovation and institutional control. ILATEN includes the mechanisms required to preserve enterprise authority over AI-assisted work. This includes identity and tenant context, capability assignment, policy evaluation, risk classification, approval requirements, segregation of duties, execution authorization, revocation, timeout, cancellation, retry constraints, and compensation or recovery behavior where applicable.

The product shall distinguish planning from permission and permission from acceptance. Intelligence components may produce analysis, recommendations, or proposed plans, but they do not authorize their own actions. Execution authority is granted only after required controls are satisfied. Completion does not imply successful validation, and successful validation does not by itself override required acceptance authority.

The platform is responsible for enforcing the authority it issues and for preventing that authority from silently expanding to adjacent systems, data, or future tasks. It must preserve the separation between control decisions and execution mechanisms. Specific isolation technologies may vary by deployment and risk profile without changing this responsibility.

ILATEN includes independent validation of outputs, artifacts, and relevant state changes before acceptance. Validation may apply structural rules, policy checks, software tests, security controls, integrity verification, quality gates, and business acceptance criteria appropriate to the task. The Validation Pipeline must remain distinguishable from the reasoning process that proposed the action.

The platform records whether execution completed, whether validation succeeded, whether exceptions remain, and whether the result was accepted or rejected. Accepted outputs may be delivered only through an approved mechanism. For software-change workflows, controlled delivery may include a reviewable change set, a separate branch, a pull request, or a verified commit according to customer policy. Delivery must not bypass ownership, review, release, or production controls defined by the organization.

ILATEN includes append-only audit behavior, cryptographically linked evidence, artifact hashing, integrity verification, correlation, provenance, access governance, and retention classification for material task records. Evidence shall connect the request, context, plan, control decisions, approvals, authority, execution events, validation results, artifacts, exceptions, and final disposition.

The product must enable authorized technical, security, risk, compliance, and audit review without requiring reliance on informal reconstruction. Evidence collection must remain proportional and must respect privacy, confidentiality, tenant isolation, data minimization, retention, and deletion obligations. Blockchain is not required by the canonical architecture; controlled append-only storage, cryptographic integrity, and accountable governance provide the required trust foundation.

Code Intelligence is within the canonical product scope because the initial commercial use case depends on accurate understanding of software repositories. The capability domain includes representation of code entities, source-file analysis, symbol extraction, dependency extraction, repository indexing, change-impact context, and the structured information required to support governed planning and validation.

Code Intelligence informs decisions and proposed work but does not grant execution authority. Its outputs remain subject to context, policy, risk, approval, execution, validation, and evidence requirements. A narrower end-to-end capability that satisfies these conditions is within scope; a broader demonstration that bypasses them is not.

ILATEN API provides authenticated programmatic access with tenant, schema, rate, replay, and correlation controls. These surfaces are access and execution channels to the same canonical trust model. They shall not create independent policy semantics, bypass control gates, or fragment audit and evidence behavior.

Enterprise scope includes organizational identity integration, tenant isolation, role and capability governance, policy administration, secrets protection, data classification, observability, monitoring, incident support, backup and recovery, change governance, secure delivery, documentation, and compliance-enablement capabilities required for responsible operation. ILATEN supports customer compliance efforts but does not convert technical controls into an automatic guarantee of legal or regulatory compliance.

Deployment may evolve across hosted, customer-controlled, hybrid, or isolated models where justified by customer requirements and product maturity. The canonical security, control, validation, audit, and evidence obligations remain applicable across deployment models. Infrastructure choices must not redefine the product’s trust boundaries.

Integrations and customer-managed environments retain their own security and operational responsibilities. ILATEN shall not claim authority over systems it does not control or guarantee outcomes that depend on undisclosed, misconfigured, or unauthorized external conditions. Shared responsibilities must be documented for each supported deployment model.

Product scope may expand into additional enterprise workflows only when the proposed capability has a defined customer problem, accountable owner, architectural fit, threat assessment, policy model, authority boundary, validation method, evidence plan, operational support model, and measurable success criteria. Expansion must preserve the Product Constitution and follow the formal Architecture Decision Record process where material architecture decisions are introduced or superseded.

Scope discipline is mandatory. ILATEN shall deepen the completeness, reliability, and enterprise readiness of the canonical trust loop before pursuing unrelated breadth. Detailed exclusions and activities intentionally outside the product mandate are defined in Section 1.11, Non-Goals.

Non-Goals protect ILATEN from uncontrolled scope expansion, category dilution, unsafe product behavior, and premature technical complexity. They identify outcomes the product shall not pursue and capabilities that are intentionally excluded from the initial commercial scope. A Non-Goal is not a statement that an adjacent capability has no value; it establishes that the capability does not justify weakening the Product Constitution, disrupting dependency order, or diverting the product from its enterprise trust mandate.

ILATEN is not intended to provide unrestricted autonomous control over enterprise systems. It shall not permit intelligence components to authorize their own actions, expand their own capabilities, bypass policy, disable validation, alter acceptance criteria, conceal failures, or erase audit and evidence history. Increased automation must remain bounded, revocable, observable, risk-aware, and accountable.

ILATEN shall not replace accountable human or institutional authority in consequential decisions. The product may support analysis, planning, approval, controlled execution, validation, and evidence, but responsibility for material legal, financial, ethical, security, operational, and production decisions remains with identified authorities. Human review shall not be reduced to symbolic confirmation where meaningful judgment is required.

ILATEN is not positioned as a foundation-model developer or a product whose value depends on owning a proprietary general-purpose model. Intelligence components are replaceable inputs to a stable enterprise control architecture. Model training may be evaluated only where a defined product requirement cannot be met through governed use of suitable components and where data, security, cost, and operational obligations are justified.

ILATEN shall not claim that probabilistic outputs are always correct, that every controlled action is risk-free, or that technical controls automatically guarantee legal or regulatory compliance. The platform supports verification, auditability, evidence, and compliance operations, but customers retain responsibility for applicable law, policy configuration, risk acceptance, and final business decisions.

The canonical approach uses append-only audit behavior, cryptographic linking, artifact hashing, integrity verification, controlled retention, and accountable access governance. A distributed ledger shall not be introduced without a specific requirement and an approved Architecture Decision Record demonstrating material value that cannot be achieved through the canonical design.

The first commercial release is not intended to cover every enterprise workflow, programming language, repository platform, operating system, infrastructure provider, or integration. Breadth shall not take priority over completion of the end-to-end trust loop. Initial support must be deliberately bounded, documented, tested, and selected according to the primary customer scenario.

The MVP does not require a complete mobile product, native applications for every platform, complex distributed orchestration, large-scale retrieval infrastructure, broad organizational memory, or self-directed production learning. ILATEN Mobile and extended local execution capabilities shall follow the maturity of the Core, secure access layer, primary operator experience, and approval model. Controlled retrieval and learning capabilities shall not modify production behavior automatically.

Kubernetes or equivalent large-scale orchestration is not a mandatory condition for the first MVP. Infrastructure complexity must be justified by measurable isolation, reliability, scale, customer deployment, or operational requirements. Technology shall not be adopted solely because it is popular or associated with enterprise software.

ILATEN shall not accept customer-specific work that silently creates a conflicting architecture, bypasses canonical controls, or produces an unmaintainable private product branch. Customer requirements may inform configurable policy, supported integrations, and roadmap decisions, but material product changes require shared architectural review and governed acceptance.

The product shall not be marketed through unverifiable claims of universal autonomy, guaranteed security, guaranteed compliance, or capabilities that have not reached the stated maturity level. Commercial urgency does not convert roadmap intent into available functionality.

Permanent boundaries derived from the Product Constitution cannot be removed through ordinary roadmap prioritization. Deferred capabilities may enter future scope only when customer value, ownership, dependency readiness, threat treatment, authority boundaries, validation, evidence, operational support, and success criteria are defined. Material changes require an Architecture Decision Record where applicable.

These Non-Goals ensure that ILATEN remains an Enterprise AI Operating System focused on trustworthy, policy-governed, verifiable operations. The product shall prefer a complete and defensible control loop over broad but ungoverned functionality.

ILATEN shall measure success through enterprise value and trust performance together. Feature volume, generated output, raw task count, or model activity are not sufficient indicators of product success. The measurement system must demonstrate that customers can adopt AI-assisted operations more effectively while policy compliance, evidence integrity, security, validation quality, accountability, and recovery remain strong.

The canonical success framework contains seven metric families: Deployment Time, Evidence Coverage, Policy Compliance, Task Success, Recovery Time, Security Incidents, and Customer Adoption. These families provide a stable measurement structure across releases and deployment models. Specific numeric targets shall be defined for the relevant product maturity level, customer environment, risk class, and reporting period using verified baselines. Targets must not be invented or represented as achieved without supporting data.

Every reported metric shall have a documented name, purpose, owner, calculation, population, data source, reporting interval, unit, exclusions, target, warning threshold, failure threshold, and evidence reference. Changes to a definition must be versioned. Historical results must not be silently recalculated under a new definition without clear disclosure.

Metrics shall be tenant-aware and risk-aware where appropriate. Aggregation must not conceal a critical failure inside a favorable average. Results should be segmented by product version, deployment model, workflow, risk class, customer cohort, and failure category when those distinctions materially affect interpretation. Security, privacy, and contractual restrictions apply to measurement data as they do to other enterprise information.

Deployment Time measures how efficiently an authorized customer or internal environment can move from approved initiation to a validated, operational ILATEN capability. It includes the elapsed time required for environment preparation, identity and tenant configuration, policy setup, supported integration, validation, operational-readiness review, and acceptance. It shall not be reduced by omitting required controls or declaring an incomplete environment operational.

Required indicators include median and percentile time to first validated deployment, time to first governed workflow, policy-configuration lead time, integration lead time, and the proportion of deployments accepted without material remediation. Paused periods caused by documented customer dependencies should be reported separately rather than silently excluded.
Evidence Coverage measures whether required evidence exists, is integrity-protected, and can be associated with the relevant material lifecycle events. The primary coverage calculation is:
**Evidence Coverage = Material events with complete and valid required evidence / Total material events requiring evidence × 100**

Coverage applies from request intake through identity and request verification, Immutable Context creation, planning, policy and capability evaluation, risk classification, approval, execution authorization, Tool Gateway activity, validation, acceptance or rejection, controlled delivery, closure, and review. Audit Engine and Evidence Chain operation is continuous across these stages; evidence shall not be measured only at task completion.

Supporting indicators include chain-integrity verification rate, artifact-hash verification rate, evidence retrieval success, required-field completeness, correlation accuracy, evidence latency, and unauthorized modification attempts. A high record count cannot compensate for missing material events or failed integrity verification.

The metric must distinguish permitted, denied, expired, cancelled, exception-approved, and violated outcomes. A correct denial is compliant behavior and must not be treated as product failure. Required indicators include policy-evaluation success, unauthorized execution attempts blocked, capability-scope violations, expired-authority prevention, approval enforcement, policy-decision reproducibility where applicable, and exception closure.

Any confirmed execution without required authorization, capability, or approval is a critical control failure regardless of aggregate compliance percentage. Exceptions must be explicit, authorized, time-bound where appropriate, and separately reported.

Task Success measures the proportion of authorized tasks that produce an accepted outcome under the defined validation and delivery conditions. Execution completion, validation success, acceptance, and delivery are separate states and must be measured separately. The primary accepted-task calculation is:
**Accepted Task Success = Tasks accepted after required validation / Authorized tasks that reached execution × 100**

A task that completes execution but fails validation is not successful. A validated result that lacks required acceptance is not delivered success. Raw task volume and generated output shall not be used as substitutes for accepted, evidenced outcomes.

Recovery Time measures the organization’s ability to restore controlled operation after task failure, component degradation, security event, data issue, deployment failure, or other defined disruption. Measures shall include time to detect, time to contain, time to restore, time to verify recovery, and time to close the associated evidence and review obligations.

Required indicators include median and percentile recovery duration by severity, restore-test success rate, rollback or compensation success, recovery-point achievement where applicable, recovery-time achievement, unresolved incident age, and recurrence after closure. Recovery is complete only when service or task state is restored to an accepted condition, integrity is verified, relevant controls are operating, and material evidence has been preserved.

Fast restoration that loses evidence, weakens policy, or leaves integrity uncertain is not successful recovery. Backup existence alone is not proof of recoverability; restoration must be tested according to defined schedules and risk.

Security Incidents measure confirmed events that compromise or threaten confidentiality, integrity, availability, authorization, tenant isolation, evidence integrity, policy enforcement, or operational control. Reporting must classify incidents by severity, affected scope, root cause, detection source, containment, customer impact, recurrence, and control failure.

Required indicators include incident frequency and severity, attempted and successful policy bypass, privilege escalation, tenant-boundary violation, secret exposure, unauthorized data access, integrity failure, audit or evidence tampering, mean time to detect, mean time to contain, remediation age, and recurrence rate. Near misses and blocked attacks should be tracked separately because they provide control-effectiveness and threat information.

There is no acceptable non-zero target for successful unauthorized privilege expansion, deliberate audit-history alteration, evidence tampering, or execution that bypasses mandatory policy and approval. Aggregate improvement cannot offset an unresolved critical incident.

Required indicators include time to first governed workflow, pilot-to-production conversion, active governed workflows, active authorized users and approvers, repeat usage, accepted tasks per active customer, customer retention, expansion across approved repositories or business units, evidence-review usage, and customer-reported value. Adoption should be segmented by maturity stage and customer cohort.

Growth achieved by weakening policy, reducing approvals inappropriately, omitting evidence, or accepting unsupported use cases is not successful adoption. Customer expansion must preserve or improve trust metrics.

No metric family shall be optimized in isolation. Deployment Time must be interpreted with control readiness. Task Success must be interpreted with validation and evidence. Customer Adoption must be interpreted with security and policy compliance. Recovery Time must include integrity and evidence restoration. A favorable commercial metric does not override a failed constitutional control.

Metrics must resist gaming. Teams shall not improve reported results by narrowing populations without disclosure, reclassifying failures, excluding denied tasks, lowering validation standards, weakening policies, delaying incident confirmation, or redefining acceptance after execution. Material data-quality limitations must accompany the report.

Each metric family shall have an accountable owner and an independent review path appropriate to its purpose. Product and engineering leadership own delivery and adoption interpretation; security owns security-event integrity; governance and audit functions review policy, evidence, and control reporting; executive leadership approves risk tolerance and material target changes.

Success metrics shall be reviewed at release, operational, customer, and executive cadences appropriate to product maturity. Threshold breaches require documented investigation, ownership, corrective action, due dates, and follow-up evidence. A critical security, policy, evidence, or integrity failure may block release, deployment, customer expansion, or scope growth regardless of favorable performance elsewhere.

The ILATEN system architecture establishes a controlled operating environment for AI-assisted enterprise work. Its primary purpose is to ensure that probabilistic reasoning cannot become operational authority without deterministic governance, explicit scope, enforceable policy, appropriate approval, constrained execution, independent validation, and verifiable evidence. The architecture therefore treats intelligence, authorization, execution, validation, acceptance, and audit as distinct responsibilities connected through defined contracts and trust boundaries.

| Execution Plane | Performs approved operations through restricted workers, sandboxed environments, device-bound execution capabilities, and controlled adapters for authorized enterprise resources. | It receives only the minimum time-bound authority required for the approved task and cannot expand its own scope. |

The AI & Intelligence Layer supplies governed reasoning capabilities to the architecture but is not an authority plane. The AI Reasoning and Recommendation Engine may interpret approved context and prepare analyses, plans, or action proposals. It grants no permission, initiates no execution, and cannot determine that its own output is acceptable. Confidence signals may inform risk evaluation and review but cannot grant permission or replace independent validation. Model Orchestration and Provider Abstraction governs model access, routing, compatibility, provider independence, and lifecycle concerns; it has no policy authority. The Policy Engine remains a deterministic Control Plane component and is defined within Section 2.3, Core Modules.

The architecture enforces four separations that cannot be collapsed for convenience. First, reasoning produces a proposal but not a permission. Second, authority is created only after deterministic identity, capability, policy, risk, and approval controls have been satisfied. Third, execution is limited to the approved operation, target, duration, data scope, and tool set. Fourth, completion of execution does not constitute acceptance; results must pass the independent Validation Pipeline and the applicable acceptance decision before controlled delivery.
