ilaten_requirement: Every transition between planes is a trust-boundary crossing and must be authenticated, authorized, schema-validated, correlated, observable, and attributable. External identities and integrations are untrusted until verified by the Secure Access Layer. Intelligence output is untrusted as an executable instruction until evaluated by the Control Plane. Execution workers and connected tools are untrusted beyond their issued capability scope. Results are untrusted until independently validated. Audit and evidence records are not trusted solely because they exist; their ordering, integrity, provenance, and retention must remain verifiable.

Tenant isolation is enforced across identity, context, policy, task state, execution, data access, observability, evidence, and administration. A tenant identifier is not merely descriptive metadata; it is part of the authorization boundary. Cross-tenant data access, policy evaluation, execution authority, evidence association, or administrative action is prohibited unless an explicitly governed platform function defines and verifies that authority.

The development system and product runtime are separate security domains. Development tools, build credentials, test environments, source-management privileges, and engineering workflows do not receive implicit authority over customer runtime operations. Runtime components shall use deployment-specific identities and narrowly scoped capabilities. Production access must remain attributable, policy-governed, reviewable, and isolated from ordinary development activity.
| Control group | Canonical stages | Required outcome |

| Governance and authorization | Policy and capability evaluation; risk classification; explicit human approval where required; issuance of time-bound and constrained execution authority. | A deterministic permit or deny outcome with recorded scope, conditions, and accountability. |
| Delivery and closure | Controlled delivery, closure, and review. | An attributable final state with required evidence, delivery controls, and follow-up obligations completed. |

The Audit Engine and Evidence Chain operate across all material events in every control group. They are not terminal post-execution functions. Evidence begins with the request and context, continues through planning, policy, risk, approval, authority issuance, execution, validation, and disposition, and concludes with controlled delivery and closure records. Failure, denial, cancellation, timeout, compensation, and rejected validation are evidence-bearing outcomes and must not disappear from the operational history.

The architecture applies secure and deterministic failure behavior. Failure to establish identity, tenant, request integrity, applicable policy, required capability, mandatory approval, execution constraints, or validation confidence results in denial, suspension, or controlled escalation according to policy. The system must not infer permission from missing information, substitute a model recommendation for authorization, bypass a failed control, or deliver an unaccepted result.

Task orchestration maintains explicit states, correlation, idempotency, timeout, cancellation, retry, and compensation behavior. Retrying a failed operation must not silently create duplicate effects or broaden the original authority. Compensation is defined only where the relevant operation supports a safe and governed compensating action; it is not treated as a universal guarantee of reversibility. Irreversible or materially destructive actions require stricter policy, approval, precondition validation, and evidence requirements.

Control availability and business availability are not interchangeable. Where a critical authorization, policy, approval, validation, audit-integrity, or evidence-integrity dependency is unavailable, the affected operation fails closed unless an explicitly approved continuity policy defines a narrower safe mode. Such a mode must remain bounded, observable, time-limited, and subject to retrospective review; it cannot disable canonical controls for convenience.

The logical architecture is deployment-neutral. Supported implementations may use shared, dedicated, private, hybrid, or customer-controlled infrastructure, subject to product scope and formal deployment decisions. Components may be distributed for scale or consolidated for operational efficiency, but tenant boundaries, identity separation, deterministic policy authority, isolated execution, independent validation, and evidence integrity must remain intact. Technology replacement is permitted when conformance is demonstrated; architectural control obligations are not replaceable implementation details.
All implementations and future architectural decisions must preserve the following invariants:
- The Policy Engine remains within the Control Plane and cannot be replaced by model judgment.
- Model Orchestration and Provider Abstraction cannot grant policy, capability, approval, or execution authority.
- Audit history is append-only, and evidence integrity must be cryptographically verifiable without blockchain dependency.
- Models, tools, infrastructure, and providers may be replaced; the canonical trust boundaries and control responsibilities may not be bypassed.

The Trust Core does not grant permission, classify risk, approve actions, perform business operations, or determine whether an output is correct. Those responsibilities remain with the applicable deterministic Control Plane components, accountable human authorities, Execution Plane, and Validation Pipeline. The Trust Core records and binds their inputs, decisions, actions, and outcomes so that the operation can be independently reconstructed and verified. Evidence integrity must never be misrepresented as proof that the underlying decision was correct, lawful, or commercially appropriate; it proves that specified records and artifacts have not been altered without detection and that their declared provenance can be evaluated.
| Responsibility | Canonical function | Required assurance outcome |

| Retention and controlled disclosure | Applies classification, access, retention, legal-hold, export, and disposal requirements across audit records, evidence metadata, and referenced artifacts. | Evidence remains available, protected, and usable for its required lifecycle without uncontrolled disclosure. |

These responsibilities must remain independent from intelligence output and execution authority. A reasoning component may emit a proposal event, and an execution worker may emit an operation result, but neither may append arbitrary trusted history, modify previously accepted records, select its own retention treatment, or declare its evidence valid. Trusted ingestion, canonicalization, ordering, persistence, and verification remain controlled platform functions.

Every material event is associated with a governed event envelope. The envelope shall contain or reference the information required to establish provenance and interpret the event, including the tenant, task and correlation identifiers; event type and schema version; producing principal and component identity; lifecycle stage; recorded and observed time where relevant; policy, capability, approval, execution, or validation references; outcome and status; artifact references or digests; idempotency data; and the integrity metadata required for chaining and verification.

Event schemas are versioned and validated. Producers cannot introduce unclassified fields or ambiguous state transitions into the trusted record. Canonicalization must produce a deterministic representation so that semantically identical records are hashed consistently and any material change produces a different digest. Ordering is established by controlled sequence information within the applicable chain scope; timestamps support interpretation but are not the sole basis for sequence because clocks may drift, events may arrive concurrently, and buffered writes may be persisted after their observed occurrence.

Sensitive values shall not be written into general audit or evidence payloads merely because they were available during execution. Secrets, authentication material, private keys, and unnecessary protected data are excluded or represented through approved references and digests. Where regulated or personal data is necessary for an evidence purpose, capture must follow data-minimization, classification, access, retention, and lawful-processing requirements. Corrections are represented by new attributable records that reference the affected record; accepted history is not silently overwritten.

The buffer or journal must preserve tenant and task scope, ordering information, idempotency identity, integrity metadata, and delivery state. It must support bounded retry, duplicate detection, backpressure, health reporting, and deterministic recovery. Producers shall not silently discard events when the Trust Core is slow or unavailable. A duplicate delivery must not create a second logical event, while a repeated business action must remain distinguishable from a transport retry. Storage consumers append records in a controlled order and expose sufficient checkpoints to identify gaps, stalled partitions, or uncommitted events.

Backpressure and failure behavior are risk-governed. When the protected ingestion boundary cannot accept a required material event, the associated operation is suspended, denied, or moved into an explicitly approved bounded safe state. High-risk execution cannot continue without the evidence capability required by policy. Lower-risk continuity behavior, where permitted, must have a defined capacity, duration, reconciliation process, and escalation threshold. No continuity mode may convert mandatory evidence into optional telemetry.

Previously accepted audit records are never edited in place. New information, correction, revocation, supersession, reclassification, recovery, or closure is expressed as a new linked event. Administrative access does not include authority to rewrite the chain. Governed retention expiry and legally required disposal are controlled lifecycle operations; they must be distinguishable from unauthorized deletion and must preserve the metadata necessary to demonstrate that disposal occurred under an approved policy.

The first record is bound to a defined genesis or trusted anchor. Each subsequent record includes or references the prior chain value, the canonical event digest, the applicable algorithm and schema versions, and the sequence information required for verification. Material artifact digests are incorporated into or referenced by the canonical event so that an artifact substitution changes the verifiable evidence state.

Cryptographic algorithms and storage technologies may evolve through controlled versioning and ADR governance. Algorithm agility must not make historical evidence unverifiable. Verification must select the correct canonicalization and cryptographic rules for the record version, validate the complete requested range, and report missing links, unexpected anchors, sequence discontinuities, digest mismatches, unsupported versions, or artifact-integrity failures without suppressing them.

ILATEN does not use blockchain as the basis of trust. The required assurance is provided through controlled append-only persistence, cryptographic linkage, authenticated event production, separation of duties, protected retention, deterministic verification, and independent review. No distributed consensus network, public ledger, token mechanism, or external blockchain dependency is required to establish the canonical evidence properties.

Evidence completeness is evaluated against the material obligations of the task, not by the mere existence of an audit row. The required evidence set varies by task type, data classification, risk, policy, integration, and outcome, but the Trust Core must be capable of binding the following lifecycle categories:
- execution commands or operations at the required level of detail, environment identity, material outputs, failures, retries, cancellation, and compensation;
- acceptance or rejection, controlled delivery, recipient or destination, closure status, and required review actions.

Completeness rules are explicit and testable. A successful task cannot be declared fully evidenced when mandatory stages, decisions, artifacts, or integrity links are absent. An event count or storage volume is not an evidence-quality measure. Evidence Coverage, defined in Section 1.12, depends on the presence, integrity, relevance, and verifiability of the required record set.

Authorized users must be able to review evidence at an appropriate level without receiving unnecessary access to protected payloads. Access is tenant-bound, purpose-limited, least-privilege, attributable, and audited. Operational personnel, customer administrators, approvers, security teams, auditors, and external assurance functions may require different views and export rights. Redaction and selective disclosure may protect sensitive content, but they must not conceal the existence of material events or falsely represent an incomplete evidence package as complete.

Evidence exports and attestations must remain portable enough for independent review and must include the metadata required to identify scope, version, integrity state, verification time, and any omissions or access restrictions. Export does not transfer authority to alter the canonical record. A derived report or customer-facing package is a controlled representation of the underlying evidence and must remain traceable to its source records.

The Trust Core is designed for failure containment and verifiable recovery. Recovery must preserve accepted event order, idempotency, chain continuity, tenant association, artifact references, and evidence status. Restored records are verified before the Trust Core returns to normal operation. A backup is not accepted as recoverable evidence until restoration and integrity verification have been tested. Detected gaps, corruption, mismatches, or unauthorized access trigger incident handling and cannot be resolved by silently rebuilding history from untrusted operational state.
All implementations shall preserve the following Trust Core invariants:
- accepted audit history is append-only and cannot be rewritten by producers, operators, intelligence components, or execution workers;

Any implementation that permits silent audit loss, mutable accepted history, unscoped evidence access, unverifiable chain gaps, execution without mandatory evidence capability, or producer-controlled verification is non-conformant. Changes to the append-only model, predecessor linkage, lifecycle coverage, evidence authority boundary, or independent verification requirement require formal architectural review and an approved ADR.

The ILATEN core modules are the logical capabilities required to govern a task from authenticated intake through controlled closure. A core module is defined by its responsibility, authority boundary, inputs, outputs, failure semantics, and evidence obligations rather than by a specific source-code package, service count, process topology, or infrastructure product. An implementation may distribute a logical module across several services or consolidate compatible responsibilities, but it must preserve the separations of reasoning, authorization, execution, validation, acceptance, and evidence established by the canonical architecture.

The module map defines the target architectural responsibilities of ILATEN. It is not, by itself, a declaration that every capability is available in every product edition or deployment. Implementation and release status must be established through verified product records. Architectural conformance requires that any implemented capability respect the module authority boundaries even when the physical topology differs from the logical model.

No module receives implicit authority from its position in the processing path. The Task Orchestrator cannot override policy. The Policy Engine cannot execute tools. The Human Approval Engine cannot expand the requested scope. The Model Gateway cannot grant permission. The Tool Gateway cannot authorize its own capabilities. An execution worker cannot accept its own result. The Validation Pipeline cannot rewrite the action it evaluates. The Audit Engine and Evidence Chain cannot be modified by the producers whose activity they record.

| Secure Access Gateway | Secure Access Layer | Establishes authenticated, tenant-bound, integrity-checked, schema-valid, rate-governed, replay-resistant request entry and correlation. | Cannot authorize business execution or bypass Control Plane evaluation. |

| Task Orchestrator | Control Plane | Maintains the canonical task state machine and coordinates planning, policy, risk, approval, authority issuance, execution, validation, delivery, cancellation, retry, timeout, and compensation. | Cannot create policy permission, fabricate approval, broaden capability, or accept failed validation. |

| Immutable Context Manager | Control Plane | Creates and preserves the authoritative tenant, identity, request, scope, classification, target, constraint, and correlation context used by downstream decisions. | Cannot mutate accepted context in place or carry a changed scope forward without re-evaluation. |

| Identity and Capability Manager | Control Plane | Resolves principals and service identities, evaluates capability eligibility, and issues, revokes, and validates task-specific, least-privilege, time-bound execution authority. | Cannot grant a capability prohibited by policy or convert role membership into unrestricted standing authority. |

| Policy Engine | Control Plane | Deterministically evaluates versioned enterprise policy against the Immutable Context, requested capabilities, target, data classification, risk inputs, and applicable constraints. | Cannot rely on probabilistic model judgment, execute actions, or treat missing policy information as permission. |

| Risk Classification Engine | Control Plane | Deterministically assigns the task risk class and required control treatment using policy-governed factors and bounded advisory signals. | Cannot independently authorize execution or allow confidence scores to replace policy, approval, or validation. |

| Human Approval Engine | Control Plane | Obtains, validates, binds, expires, revokes, and records explicit human decisions where policy or risk requires accountable approval. | Cannot reuse approval for a materially changed plan, context, target, capability, or validity period. |

| Model Gateway | Control Plane boundary to AI & Intelligence Layer | Provides governed access to reasoning capabilities and enforces approved context, routing constraints, request metadata, correlation, and output provenance. | Cannot grant policy, capability, approval, execution, validation, or acceptance authority. |

| Tool Gateway | Control Plane boundary to Execution Plane | Mediates every governed tool invocation, validates active authority and parameters, applies tool-specific constraints, and records the invocation and outcome. | Cannot expand authority, invoke unregistered operations, or permit direct execution paths that bypass it. |

| Restricted Execution Workers | Execution Plane | Perform approved operations in isolated workers or device-bound execution sessions with constrained filesystem, network, process, credential, tool, duration, and resource access. | Cannot change policy, approve themselves, obtain broader credentials, or declare their output accepted. |

| Validation Pipeline | Independent assurance boundary | Evaluates results through ordered, versioned, independently governed validation rules and produces an explicit pass, fail, or otherwise policy-defined outcome. | Cannot be skipped by the executor, convert an execution result into permission, or conceal failed checks. |

| Evidence Chain and Artifact Integrity | Trust and Evidence Plane | Cryptographically links canonical records, binds artifacts to digests and provenance, and supports independent integrity and completeness verification. | Cannot replace policy authorization, human accountability, or result validation. |

The Bootstrap Validator prevents the platform from accepting governed work when mandatory trust dependencies or task preconditions are absent or invalid. Required checks include configuration schema and version, deployment identity, tenant-isolation prerequisites, policy availability, cryptographic capability, Trust Core ingestion readiness, execution-boundary configuration, and mandatory integration contracts. For repository-scoped work, the validated baseline includes the intended repository root, branch, configured origin, and baseline commit or equivalent immutable source reference. The validator fails closed for conditions that would make authorization, execution, validation, audit, or evidence unreliable. It reports explicit diagnostic state and generates material audit events; it does not self-remediate by disabling controls, creating default credentials, changing branches, or substituting a different repository state.

The Task Orchestrator owns the canonical lifecycle state machine. It accepts an eligible request from the Secure Access Gateway, requests creation of the Immutable Context, invokes the governed proposal path, submits the proposal and context for policy and risk evaluation, coordinates required approval, requests constrained authority, dispatches authorized work through the Tool Gateway, initiates independent validation, records acceptance or rejection, and coordinates controlled delivery and closure. Every transition has defined preconditions, permitted successors, timeout behavior, cancellation behavior, and material evidence requirements.

The Orchestrator coordinates decisions but does not make decisions assigned to other modules. A denial from the Policy Engine, missing required approval, invalid capability, failed Tool Gateway check, or failed Validation Pipeline result cannot be converted into success by orchestration logic. Retry applies only where the action and policy permit it and must preserve idempotency and the original authority boundary. Compensation is invoked only through an explicitly authorized and evidence-bearing path.

The Immutable Context Manager creates the authoritative decision context before proposal and authorization. The context identifies the tenant, requesting principal, request and purpose, approved target scope, data classification, applicable environment, repository or resource references where relevant, constraints, correlation, and the versions or references required to reproduce control decisions. Sensitive payloads may remain in protected stores and be represented by integrity-bound references rather than copied into the context.

Accepted context is immutable. A material change to identity, tenant, purpose, plan scope, target, environment, data classification, requested capability, or protected artifact reference creates a new context version or a new task according to policy. The changed context must re-enter the applicable proposal, policy, risk, approval, and authority stages. Immutability prevents approval or capability issued for one operation from being reused after the operation has materially changed.

The Policy Engine is a deterministic Control Plane component. It evaluates explicit, versioned rules against the Immutable Context and governed inputs and produces a structured decision such as permit, deny, require approval, require additional controls, or require clarification, as defined by the policy model. The decision includes the policy version, evaluated scope, applicable obligations, denial or escalation reasons, required approval class, capability constraints, evidence requirements, and validity conditions.

ilaten_requirement: The Human Approval Engine implements explicit accountable authorization where required by policy or risk. Approval is bound to the exact material state reviewed. Separation-of-duty rules may prohibit a requester, proposer, executor, or validator from approving the same high-risk action.

The approval mechanism must support approve, deny, request clarification, expiry, revocation, delegation where formally governed, and escalation according to policy. Silence is not approval. Emergency or continuity approval remains an explicit policy-defined process with narrower scope, shorter validity, stronger evidence, and mandatory review; it is not a bypass channel.

The gateway does not transform intelligence output into authorization. A model selection, confidence value, structured response, or apparently complete plan has no execution authority until it has passed the deterministic policy, capability, risk, and approval path. Provider availability or model failure may cause retry, alternative governed routing, clarification, or task failure, but it cannot justify weaker policy or direct tool access. Model Orchestration and Provider Abstraction remains provider-independent and has no Policy Engine responsibility.

The Tool Gateway is the exclusive governed path from authorized task control to supported execution operations. For every invocation, it verifies the active task and tenant, capability validity, approved tool and operation, target, parameters, path or resource boundaries, time window, usage limits, data classification, policy obligations, and required evidence state. It rejects unknown tools, unregistered operations, invalid parameters, expired or revoked authority, target drift, path escape, privilege expansion, and direct invocation attempts that lack the required control context.

Tool adapters expose explicit contracts and cannot inherit unrestricted ambient authority from the host environment. Each adapter defines supported operations, input and output schemas, side effects, credential requirements, idempotency behavior, timeout and cancellation semantics, compensation support, audit detail, and error classification. Tool output is treated as an execution result, not as trusted evidence of success or acceptance.

Execution workers cannot call enterprise resources outside the Tool Gateway contract, retain credentials beyond the authorized period, modify the Immutable Context, alter policy or approval records, suppress material telemetry, or write trusted audit history directly. A worker failure, timeout, partial side effect, or isolation breach signal causes controlled task transition, evidence capture, and the applicable containment, compensation, validation, and incident response behavior.

The Validation Pipeline is independent from the component that prepared the plan and the environment that executed it. It receives the execution result, applicable context, acceptance criteria, policy obligations, artifact references, and required validation rule set. Rules execute in a defined order with explicit versions, inputs, outputs, severity, and pass or fail semantics. Validation may include structural, functional, security, policy, integrity, quality, and domain-specific checks appropriate to the task.

Execution completion never implies validation success. A failed mandatory rule produces rejection or another explicitly policy-defined non-acceptance state. A validation waiver, where permitted, requires separate authority, documented rationale, bounded scope, expiry where applicable, and Trust Core evidence. The executor cannot disable, rewrite, reorder, or self-certify the required rule set.

Following acceptance, the Task Orchestrator coordinates controlled delivery only for results that satisfy the required validation and acceptance conditions. It verifies the approved destination or recipient, delivery method, artifact identity, current authorization, evidence completeness, and any release conditions before invoking the applicable governed delivery interface. Delivery outcome is recorded independently from execution and validation outcome. Failure to deliver does not erase a valid result, and a delivery attempt does not make an invalid result acceptable.

Every core module emits material events through the protected Trust Core ingestion path described in Section 2.2. Audit and evidence capture is continuous and includes entry decisions, bootstrap state, context creation, proposal provenance, policy decisions, risk classifications, approval actions, capability issuance and revocation, model and tool boundary activity, execution transitions, validation results, delivery, closure, denial, failure, cancellation, timeout, retry, and compensation. Core modules may read authorized evidence necessary for their function, but they cannot rewrite accepted history.

ILATEN Companion may contain both an experience-facing control surface and a device-bound execution capability within one distributed product installation. These are separate logical components with separate identities, privileges, update controls, and communication paths. The user interface cannot invoke local tools directly. It submits governed intent through the Secure Access Layer, while the device-bound execution component accepts only time-bound operations issued through the Tool Gateway after the canonical control path has completed.

The component interaction path is directional and authority-preserving. A supported request enters through an Experience Layer surface or authenticated enterprise integration and crosses the Secure Access Layer. The Task Orchestrator establishes the task and requests an Immutable Context. The AI Reasoning and Recommendation Engine may then be invoked through the Model Gateway to produce a plan or action proposal. The proposal returns to the Control Plane for Policy Engine evaluation, Risk Classification, capability determination, and Human Approval where required.

When the required controls are satisfied, the Identity and Capability Manager issues constrained task authority. The Task Orchestrator sends the authorized operation to the Tool Gateway, which revalidates the capability and dispatches the permitted invocation to the appropriate restricted worker and registered adapter. The execution result and artifact references are passed to the independent Validation Pipeline. The Task Orchestrator records and advances the task according to the acceptance or rejection disposition produced under the applicable validation and policy rules, then coordinates controlled delivery and closure only for an accepted result.
The following direct paths are prohibited:

Component interfaces are explicit, versioned, authenticated, tenant-bound, and schema-governed. Each control-path request carries or references the tenant identifier, task identifier, correlation identifier, requesting or producing principal, Immutable Context version, operation or event type, schema version, idempotency identity where applicable, and the policy, approval, capability, artifact, or validation references required by the receiving component. Components reject incomplete, conflicting, unsupported, expired, or out-of-scope contracts rather than infer missing authority.

| Event | Records an immutable material fact that has occurred. | An event is attributable, versioned, append-only, and suitable for Trust Core ingestion; it cannot be used to conceal a command or retroactively create permission. |

Communication style is selected according to authority, latency, durability, and failure requirements. Control-critical checks that determine whether an operation may proceed require a current, attributable result before the state transition is committed. Identity verification, policy outcome, active capability validation, required approval status, Tool Gateway authorization, mandatory validation outcome, and final acceptance therefore cannot be satisfied by stale derived state or an unverified asynchronous notification.

Material state transitions and their required Trust Core events must be atomically or recoverably coupled. A successful control transition cannot remain permanently without its required evidence, and an event cannot falsely represent a transition that was not committed. The implementation may use any conformant transactional or journaling mechanism that provides deterministic recovery, gap detection, and reconciliation without rewriting accepted history.
| Policy definitions and decisions | Policy administration authority and Policy Engine | Consumers use the exact referenced version and cannot reinterpret a decision as broader permission. |
| Validation result | Validation Pipeline | Executor and planner cannot alter the outcome or rule evidence. |

Authorization-relevant state requires consistency sufficient to prevent stale permission, cross-tenant access, reuse of revoked authority, or acceptance against an outdated result. Reporting, analytics, search indexes, dashboards, and other derived views may be eventually consistent when they are clearly non-authoritative. A derived view cannot be used to approve, execute, validate, or deliver an action unless its source state is revalidated through the owning component.

The canonical component architecture supports progressive deployment composition. An initial deployment may use a modular application with isolated workers and independently protected trust storage. Larger deployments may separate access, orchestration, policy, intelligence, execution, validation, audit, evidence, and integration components for scale, residency, or operational ownership. Both forms are conformant only when the logical identities, access controls, state ownership, interface contracts, and prohibited paths remain intact.

Replaceable components are isolated behind stable contracts. Model providers are accessed through Model Orchestration and Provider Abstraction; tools and enterprise systems are accessed through registered Tool Gateway adapters; deployment technologies and storage engines may change while preserving logical behavior. Replacement requires compatibility, security, policy, validation, evidence, performance, resilience, and migration verification. A provider or technology change cannot alter authority semantics or historical evidence interpretation.

New experience surfaces connect through the Secure Access Layer. New reasoning capabilities connect through the Model Gateway. New execution capabilities require a registered Tool Gateway contract and isolated worker support. New validation rules enter through the governed Validation Pipeline. New evidence consumers use controlled read or verification interfaces. Any proposed component that creates a parallel route around these extension points is non-conformant.

Interface evolution uses explicit schema and behavior versioning, compatibility testing, controlled deprecation, migration evidence, and rollback or compensation planning where applicable. A breaking change that affects identity propagation, tenant isolation, policy interpretation, approval binding, capability validation, execution boundaries, validation independence, state ownership, or Trust Core integrity requires formal architectural review and an approved ADR.
All implementations shall preserve the following invariants:
- experience, intelligence, execution, validation, and evidence components cannot create authority outside the Control Plane;
- telemetry and derived views cannot replace authoritative state or canonical evidence;
- physical consolidation or distribution cannot weaken logical separation, tenant isolation, failure containment, or evidence integrity;
- component replacement and extension occur only through governed interfaces and cannot create bypass paths.

An implementation is non-conformant if it relies on direct database mutation across component ownership boundaries, allows an intelligence or experience component to invoke tools directly, permits execution workers to change task authority, uses stale derived state for authorization, merges execution with acceptance, treats telemetry as the canonical audit record, or loses required evidence during component failure. These component constraints remain binding across all supported deployment models.

Every runtime task is finite and attributable. It has a tenant, requesting principal, task identifier, Immutable Context, explicit lifecycle state, applicable policy and risk decisions, defined approval status, bounded capabilities, execution environment, validation obligations, evidence requirements, timeout and cancellation behavior, and final disposition. Background processing may continue after an interactive session ends, but it remains attached to the governed task and cannot exceed the scope, duration, or authority established for that task.

| Experience Runtime | Hosts approved interactive surfaces and operator workflows, including ILATEN Console and the control surface of ILATEN Companion where applicable. | Holds user-session authority only; it cannot retain task execution credentials or invoke local or enterprise tools directly. |

| Secure Access Runtime | Terminates supported authenticated interfaces, establishes tenant and service context, validates requests, protects real-time channels, and applies rate, abuse, integrity, idempotency, and replay controls. | External traffic cannot cross directly into Control, Execution, Validation, or Trust storage components. |

| Control Runtime | Hosts task orchestration, Immutable Context, policy, risk, approval, identity, capability, Model Gateway, and Tool Gateway responsibilities. | Owns governed state progression and authority issuance but cannot perform unrestricted business execution or self-approve validation. |

| Validation Runtime | Executes the required validation rules independently of the planner and executor. | Receives immutable result and artifact references, cannot modify the execution result, and cannot issue execution authority. |

| Trust Runtime | Hosts protected event ingestion, buffered append-only audit persistence, Evidence Chain processing, artifact-integrity verification, and governed evidence access. | Operates continuously across all zones; producers cannot rewrite accepted history or control their own verification. |

Runtime state is classified according to its authority, mutability, lifetime, and recovery requirements. The classes are kept distinct so that temporary worker state, derived telemetry, and intelligence context cannot be mistaken for authoritative task state.

| Audit, evidence, and artifact-integrity state | Material events, chain links, artifact digests, verification status, retention, and evidence-package references. | Owned by the Trust Runtime; append-only or otherwise integrity-governed for the required lifecycle. |

| Operational telemetry and derived views | Metrics, traces, diagnostic logs, dashboards, search indexes, and non-authoritative projections. | Owned by platform and observability capabilities; retention may differ and state cannot be used as execution authority without source revalidation. |

Task state transitions use explicit compare-and-advance or equivalent concurrency protection. A delayed worker result, approval response, cancellation, or retry cannot overwrite a newer terminal or superseding state. Each transition identifies the expected current state and relevant context version. Conflicts produce reconciliation or controlled rejection rather than last-write-wins authority changes.

The Control Runtime schedules tasks according to tenant quotas, risk class, resource requirements, execution locality, data-residency constraints, approval readiness, dependency availability, and operational priority. Scheduling priority affects when an eligible task may run; it cannot make an ineligible task executable, bypass a control, reduce evidence requirements, or grant access to a different tenant’s capacity or data.

The lease binds the worker identity, tenant, task, capability, permitted adapter and operation, resource class, environment, validity period, heartbeat requirements, cancellation channel, and evidence correlation. A worker cannot pull arbitrary tasks or reuse a lease for a different operation.

Concurrency is bounded at tenant, task type, adapter, target system, risk class, and platform levels as required. Limits prevent resource exhaustion, target overload, rate-policy violation, and correlated failure. Two tasks that could modify the same protected target require explicit concurrency control, serialization, optimistic conflict detection, or another governed consistency mechanism appropriate to the resource. Scheduling does not assume that independent requests are safe to execute concurrently.

The Tool Gateway remains the mandatory mediation point for supported enterprise operations. A worker may contain local runtime functions necessary to perform its approved task, but it cannot establish an unregistered side channel to source repositories, deployment targets, collaboration systems, data platforms, or other enterprise resources. Network egress and adapter access are restricted to the destinations and operations permitted by the active capability and deployment policy.

Credentials are late-bound and short-lived wherever the integration model permits. They are delivered only to the component and task that require them, are excluded from plans and general logs, and are revoked or rendered unusable after expiry, cancellation, incident containment, worker termination, or task closure. A worker may not copy credentials into artifacts, evidence payloads, persistent caches, or another execution environment.

Runtime communication uses authenticated component identities, tenant-bound contracts, encrypted channels, explicit schema versions, correlation, deadlines, and typed outcomes. Long-lived connections and real-time channels are continuously associated with the authenticated session and tenant; reconnecting does not preserve expired authority. A refreshed user session, worker channel, or device connection must re-establish current identity and authorization state.

A device-bound executor that loses connectivity cannot accept new governed operations or extend existing authority on its own. An already active operation follows the policy-defined disconnection behavior: pause, cancel, complete a bounded local step, or enter a safe containment state. Cancellation is a stateful control action. It stops future progression, revokes or prevents further capability use, signals active workers, and records the request and resulting state. Cancellation cannot guarantee reversal of an action that has already produced an irreversible external effect. Retry is allowed only when the operation, adapter contract, target state, capability validity, and policy permit it. A retry cannot silently acquire broader permission, a longer capability, a different target, or a changed plan. Exhausted retry produces an explicit failure or escalation state.

Backpressure propagates across component boundaries. Access components may reduce admission; orchestration may defer eligible work; model and tool gateways may limit concurrent calls; workers may reject assignments they cannot isolate; validation may queue accepted inputs without declaring success; and the Trust Runtime may suspend evidence-dependent operations when protected ingestion capacity is unavailable. Queue state is tenant-bound, observable, bounded, and governed by expiry and fairness rules.

Degraded modes are explicit policy objects with defined entry criteria, permitted operations, duration, compensating controls, evidence requirements, exit criteria, and mandatory review. A degraded mode cannot be created dynamically by the failing component and cannot weaken non-negotiable controls. Read-only access, status visibility, or safe cancellation may remain available while new execution is suspended.

Workers that restart or reconnect do not assume their prior lease remains valid. They present their identity, task, lease, last acknowledged operation, material result references, and evidence correlation for verification. Development may use representative test environments and synthetic or appropriately governed data, but it cannot depend on direct mutation of production task state or audit history. Emergency production intervention remains a governed runtime action, not an extension of ordinary development privilege.

An implementation is non-conformant if it permits indefinite autonomous operation, relies on a user session as execution authority, gives a worker standing credentials, resumes expired work without revalidation, treats timeout as proof of no side effect, retries non-idempotent actions without reconciliation, bypasses isolation during capacity pressure, allows development access to become production authority, or closes a task successfully while runtime outcome or evidence remains uncertain.

The ILATEN execution flow defines the canonical sequence by which enterprise intent becomes a controlled, validated, evidenced, and dispositioned outcome. The flow is a governed state machine, not a direct request-to-tool pipeline. Each stage has required inputs, an accountable component, explicit completion criteria, permitted successor states, failure behavior, and Trust Core obligations. A task advances only when the gate for the current stage has been satisfied.

The flow separates proposal from permission, permission from execution, execution from validation, and validation from acceptance. Intelligence may prepare a plan, but it cannot authorize or execute it. A policy decision may permit progression, but it does not itself perform the operation. A worker may produce a result, but it cannot validate or accept that result. Successful validation may support acceptance, but controlled delivery occurs only after the applicable disposition and delivery conditions are satisfied.

| Evidence-only | Captures an attributable fact, measurement, or provenance element required for assurance. | Missing required evidence prevents completeness even when no defect is detected. |

Implementations may use equivalent terminology, but they must distinguish blocking, conditional, advisory, and evidence-completeness behavior. Rule severity cannot be lowered at runtime to obtain a passing result. A rule that is not applicable records the evaluated condition and rationale. A rule that was expected but not executed is not silently treated as not applicable.

Rules shall be deterministic wherever the validation objective permits. Given the same validated inputs, rule version, configuration, dependency versions, and controlled environment, a deterministic rule must produce the same result. Environmental facts that affect the outcome are explicit inputs rather than hidden state. Time, external target state, network dependency, or probabilistic assessment is recorded when it prevents strict reproducibility.

Where a validation rule depends on an external or time-varying system, the rule declares that dependency, captures the observed state or authoritative reference, applies bounded retry where permitted, and reports uncertainty. A favorable result from one attempt cannot be selected while contradictory attempts are discarded. Divergent results remain evidence and produce an explicit unstable, incomplete, or failed state according to policy.

Rule order is versioned and dependency-driven. A rule may depend on integrity verification, environment readiness, artifact preparation, or an earlier result. Independent rules may run concurrently for efficiency, but parallel execution cannot change logical outcome, evidence completeness, or ordering requirements. The pipeline records start, completion, dependency, and result relationships for every rule.

Fail-fast behavior is permitted only when continuing would be unsafe, meaningless, prohibited, or unnecessarily expose protected data. The blocking result is recorded, and every unexecuted required rule is marked with an explicit reason. Where safe and useful, the pipeline continues after a failure to produce a complete defect and evidence set. Stopping early cannot be used to conceal additional known failures or create the appearance of full validation coverage.

Tenant workspaces, caches, temporary files, rule output, and diagnostics remain isolated. A rule cannot use artifacts or results from another tenant or task unless an explicit governed shared reference permits it. Cleanup is verified and evidenced even when the pipeline fails.
Every rule produces a structured outcome. Implementations may use equivalent labels, but the semantics must distinguish at least:

| Not Applicable | The rule’s versioned applicability condition was evaluated and did not apply to the subject. | Requires recorded condition and rationale; cannot be assigned merely to avoid execution. |

The aggregate validation status is computed from the complete rule-result set, rule classifications, dependency state, evidence completeness, and authorized waivers. It is not a simple average, confidence score, majority vote, or count of passing checks. One failed mandatory control cannot be offset by numerous advisory passes. Missing or erroneous mandatory validation prevents a passing aggregate status.

The aggregate result includes the status, blocking rules, non-blocking findings, incomplete checks, authorized waivers, integrity state, limitations, rule-set version, artifact digests, environment reference, and evidence package. The calculation is deterministic and independently testable. The Task Orchestrator records the returned status but cannot recalculate it using different weights or omit unfavorable rules.

The Validation Pipeline emits material events throughout the run, not only a final summary. Required evidence includes contract acceptance, input and artifact verification, rule-set resolution, runner identity, environment and dependency versions, rule start and completion, inputs or protected references, outcome, findings, timing, errors, logs or report references, waiver evaluation, aggregate calculation, publication, and cleanup.

For software-development workflows, Code Intelligence may supply the repository baseline, changed files, code entities, symbols, dependency relationships, impacted components, language or framework context, and candidate tests. This information can improve validation scope, ordering, and efficiency. It remains a governed input rather than authority to remove required checks.

Impact analysis must be bound to the exact repository baseline and proposed artifact. An incomplete index, unsupported language, parse failure, unresolved dependency, or uncertain change boundary expands validation or produces an explicit limitation; it does not justify a smaller rule set. The minimum policy-defined checks run regardless of confidence in the impact analysis.

Repository validation may include baseline integrity, change-scope verification, syntax and parsing, formatting, linting, type analysis, unit and integration tests, dependency-policy checks, security analysis, secret detection, artifact build verification, and change-specific acceptance criteria where supported. Tool names and implementations remain replaceable; the required assurance outcome, rule evidence, and quality gates are canonical.

A validation waiver is an explicit governed exception, not a change to the observed rule result. The original failure, error, or unavailable check remains visible. Policy defines whether a rule is waivable, who may approve the waiver, the maximum scope and duration, required rationale, compensating controls, evidence, review, and expiry. Non-waivable controls cannot be overridden by operational convenience or delivery pressure.

The executor, proposal producer, validation rule, and pipeline runner cannot approve their own waiver. Separation of duty applies according to risk. A waiver is bound to the tenant, task, exact artifact digest, rule and version, context, target, reason, approver, conditions, and validity period. A changed artifact, rule, target, or context invalidates the waiver unless policy explicitly establishes continuing applicability.

Waiver approval does not automatically produce acceptance. Stage 11 evaluates the waived condition, remaining risk, policy obligations, evidence completeness, and any required accountable disposition. Expired, revoked, ambiguous, or incompletely evidenced waivers are treated as absent.

Retry is governed at rule and pipeline levels. A transport or transient infrastructure retry may occur when the rule contract permits it, but all attempts and outcomes are retained. Retry cannot change the artifact, rule version, configuration, environment class, or acceptance criterion without creating a new validation contract. A rule is not repeatedly executed until a favorable result appears.

When an external or nondeterministic factor produces inconsistent results, the pipeline records the divergence and applies the policy-defined unstable or incomplete status. Quarantining a suspected validator, rule package, cache, or artifact may be required. A cache result is reused only when it is tenant-appropriate, content-addressed, rule-version exact, environment-compatible, integrity-verified, and permitted by policy; the cache hit and source evidence are recorded.

The Validation Pipeline does not remediate the subject. A failed result may make the task eligible for a separately governed remediation proposal. That proposal is bound to the failed artifact and evidence and must pass the applicable policy, risk, approval, capability, execution, and validation stages. The original failed validation remains append-only evidence and is never replaced by the later successful run.
All implementations shall preserve the following invariants:
- the executor and intelligence layer cannot select, remove, reorder, weaken, suppress, or waive mandatory rules;
- aggregate status is deterministic, policy-governed, evidence-bearing, and cannot be recalculated by the Task Orchestrator;
- Code Intelligence may refine validation scope but cannot reduce the mandatory policy baseline or conceal uncertainty;

An implementation is non-conformant if it validates a different artifact from the one considered for delivery, allows an executor to choose its checks, treats rule errors as passes, suppresses failed attempts, retries until success without preserving divergence, uses an expired waiver, permits a validator to alter the subject, computes aggregate status from an average that masks blocking failures, auto-remediates without renewed authorization, or allows acceptance to proceed while mandatory validation or evidence remains incomplete.

Cryptographic integrity is not equivalent to semantic correctness. A valid chain proves that the verified canonical records and bound artifacts have not changed without detection under the defined cryptographic and storage assumptions. It does not independently prove that a producer told the truth, that an external action occurred exactly as claimed, that a policy decision was legally correct, that validation coverage was sufficient, or that every required event was captured. Producer authentication, schema validation, evidence-completeness rules, independent validation, external references, attestations, and governance remain necessary.
Each Evidence Chain entry is based on a canonical evidence record. The physical representation may vary, but the logical fields and integrity relationships must be preserved.

| Chain scope and record identity | Uniquely identifies the governed chain, tenant-bearing scope, record, and applicable partition or task relationship. Record identity is stable and cannot be reassigned. |

The canonical event body excludes the current chain value to avoid recursive calculation but includes the predecessor relationship, record identity, sequence, tenant and task scope, semantic content or protected digest, relevant artifact manifest, and version metadata. Fields excluded from the integrity calculation must be explicitly defined, non-authoritative, and incapable of changing the meaning, scope, order, provenance, or evidence interpretation of the record.

Each chain has an explicit scope. A scope may correspond to a task, a tenant-controlled partition, an evidence-retention domain, or another formally governed unit selected for scalability and assurance. The architecture does not require one global chain, but every material record must have one unambiguous primary chain scope, and the partitioning model must support complete task reconstruction and tenant isolation. Tenant-bearing records cannot be moved into another tenant’s chain or combined into an unrestricted shared chain.

Every chain begins from a defined genesis value or trusted anchor. The genesis record identifies the scope, creation authority, schema and cryptographic versions, creation time, and any relationship to a higher-level checkpoint or platform attestation. A chain cannot begin from an undocumented null state. Restart, migration, partition rollover, retention transition, or algorithm change creates an explicit linked checkpoint or successor relationship rather than silently resetting history.

Sequence is assigned by the controlled append authority within the chain scope. Producer timestamps may arrive late, out of order, or concurrently. A late event is appended at the next valid sequence with its original observed time, ingestion time, and late-arrival status; it is not inserted into an earlier chain position. This preserves cryptographic ordering while retaining the facts required to reconstruct temporal context.

Canonicalization converts the logical evidence record into deterministic bytes. It defines field inclusion, field order, data types, character encoding, numeric representation, timestamp representation, null and optional-field treatment, collection ordering, normalization, schema version, and protected-reference encoding. A semantically material change must produce different canonical bytes. Two conformant verifiers using the same record and canonicalization version must produce the same digest.

Material events enter through an authenticated, schema-governed, tenant-bound ingestion contract. The protected ingestion boundary validates producer identity, event identity, tenant and task scope, schema, classification, idempotency, artifact references, and the minimum provenance required for the event type. Invalid or cross-tenant events do not enter the accepted chain path.

The append authority resolves the chain scope and current verified predecessor, assigns the sequence, canonicalizes the record body, calculates the chain value, persists the audit and chain state, and records the artifact-integrity relationship. Acknowledgement states distinguish protected ingestion from completed append and completed verification. Components cannot claim a fully chained event when only local production or transient receipt has occurred.

Batching and asynchronous append are permitted for throughput when the order, predecessor relationship, durability, tenant isolation, failure detection, and per-record verifiability remain intact. A batch cannot become an opaque object that prevents verification of individual material events. Partial batch failure is explicit and recoverable without rewriting already accepted links.

Composite artifacts use a deterministic manifest that binds their members, order where material, individual digests, and package-level digest. Chunking may be used for large objects when the chunking and root-digest method are versioned and verifiable. A verifier must be able to detect missing, added, reordered, or substituted members. Packaging format and compression are treated explicitly so that verification does not depend on ambiguous reconstruction.

The artifact presented to validation, acceptance, and delivery must resolve to the same integrity identity. A transformation such as redaction, conversion, signing, packaging, localization, or destination-specific rendering creates a derived artifact with its own digest and lineage. The derived artifact is not assumed valid merely because its source was validated; the applicable transformation and delivery-readiness checks must be governed and evidenced.
| Task evidence verification | Confirm that the records and artifacts required for the task’s lifecycle, policy, risk, validation, and outcome are present and integrity-valid. |

Where required, an authorized trust service may sign or attest to a checkpoint, evidence package, artifact manifest, or verification result. The attestation proves that the identified signer asserted the specified integrity state under a governed key and policy. It does not expand the underlying evidence or transform an incomplete chain into a complete one. Expired, revoked, compromised, or unsupported signing credentials are reported according to the verification policy.

Evidence packages are portable controlled representations of canonical records. A package includes a manifest, scope, chain and record versions, included and omitted sequence ranges, artifact identities, protected references or embedded permitted content, verification rules, terminal values, checkpoints, redaction information, classification, and access or retention conditions. An export cannot present a selective subset as a complete history without declaring the selection criteria and omissions.

Independent verification must not require access to internal mutable application state. It may require protected access to classified records or artifacts, but the package and verification specification contain the information necessary to reproduce the permitted integrity checks. Export and verification access remain tenant-bound, purpose-limited, attributable, and audited.

Redaction produces a derived representation and does not change the original chain entry. The export manifest identifies which fields or artifacts were withheld, the authority and reason for redaction, and whether full verification requires access to the protected original. A redacted record cannot be hashed as though it were the original canonical content. Verification may confirm the original digest and the integrity of the redaction manifest without disclosing the protected value.

ilaten_requirement: Evidence retention is governed by tenant policy, contract, classification, legal obligation, task type, risk, investigation, legal hold, and assurance purpose. Audit metadata, chain records, protected payloads, artifact content, checkpoints, exports, and telemetry may have different retention periods. The chain design must identify which verification claims remain possible after any governed disposal.

Historical verifiability is tested through scheduled and risk-based verification, restore exercises, migration checks, and algorithm-support review. A backup is not accepted as trustworthy merely because it exists. Restored records must reproduce the expected chain values and artifact relationships before they are used as canonical evidence.

The verifier detects and classifies missing records, sequence gaps, duplicate or conflicting identities, predecessor mismatch, canonicalization failure, unsupported version, chain-hash mismatch, invalid signature or attestation, artifact-digest mismatch, broken manifest, inaccessible required content, cross-tenant reference, and incomplete evidence sets. Detection produces a material security and integrity event; it is not reduced to a diagnostic warning when assurance depends on the affected data.

Recovery begins from a verified genesis, checkpoint, backup, replica, or other approved source. It does not regenerate a preferred history from mutable task state or producer memory. Restored content is verified before use. If continuation from a recovered point is required, the transition is represented through an explicit recovery, successor, or checkpoint record that preserves the relationship to the affected history. The original suspected or corrupted state is not silently overwritten.

The chain cannot prove an event that was never submitted or accepted. Evidence-completeness rules and reconciliation are therefore required to detect missing expected events. It cannot prove that an authenticated producer observed reality correctly; independent artifacts, target-system references, validation, human review, or attestations may be required. It cannot establish non-repudiation unless the applicable signature, identity, key custody, and legal conditions support that claim.

ILATEN does not use blockchain as the trust mechanism. The required properties are achieved through authenticated event production, controlled append-only persistence, cryptographic predecessor linkage, artifact digests, tenant isolation, separation of duties, protected checkpoints, deterministic verification, retention governance, and independent assurance. Distributed consensus, public ledgers, tokens, and blockchain infrastructure are neither required nor treated as substitutes for enterprise control.
All implementations shall preserve the following invariants:
- transport retry cannot create duplicate logical evidence, and conflicting reuse of an event identity is rejected and evidenced;

An implementation is non-conformant if it permits mutable chain entries, calculates hashes over ambiguous serialization, allows producers to choose predecessor or final sequence, reuses event identities with different content, inserts late events into prior positions, validates one artifact digest while exporting another, presents a selective export as complete, hides unsupported verification, rebuilds history from untrusted state, stores tenant evidence in an unrestricted shared scope, or claims that a valid chain proves the semantic truth of its records.

The Audit Engine records material events but does not authorize activity, classify risk, grant capabilities, execute tools, validate outputs, or decide task acceptance. Those responsibilities remain with their designated authoritative components. The Audit Engine must not become an alternative policy path or a mechanism through which failed authorization can be bypassed. Audit processing may enforce ingestion integrity, schema conformance, tenant binding, and retention rules, but it does not reinterpret a business or control decision made by the responsible component.

The Audit Engine and Evidence Chain are related but distinct. The Audit Engine provides the semantic event model, lifecycle coverage, attribution, correlation, access, search, reporting, retention, and governance required for enterprise auditability. The Evidence Chain provides cryptographic continuity and tamper-evident verification for protected records and artifacts. An audit event may be bound into the Evidence Chain, but a valid cryptographic binding proves record integrity and continuity rather than the factual truth, business correctness, or regulatory sufficiency of the event's claims.

Audit architecture shall remain implementation-independent. An implementation may use different persistence, indexing, archival, or analytical technologies provided that it preserves the invariants defined in this section, the Evidence Chain requirements in Section 2.9, tenant isolation, protected append semantics, deterministic correlation, and verifiable lifecycle coverage.

ilaten_requirement: The canonical audit event taxonomy defines the minimum classes of activity that the platform must be able to record. Each event type shall have a designated owning domain, documented materiality rule, versioned schema, severity classification, retention classification, and relationship to the canonical operational flow. Product modules may extend the taxonomy, but they must not redefine or weaken the meaning of canonical event classes.
- **Immutable Context events:** context creation, authority-scope binding, approved context extension, reference resolution, context integrity verification, and rejection of unauthorized mutation.

- **Reasoning and recommendation events:** invocation of the governed intelligence capability, plan or action proposal creation, model or provider selection, model-access policy application, proposal revision, and rejection of an invalid or unsupported proposal. These events must not imply that the intelligence capability granted permission or initiated execution.

- **Tool Gateway and execution events:** tool resolution, adapter selection, environment preparation, worker assignment, isolated execution start, controlled external interaction, output receipt, execution termination, cleanup, resource-limit enforcement, and prohibited route denial.

- **Evidence and integrity events:** evidence registration, artifact digest binding, chain append, checkpoint creation, verification request, verification outcome, gap detection, integrity failure, and unsupported historical verification condition.

Every event family must include adverse and exceptional outcomes. An unsuccessful attempt to obtain authority, access protected data, invoke a prohibited tool, reuse a capability, alter an audit record, cross a tenant boundary, or suppress evidence is independently material even when the attempted action has no business effect. Successful-path-only auditing is non-conformant.

All audit events shall conform to a canonical envelope. Event-specific payloads may extend the envelope, but they may not remove mandatory attribution, tenant, ordering, outcome, classification, or integrity fields. Fields that do not apply to an event must be represented according to the schema contract rather than populated with ambiguous placeholder values.
| Field group | Required semantics |

| Producer attribution | Authenticated producer identity, producing component, service or workload identity, deployment environment, instance or execution boundary, and attestation metadata where required |

Identifiers shall be opaque where business meaning is not required. Direct credentials, private keys, access tokens, raw secrets, unrestricted sensitive payloads, and reusable capability material must never be written into the audit record. Where accountability requires association with sensitive content, the event shall use a protected reference, digest, classification marker, or separately controlled payload whose access is narrower than access to the event envelope.

Reason codes must be stable, documented, and suitable for automated analysis. Free-form descriptions may supplement a reason code but may not replace it. Human-entered comments shall be treated as untrusted data, classified appropriately, and protected against disclosure or interpretation as executable instructions.

Audit events originate in the component that observes or owns the material activity. Producers are responsible for accurate event construction, correct tenant binding, causal references, and timely submission. Producers do not control the canonical append sequence, retention decision, Evidence Chain predecessor, or post-ingestion mutability of the record.

Depending on the event family, it may be a tenant, task, capability, execution, approval, policy publication, or other governed stream. Global physical ordering across all tenants is not required, but all records needed to reconstruct a governed task must have deterministic correlation and an unambiguous logical relationship.

Causal parent references identify why an event occurred, while correlation identifiers connect events belonging to the same request, task, execution, review, or incident. A retry must refer to the original attempt and receive its own attempt identity. A compensation event must identify the action it compensates. A late-arriving event is appended at the current canonical position with its original observation time and late-arrival status; prior history is never rewritten to insert it retroactively.

Submission of the same event identity with the same canonical content is idempotent and must not create a second semantic event. Reuse of an event identity with different content is an integrity conflict and must be rejected, recorded, and investigated according to severity. Producer-generated sequence hints may be preserved for diagnosis but cannot override canonical sequence assignment.

Time sources used for security-sensitive ordering, expiry, approval, capability use, retention, and incident reconstruction shall be governed and monitored. Events shall disclose time uncertainty or degraded clock quality when it could affect interpretation. Human-readable local time may be presented in reports, but canonical records shall use an unambiguous time representation.

Audit materiality determines which activities must produce canonical events. Materiality is governed by event type, data classification, risk tier, authority change, tenant impact, security relevance, contractual requirement, and lifecycle significance. It is not left to individual developers or runtime producers to decide at their discretion.
At minimum, every governed task shall provide sufficient audit coverage to reconstruct:
- whether human approval was required, who decided, what was reviewed, and whether the approval remained valid at use time;

The audit event catalog shall define expected relationships between event types. For example, a successful capability use must relate to a valid issuance; an execution start must relate to an authorized proposal and policy decision; a result release must relate to an accepted validation disposition; and a closed task must either contain the mandatory lifecycle events or carry a governed exception explaining their absence.

Completeness is evaluated semantically, not by event volume. A large quantity of service logs cannot compensate for a missing approval decision or absent execution-authority record. Conversely, audit architecture should avoid recording redundant low-value detail that increases exposure and obscures material events. Coverage rules must be testable, measurable, versioned, and appropriate to the applicable risk class.

Auditability does not authorize unrestricted collection. The audit architecture follows privacy by design, data minimization, purpose limitation, tenant isolation, and least-privilege disclosure. Event schemas shall capture the minimum content necessary to support accountability, investigation, verification, legal obligations, and controlled operational use.

The Repository Code Index is published only after the accepted entity and relationship sets have been reconciled for the target baseline.

Working-tree state, uncommitted content, generated files, vendored dependencies, symbolic links, submodules, archives, and externally resolved packages require explicit treatment. Every derived entity and relationship retains a transitive reference to the repository baseline and analysis run. A query result without baseline identity is incomplete. Combining entities from different baselines into a single repository snapshot is prohibited unless the result is explicitly defined as a comparison view and preserves the identity of each source snapshot.

The Code Entity Model is the canonical semantic contract for repository-derived information. It separates durable identity from presentation and analyzer-specific representation. The model shall support at least repositories, source snapshots, files, directories where material, symbols, declarations, definitions, references, imports, exports, packages, modules, dependencies, configuration entities, generated artifacts, analysis runs, diagnostics, and change sets.

Each entity contains a stable identity within its repository baseline, tenant binding, entity type, schema version, source location or protected reference, language or format classification where applicable, integrity reference, producer and analyzer provenance, creation time, analysis status, and applicable confidence or completeness markers. Source locations use deterministic coordinates appropriate to the content type. For text source, a location may include normalized path, byte or character range, line and column range, and an integrity reference to the analyzed file. Symbol entities distinguish language-level identity from human-readable names. Optional fields must carry explicit absence or unsupported semantics; they must not be populated with inferred values presented as facts.

Relationship entities are typed, directional, and baseline-bound. Each relationship identifies its source entity, target entity or unresolved target description, relationship kind, extraction method, confidence class, evidence locations, and resolution status. Multiple relationships between the same entities may coexist when they represent different semantics. Relationship deduplication must preserve distinct evidence and must not collapse conflicting analyzer findings without recording the conflict.

The model evolves through explicit schema versions and compatibility rules. Historical indexes remain interpretable under the model version used to produce them. Analyzer implementations may expose additional fields, but consumers must be able to distinguish canonical fields from extensions.

For each candidate file, the analyzer determines the normalized repository-relative path, content identity or digest, size, detected encoding, line-ending representation where material, language or format classification, generated or vendored status where determinable, binary or text status, analysis eligibility, and diagnostic state. The analyzer rejects or quarantines paths that escape the verified repository boundary, unsafe symbolic-link resolution, malformed archives, prohibited device paths, unsupported encodings where safe normalization is impossible, excessive resource consumption, and content that violates policy. Excluded files remain represented at the level required to explain coverage; they are not silently omitted from repository completeness claims.

Normalization must be deterministic and must not change program meaning. Byte-order marks, line endings, Unicode normalization, and decoding errors require explicit rules. The analyzer shall preserve a reference to original bytes even when a normalized analysis view is used. Generated, vendored, minified, encrypted, compressed, or machine-produced files may be classified for separate treatment. Parser errors are local unless policy or analyzer rules require the entire file or run to fail. Dependency Extraction does not claim to reproduce all runtime behavior. Every Code Intelligence output shall be traceable to the exact repository snapshot, source file bytes, analysis configuration, entity-model version, analyzer identity and version, and analysis run that produced it. Provenance is part of the data contract rather than optional diagnostic metadata.
