ilaten_requirement: Test planning shall begin with product and system risk rather than historical test lists. The assessment considers consequence of failure, likelihood, exposure, detectability, reversibility, novelty, complexity, change size, data sensitivity, tenant reach, privilege, external action, regulatory impact, customer dependency, availability objective, and evidence criticality.
Each material risk shall determine:
- required test levels and techniques;
- required independence and specialist review;

Risk-based testing shall not be used to omit mandatory controls. Low observed defect history does not make an authorization boundary low risk. A small code change may require extensive testing when it affects shared identity, policy, tenant, evidence, data migration, cryptography, or release infrastructure. Conversely, a large mechanical change may require narrower behavioral testing when equivalence can be established with strong evidence.

Every material requirement shall be uniquely identifiable and testable or shall state why another assurance method is required. Ambiguous, contradictory, unverifiable, or missing requirements are defects in the Test Basis and shall be resolved before a test result is represented as conformance.

Bidirectional traceability shall connect requirement or risk to test condition, test case or automated check, execution result, defect, remediation, and acceptance. Traceability depth shall be proportionate to impact. Generated matrices may support this relationship, but link presence does not prove that a test meaningfully covers the requirement.

When a requirement changes, impact analysis shall identify affected tests, fixtures, data, baselines, results, documentation, and customer commitments. Tests shall not be silently changed to match unintended implementation behavior.

Architecture and implementation shall enable verification without weakening production controls. Testability includes observable state transitions, deterministic interfaces where required, stable identifiers, injectable failure points under authorization, controllable time, reproducible data, bounded concurrency, inspectable policy outcomes, correlation across events, and safe reset or cleanup.

Test hooks shall be explicitly designed, scoped, authenticated, authorized, disabled or removed from production where required, and reviewed for abuse. A hidden administrative bypass, hard-coded credential, unrestricted debug interface, or fail-open test mode is prohibited.

Systems shall emit enough structured telemetry and evidence to distinguish input rejection, policy denial, approval absence, capability failure, execution failure, validation rejection, acceptance decision, cancellation, and delivery result. Observability created for testing shall follow privacy, security, minimization, and retention requirements.

A component that cannot be tested independently may indicate excessive coupling or unclear responsibility. Testability concerns that require structural change shall enter ADR governance rather than being resolved through uncontrolled production instrumentation.

Early testing reduces defect propagation but does not eliminate the need for integrated and operational validation. A mocked component cannot establish end-to-end authority. A staging success cannot establish production resilience. A unit test cannot demonstrate tenant isolation across deployed services. Each level provides distinct evidence.

Continuous testing shall select the fastest reliable checks appropriate to each change stage while preserving deeper scheduled, pre-release, and periodic assessments. Section 4.7 defines pipeline orchestration. This section requires that test selection be risk-aware, attributable to the exact source and build, and resistant to silent omission.
Changes to tests, test data, baselines, or test infrastructure shall receive the same review discipline as production changes where they influence acceptance evidence.

Static checks shall use approved configurations, versions, rule sets, and suppression policies. A scan result is bound to its input and rule set. Passing static analysis does not prove runtime correctness or absence of vulnerability. Failing results shall be triaged by competent reviewers rather than dismissed solely because a tool reports a possible false positive.

Suppressions shall identify exact finding, reason, owner, scope, expiry or review trigger, and compensating evidence. Broad file-, repository-, category-, or severity-wide suppression is prohibited unless explicitly justified and governed. Generated code, vendored content, test code, examples, and infrastructure definitions shall not be assumed safe merely because they are excluded from a default scan.

Unit tests verify the smallest practical behavior in isolation. They shall be fast, deterministic, independent, readable, and focused on externally meaningful behavior or stable internal contracts. Unit tests should cover normal cases, boundaries, invalid input, state transitions, error propagation, cancellation, and relevant resource cleanup.

Test doubles may isolate dependencies but shall preserve the contract characteristics material to the test. Excessive mocking of internal calls creates implementation-coupled tests and can hide integration failure. Security or policy outcomes shall not be validated solely by asserting that a mock method was invoked.

Unit tests for deterministic modules shall assert exact results where the contract is exact. Time, randomness, locale, filesystem ordering, environment variables, network behavior, and concurrency shall be controlled. A test that passes only in one execution order or local environment is defective.

Unit coverage is necessary for maintainability but does not establish integrated trust or customer fitness. A numerical coverage target shall not encourage trivial assertions or discourage meaningful integration tests.

Service tests shall use realistic protocol behavior, serialization, authentication context, tenant context, retry, timeout, and concurrency. Internal implementation access may support diagnosis but shall not replace black-box verification of the published contract.

Stateful components shall be tested for initialization, empty state, normal evolution, restart, duplicate input, interrupted operation, corruption handling, schema change, retention, and cleanup. Tests shall verify both state and emitted audit or evidence events where material.
Component tests shall identify what remains unverified because dependencies are simulated. Those limitations determine required contract, integration, system, and operational tests.

Contracts shall test required and optional fields, defaults, unknown fields, enumeration extension, ordering, idempotency, error taxonomy, version negotiation, authentication, authorization, tenant scope, rate behavior, timeout, retry, pagination, and deprecation as applicable.

Consumer expectations shall not silently narrow or expand provider authority. A provider passing its own tests does not prove compatibility with all registered consumers. Contract registries or compatibility matrices shall identify supported versions and tested pairs.

Breaking-change detection shall distinguish syntactic compatibility from semantic compatibility. A field may remain present while its meaning, unit, privacy classification, default, or authorization effect changes. Material semantic change requires explicit version and migration governance.

Integration scope shall include normal operation and failures such as unavailable dependency, partial response, malformed payload, stale credential, expired capability, duplicate event, reordered message, network partition, timeout, rate limit, schema mismatch, provider degradation, and recovery after restoration.

Tests shall verify that failure does not create unauthorized fallback. A policy service timeout shall not grant permission. An audit backpressure condition shall follow the defined durable-admission behavior. A model-provider failure shall not bypass data-destination restrictions. A validation dependency failure shall not cause an unvalidated result to be accepted.

External integrations shall be tested against controlled sandbox or contract environments and periodically against authorized real endpoints where necessary. Provider test environments shall not be assumed to reproduce production semantics without evidence.

System tests evaluate the integrated ILATEN product against end-to-end requirements in a representative deployment. They shall cover the canonical operational flow from request intake through controlled delivery, closure, and review.
End-to-end scenarios shall establish that:
7. explicit human approval is obtained where required;

Audit Engine and Evidence Chain behavior shall be verified across all material stages rather than only after execution. System testing shall include rejection, cancellation, timeout, partial execution, compensation, duplicate request, replay, and recovery paths.

Acceptance testing determines whether the defined product, release, deployment, or customer scope satisfies approved business, operational, security, usability, contractual, and risk criteria. Acceptance scenarios shall be understandable to the accountable stakeholders and traceable to the acceptance basis.

Acceptance shall not be reduced to a demonstration of the preferred path. It includes material limitations, shared responsibility, administrative setup, failure communication, approval experience, evidence retrieval, recovery, and support readiness.

Customer acceptance may be executed in a customer-controlled environment, but test authority, data use, change window, production safeguards, evidence access, and defect treatment shall be agreed in advance. Customer sign-off does not waive ILATEN's internal security or quality obligations, and internal acceptance does not replace customer acceptance where contractually required.

Unresolved acceptance findings shall be classified as blocking, accepted residual risk, deferred scope, or rejected change through competent authority. Silence, attendance, or elapsed time is not acceptance.

Regression testing determines whether a change has adversely affected previously accepted behavior. The regression set shall be risk-based, versioned, maintained, and traceable to product capabilities, architecture invariants, historical defects, incidents, customer commitments, and high-risk integrations.

Change impact analysis shall select tests based on modified code and configuration, dependency graph, data and schema changes, interface consumers, deployment profile, policy, security boundaries, and operational history. Selection based only on modified filenames is insufficient for shared or dynamically bound behavior.

Every escaped material defect shall produce a regression test or a documented reason why another preventive or detective control is more appropriate. Tests shall reproduce the failure mechanism, not merely the visible symptom.

The regression suite shall be reviewed for obsolete, duplicate, low-value, and over-coupled cases. Removal requires evidence that the covered risk no longer applies, has moved to another controlled test, or is accepted through governance. Suite duration alone is not sufficient reason to remove critical coverage.

Exploratory work is especially valuable for administrative workflows, complex policy interactions, novel integrations, usability, adversarial input, recovery, and emergent reasoning behavior. It shall complement rather than replace repeatable verification of mandatory requirements.

Findings shall be reproducible where possible and recorded with environment, version, inputs, observations, impact, and evidence. A material finding shall become a defect, risk, test case, threat-model update, or requirement change as appropriate.

Scenario testing shall represent realistic enterprise sequences across roles, tenants, approvals, time, failures, and recovery. A scenario shall not combine so many variables that cause and coverage become impossible to interpret.

Test designs shall use techniques appropriate to the risk and behavior. Applicable techniques include equivalence partitioning, boundary-value analysis, decision tables, state-transition testing, use-case testing, cause-effect analysis, combinatorial testing, pairwise selection, classification trees, error guessing, checklist-based testing, property-based testing, model-based testing, metamorphic testing, fuzzing, differential testing, mutation testing, concurrency testing, and fault injection.

Technique selection shall be documented for material scope. Boundary and decision logic require more than representative happy-path examples. Stateful authorization and approval require transition testing. Large input spaces may require combinatorial or property-based approaches. Parser, protocol, and file ingestion paths may require fuzzing. Systems without a simple oracle may require metamorphic or differential methods.

Generated cases shall remain reviewable and reproducible. A large case count does not imply meaningful coverage if the generation model omits the critical states. Random seeds, distributions, constraints, shrink results, and failing examples shall be preserved where relevant.

Deterministic control components shall produce the same decision for the same canonical input, policy version, configuration, and system state. Tests shall bind exact inputs and versions and shall verify canonical serialization, decision outcome, reason code, obligations, capability scope, expiry, tenant, and evidence.

The Policy Engine shall be tested as an authoritative deterministic Control Plane component. Test suites shall cover permit, deny, conditional, conflicting policy, missing policy, invalid policy, stale version, unknown capability, risk escalation, required approval, expired approval, and unavailable dependency. Ambiguity or internal failure shall follow the approved fail-closed behavior.

Deterministic controls shall not depend on probabilistic model output for authority. Reasoning output may be an input proposal, but permission tests shall demonstrate that manipulated, inconsistent, or persuasive text cannot override identity, policy, capability, approval, or risk controls.

Golden baselines may support deterministic testing but shall not be updated automatically merely because output changed. Baseline change requires semantic review and traceability to an approved requirement or decision.

The AI Reasoning and Recommendation Engine shall be evaluated as a probabilistic advisory capability. Tests shall assess usefulness, factual grounding, instruction adherence, uncertainty handling, plan quality, harmful or prohibited recommendations, data handling, robustness, consistency, and escalation behavior. They shall never treat model confidence or fluent output as authorization, validation, or evidence of correctness.

Evaluation sets shall represent intended use, high-risk use, prohibited use, edge cases, multilingual inputs where supported, ambiguity, incomplete context, adversarial instructions, conflicting sources, long context, provider variation, and known failure classes. Sets shall be versioned, classified, protected against contamination, and reviewed for representativeness.

Because outputs may vary, results shall use defined scoring rubrics, repeated trials, sample sizes, confidence intervals or other uncertainty representation where appropriate, and human evaluation for criteria that cannot be established mechanically. Pass thresholds shall reflect consequence and shall not be selected after observing results.

Evaluation shall distinguish the quality of a proposal from the effectiveness of deterministic controls around it. A poor proposal correctly denied is a reasoning-quality failure but a control success. A high-quality proposal executed without required authority is a critical system failure.

Model orchestration tests shall verify provider selection, approved model and version constraints, data-destination policy, regional and tenant restrictions, credential isolation, request transformation, response normalization, timeout, retry, rate behavior, fallback, circuit breaking, cost controls, telemetry, and provider retirement.

ilaten_requirement: Identity testing shall cover enrollment, proofing where applicable, credential issuance, authentication, federation, session creation, renewal, revocation, recovery, logout, device or workload identity, and lifecycle events. Tests shall include valid, invalid, expired, revoked, replayed, duplicated, downgraded, malformed, and cross-tenant credentials.

Identity propagation across components shall preserve subject, tenant, delegation, purpose, and correlation.

Authorization testing shall evaluate subject, tenant, role, attribute, resource, action, purpose, context, risk, policy version, and explicit denial. Tests shall include horizontal and vertical privilege escalation, confused deputy behavior, stale grants, missing attributes, conflicting roles, delegated authority, boundary values, and attempts to bypass enforcement through alternate interfaces.

Evidence retention shall follow the approved record-class-specific schedule. Personal data, customer data, secrets, full payloads, and exploit detail shall be minimized. Legal holds and justified extensions shall be documented, authorized, scoped, and reviewed.

Test reports shall state the decision-relevant result before activity volume. They shall identify scope, version, environment, executed and omitted tests, pass and fail results, defects, risk coverage, residual uncertainty, waivers, evidence location, and recommendation.

Each material test phase shall define entry conditions such as approved Test Basis, stable scope, available build, known configuration, prepared environment, authorized data, ready dependencies, required access, and resolved blockers. Resumption requires correction, verification of the test context, and accountable authorization. Schedule pressure shall not convert a suspended test into a pass.

Independent verification shall be used where consequence, customer expectation, certification scope, regulatory obligation, contractual requirement, or conflict of interest warrants it. Independence may be organizational, technical, procedural, or external and shall be strong enough for the risk.

External assessment shall follow authorization, confidentiality, data protection, rules of engagement, vulnerability handling, evidence, and communication controls. The assessment method, competence, independence, date, and tested scope shall be recorded.

Production tests shall use dedicated synthetic identities and data, explicit tenant scope, rate and resource limits, tagged telemetry, cleanup, abort conditions, owner, window, and incident escalation. They shall not invoke real customer workflows, external side effects, destructive tools, payments, communications, or regulated processing without specific authorization.

Synthetic monitoring shall distinguish test events from customer events while exercising the material control path. A health endpoint that bypasses identity, policy, storage, or dependencies does not demonstrate end-to-end service health.

Production observation may reveal behavior but shall not be used as uncontrolled experimentation. Privacy notices, contracts, customer expectations, and applicable legal requirements govern any experiment involving real users or data.

The Engineering Standards Register shall identify the adopted reference, exact edition or version, publication status, scope, implementation profile, owner, review date, and any deviations. Draft, withdrawn, superseded, and final publications shall be distinguished.

A reference framework shall not be copied wholesale without applicability analysis. Framework requirements may be narrower, broader, technology-specific, or based on different roles and deployment assumptions. ILATEN-specific tenant, policy, capability, approval, execution, validation, audit, evidence, and human-accountability requirements remain mandatory even where an external framework is silent.
Testing metrics shall evaluate risk reduction and decision quality rather than activity volume. Relevant indicators include:
- test evidence missing provenance or exact build binding;

Pass count, test count, code-coverage percentage, automation percentage, and absence of reported defects are not maturity measures alone. Metrics shall identify definition, source, period, denominator, exclusions, and owner and shall be protected against manipulation.

Debt shall be registered with affected requirements and risks, impact, owner, treatment, target date, and release consequence. Critical authority, tenant, evidence, cryptographic, data-integrity, recovery, and external-action coverage shall not remain undocumented debt.

Temporary debt may be accepted only through the applicable risk process. A test skipped repeatedly becomes a control gap, not an informal exception. Investment decisions shall prioritize consequence and defect-prevention value rather than the age or size of the test suite.

Remediation shall improve the test basis, system testability, environments, data, automation, and ownership as necessary. Adding more cases is not always the correct treatment for an unclear requirement or unobservable architecture.

An exception to this strategy shall identify the exact requirement, affected product and versions, risk, omitted or modified testing, reason, alternatives, compensating evidence, owner, approver, start date, expiry or review date, and remediation plan.

An exception cannot authorize false reporting, conceal a failed test, treat a non-executed test as passed, bypass mandatory law or contract, expose customer data or secrets, remove human accountability, weaken tenant isolation, move authority to probabilistic reasoning, permit unvalidated external action, or redefine accepted architecture.

Where testing is technically infeasible, the owner shall use another controlled assurance method such as formal analysis, independent review, proof, inspection, monitored pilot, or bounded operational control and shall document the residual uncertainty. `Cannot test` is not itself risk acceptance.
- human approval remains explicit, informed, attributable, scope-bound, and resistant to post-approval mutation where required;

An implementation, test process, or release assessment is non-conformant if it tests only successful paths; treats unit coverage as proof of end-to-end trust; lets reasoning output authorize or validate itself; moves the Policy Engine into the intelligence layer; invokes a governed tool outside the Tool Gateway; accepts a result after Validation Pipeline failure or uncertainty without authorized handling; tests Audit Engine or Evidence Chain only as a final step; treats a chain hash as proof of completeness; validates tenant isolation through an application query alone while ignoring asynchronous, operational, backup, or recovery paths; uses production credentials or unapproved customer data in routine tests; hides a failure through retry, suppression, deletion, quarantine, or baseline refresh; automatically updates expected results because implementation changed; represents a blocked or non-executed test as passed; claims production performance from an unrepresentative benchmark; claims resilience from configuration without recovery exercise; claims accessibility from automated scanning alone; claims provider interchangeability from connectivity alone; omits exact build, configuration, environment, data, or suite provenance; allows an implementer to be the sole approver of a high-impact control where independence is required; releases with an expired exception through inaction; or uses test count, pass rate, coverage percentage, or tool output as a substitute for risk-based assurance.

Quality Gates shall preserve the canonical ILATEN trust model. A gate shall never transfer authority to probabilistic reasoning, treat a code merge as release approval, treat a deployment as acceptance, or treat generated evidence as self-validating. Gate quality is measured by the risks it controls and the integrity of its decisions, not by pipeline complexity or check count.
1. **Default deny.** A required gate that has not produced a valid decision prevents progression.
6. **One-way evidence binding.** Evidence supports a decision; the desired decision shall not determine which evidence is retained.

A gate receives authority from the approved governance model, not from the software platform that executes it. The repository provider, workflow engine, scanner, test framework, artifact registry, model, or dashboard may calculate and display a result but shall not define its own authority.

Gate requirements follow the documentation authority hierarchy established in Section 4.4. Applicable law and binding obligations govern first, followed by the Product Constitution, this canonical handbook, accepted ADRs, approved standards, product and interface requirements, and implementation-level rules. A lower-order gate cannot waive a higher-order requirement.
Each gate shall declare one enforcement mode:
- **Approval-Required:** progression requires an accountable human or committee decision based on defined evidence;
- **Advisory:** the result informs a decision but does not independently block; advisory use shall be justified by risk;

Enforcement mode shall not be weakened automatically because a platform cannot implement blocking. A manual control may be required until technical enforcement exists. A gate labeled advisory for convenience cannot satisfy a requirement that the authoritative profile defines as blocking.

An observational gate is not a substitute for a pre-transition blocking gate where harm cannot be acceptably reversed. Conditional progression shall identify who verifies the conditions and what occurs if they are not met.

Gate selection and thresholds shall be defined through approved Quality Profiles. Profiles may vary by product maturity, component criticality, deployment model, data classification, tenant reach, privilege, external side effect, public interface, regulatory scope, and release channel.
At minimum, the profile shall identify:
- required evidence producers and independence;
- required checks, techniques, thresholds, and freshness periods;
- supported exceptions and prohibited exceptions;
- required environments and deployment profiles;

A lower-risk profile shall not be selected by the change author solely to avoid controls. Classification changes require authorized review and evidence. Shared identity, policy, capability, approval, Tool Gateway, tenant, cryptographic, evidence, release-infrastructure, and recovery components normally require the highest applicable scrutiny because their failure can affect many downstream consumers.
Profiles shall remain implementation-independent where possible. Tools implement the profile; they do not define it.
Every governed gate shall have a stable Gate ID and a controlled Gate Definition Record. The record shall include:
- required inputs, evidence, checks, thresholds, and freshness;
- source, artifact, environment, configuration, policy, schema, and dependency binding rules;
- waiver eligibility, prohibited waiver conditions, and expiry;

A gate decision shall bind the exact object evaluated. For source changes, this includes repository identity, branch or change identity, commit or tree, relevant submodules or external source, and policy configuration. For artifacts, it includes immutable digest, package identity, provenance, composition, signing state, and intended release.

Environment-dependent gates additionally bind infrastructure definition, runtime configuration, policy version, schema version, deployment profile, region, identity, dependencies, test data, and relevant feature controls. A result from one environment shall not be silently applied to another.

Mutable tags, branch names, filenames, URLs, labels, or display versions shall not be the sole binding. If an artifact changes after evaluation, the gate result is invalid for the new bytes. If a configuration or policy changes materially, affected gates shall re-run or receive an explicit impact decision.
Gate evidence shall be protected against substitution. The system shall prevent a passing result for one artifact from being attached to another release, tenant, environment, or deployment.
- **Inconclusive:** evaluation completed but the evidence cannot support a reliable pass or fail decision;

`Skipped`, `Not Run`, `Unavailable`, `Timed Out`, `Allowed to Fail`, `Neutral`, or an absent result shall map to Blocked, Inconclusive, Cancelled, or Failed according to the Gate Definition; none maps automatically to Passed.
Failed and blocked outcomes remain in history after a later pass. A pass shall not erase prior evidence or make a previously deployed non-conforming artifact retroactively conformant.

Every gate result shall have a defined validity scope and, where risk can change with time, a freshness period. Static source and build evidence may remain valid for immutable inputs, while vulnerability, supplier, legal, threat, environment, credential, model, and operational assessments may expire.

Implementation shall not begin for material scope until the Definition Gate confirms a clear product outcome, accountable owner, intended audience, scope, non-goals, requirements, acceptance criteria, risk classification, data and tenant implications, dependencies, and lifecycle expectations.

The gate shall identify whether an ADR, threat model, privacy assessment, compliance applicability assessment, customer review, accessibility profile, or operational objective is required. Requirements shall be testable or assigned another approved assurance method.

Roadmap intent, research hypothesis, customer request, and current release commitment shall be distinguished. A feature shall not enter implementation under an ambiguous label that could create an unsupported public or contractual promise.

The Definition Gate fails or blocks when material requirements conflict with the Product Constitution, canonical architecture, legal obligation, product scope, or available decision authority. Architecture shall not be redesigned implicitly to rescue an unapproved requirement.

Required evidence may include architecture views, interface definitions, data flows, threat model, privacy and compliance assessment, capacity assumptions, recovery design, migration plan, cost analysis, and accepted ADR. The gate shall identify unresolved assumptions and transition architecture.

The gate shall reject any design that silently moves the deterministic Policy Engine into the intelligence layer; grants authorization or execution authority to the AI Reasoning and Recommendation Engine; gives Model Orchestration and Provider Abstraction policy authority; bypasses capability, approval, Tool Gateway, independent Validation Pipeline, Audit Engine, or Evidence Chain; collapses Development System and Runtime System; or changes the canonical Code Intelligence sequence without an authorized ADR.

The Source and Change-Integrity Gate establishes that a proposed change originates from the registered canonical repository, is bound to an exact verified baseline, has authorized authorship, and contains only the intended scope. It shall evaluate repository status, change provenance, unauthorized generated or vendored content, protected paths, sensitive files, and unexpected binary or large-file changes.

The gate shall detect ambiguous repository root, wrong remote, wrong baseline, unregistered fork, untracked material files, hidden nested repositories, modified submodule references, case-only path collisions where relevant, and source outside the approved workspace.

A change shall not pass because its textual diff is small. Generated output, lockfiles, build definitions, policies, infrastructure, migrations, security settings, documentation, and test changes may carry high consequence.

The Coding Gate evaluates conformance to Section 4.1 and the applicable repository profile. It may include formatting, linting, strict type analysis, schema checks, compilation, policy validation, dead-code detection, complexity signals, unsafe-language patterns, configuration validation, and required code-generation consistency.

Thresholds shall reflect language, component, maturity, and risk. A warning that is advisory in an isolated prototype may be blocking in a Trust Core or public-interface component. Rule severity shall be governed rather than inherited blindly from a tool default.

Suppressions shall be exact, attributable, justified, time-bound or reviewable, and visible to the gate. A blanket suppression, disabled rule set, altered baseline, or excluded path shall itself be evaluated as a change.
Static-analysis success does not establish runtime correctness or security. The gate shall not inflate tool coverage into a broader assurance claim.

The Review Gate establishes that the exact change received the required competent review and approvals before integration. Reviewer count alone is insufficient; the required roles depend on product, architecture, security, privacy, data, operations, accessibility, documentation, and release impact.

The gate shall verify current reviewer authority, independence where required, resolution of material comments, re-review after material modification, and absence of self-approval prohibited by policy. An approval attached to an earlier revision shall not automatically apply after substantive change.

Automated suggestions, generated review summaries, or absence of comment do not constitute accountable review. A reviewer shall be able to determine the actual change, affected requirements, tests, risks, and evidence.

The Test Gate consumes evidence produced under Section 4.5. It shall verify required test levels, risk scenarios, test suite version, environment, data, artifact binding, results, defects, flakiness, omissions, and evidence integrity.

The gate shall distinguish Passed, Failed, Blocked, Inconclusive, Quarantined, and Not Run results. A high aggregate pass rate does not compensate for one failed mandatory authorization, tenant, policy, evidence, migration, recovery, or security test.

Required thresholds and coverage dimensions belong to the applicable Quality Profile. They shall not be weakened after observing a failure. Changes to tests, fixtures, expected results, or coverage exclusions shall be reviewed as part of the same decision.

The gate shall fail or block when a critical requirement has no test or approved alternate assurance method, when a supported configuration is untested without disclosure, or when a coverage exclusion hides material behavior.
Teams shall not add trivial assertions, split cases artificially, or avoid testable code to satisfy a metric. Metric optimization that reduces assurance is a gate-system defect.

The gate shall classify findings by consequence, exploitability, exposure, affected scope, available mitigation, and uncertainty. Tool severity is an input, not final risk authority. Known-exploited or remotely exploitable vulnerabilities, tenant escape, authorization bypass, secret exposure, unsafe external action, or evidence compromise require treatment proportionate to impact regardless of aggregate scan score.

A clean scan does not prove absence of vulnerability. A supplier assertion does not prove ILATEN configuration. A penetration test has a defined scope and freshness and shall not be generalized to untested versions or deployment profiles.
Security exceptions shall be narrowly scoped and cannot authorize a known critical failure that violates law, contract, tenant isolation, human accountability, or the canonical trust model.

The Secret Gate prevents credentials, private keys, tokens, session material, recovery codes, customer secrets, and prohibited sensitive values from entering source, artifacts, logs, examples, documentation, packages, or publications.

Scanning shall cover changed content and, where risk requires, history, generated output, archives, binaries, document metadata, embedded objects, screenshots, and infrastructure state. Pattern matching shall be supplemented by entropy, context, provider validation, or manual review as appropriate.
Test placeholders shall be unmistakably non-functional. A scanner suppression for a synthetic value shall be exact and reviewed; broad exclusions are prohibited.

The gate shall distinguish an installed vulnerability from reachable or exposed risk without treating lack of proven reachability as proof of safety. Uncertainty, runtime loading, optional paths, plugin behavior, and build-time compromise shall be considered.

Dependency waivers shall bind exact package, version, component, use, vulnerability or issue, environment, compensating control, owner, expiry, and upgrade plan. A global ignore by vulnerability identifier is prohibited when another product or path may be exposed.

Required evidence may include source identity, build definition, builder identity, isolated or controlled build context, dependency resolution, software bill of materials, artifact digest, signature, timestamp, provenance attestation, reproducibility result, and policy evaluation.

Provenance shall be generated by a trusted build control plane or another approved authority rather than supplied solely by the untrusted build requester. Signature verification shall include trust, identity, scope, time, revocation, and subject digest; the presence of a signature file is insufficient.

An attestation proves only the claims it contains under its trust assumptions. It does not prove source correctness, security, license compliance, or approval. Gate language shall preserve this limitation.

Where required by the Quality Profile, the Build Gate shall evaluate whether the artifact is produced from declared inputs under controlled conditions and whether an independent rebuild yields the expected equivalence.

The gate shall identify network access, mutable dependencies, timestamps, locale, environment variables, nondeterministic ordering, random inputs, host tools, external state, and generated metadata that affect output. Non-reproducibility shall be diagnosed rather than hidden by signing whichever artifact was produced.

Bit-for-bit identity may not be practical for every technology. The approved profile shall define the equivalence property and excluded nondeterministic fields. Exclusions shall not conceal executable or security-relevant difference.

Only artifacts that pass the applicable build, provenance, composition, vulnerability, license, signature, and policy checks may enter an authoritative registry or release repository. Admission shall bind immutable digest and approved namespace.

The gate shall prevent overwriting immutable release artifacts, promoting artifacts built from unregistered source, using personal or untrusted registries, accepting mutable tags as identity, and mixing environments or tenants in a shared artifact path without approved separation.

Quarantined or rejected artifacts shall be isolated, visibly classified, and retained or disposed of according to evidence and security needs. They shall not remain discoverable as approved alternatives.

Automated license identification supports discovery but does not resolve ambiguous, custom, missing, dual, or conflicting terms. Legal review is required where interpretation or product distribution consequence is material.

The gate shall verify required notices and source-offer or attribution obligations in the actual distribution package. A repository-level license file does not automatically cover every included asset.

Architecture conformance checks shall evaluate component ownership, allowed dependencies, trust boundaries, data flow, interface contracts, deployment constraints, and accepted ADR obligations. Machine checks should enforce structural rules; human review addresses semantic intent.

The gate shall confirm that the Policy Engine remains deterministic Control Plane authority; reasoning produces proposals without permission or execution authority; Model Orchestration and Provider Abstraction does not decide policy; Tool Gateway remains the exclusive controlled external-action path; Validation Pipeline remains independent; and Audit Engine and Evidence Chain span all material stages.

Development System and Runtime System separation and the Code Intelligence order—Code Entity Model, Source File Analyzer, Symbol Extraction, Dependency Extraction, and Repository Code Index—shall remain enforced.

Changes affecting identity, authentication, session, tenant, authorization, delegation, administrative access, or workload identity require a dedicated high-rigor gate. Evidence shall include positive and negative testing, privilege analysis, trust-boundary review, failure behavior, audit, and recovery.

The gate shall block horizontal or vertical privilege escalation, cross-tenant access, ambiguous tenant context, stale or replayed credential acceptance, unsafe fallback, broad service identity, unreviewed support access, and inconsistent enforcement across alternate interfaces.
Access change shall identify the actual principals, resources, actions, purpose, environments, and duration affected. A role name or group membership alone does not demonstrate least privilege.
The gate shall verify that denied requests produce no prohibited side effect and that material denial events remain observable and attributable.

The Policy Gate establishes that policy definitions are valid, versioned, reviewed, test-covered, and applied by the deterministic Policy Engine. It shall evaluate conflicting rules, default behavior, unknown attributes, unavailable dependencies, version drift, and rollback or forward recovery.

ilaten_requirement: The Execution-Control Gate establishes that every governed external action is registered, policy-eligible, capability-bound, approved where required, isolated, resource-constrained, observable, independently validated, and attributable.

Evidence shall cover tool identity, contract, schema, side effects, destination, tenant, credentials, network and filesystem access, timeout, cancellation, idempotency, compensation, failure, output capture, and evidence. Direct invocation or an alternate route around Tool Gateway is prohibited.
Changes to a tool's side effects, destination, permissions, sandbox, handler, or validation obligations shall invalidate prior approval even when the tool name remains unchanged.
The gate shall reject unbounded command execution, hidden administrative bypass, mutable remote code, unsafe path resolution, unregistered tools, and use of a capability outside its exact scope.

The gate shall bind validator identity and version, validation inputs, rule results, unavailable rules, conflicts, timeouts, severity, explanation, and evidence. Execution success is not validation success. Reasoning self-assessment is not independent validation.

Acceptance shall be an explicit attributable decision. Accepted, Rejected, Held for Review, and Conditionally Accepted states shall produce different controlled outcomes. Rejected or unresolved results shall not proceed to delivery.
The gate shall evaluate unexpected side effects, incomplete outcomes, unverified output, stale evidence, tenant mismatch, and post-execution state, not only the returned response.

The gate shall evaluate event schema, identity, tenant, correlation, sequence, timestamp, source, decision, outcome, failure, append-only behavior, buffer or backpressure state, checkpoints, reconciliation, retention, export, and verification. Denied, failed, cancelled, recovered, and superseded actions are included.

Hash continuity or signature validity is necessary only where the profile requires it and is never sufficient to prove completeness, authorization, correctness, or truthful origin. The gate shall address events lost before durable admission, fork, truncation, duplicate, missing sequence, unavailable signer, and restore continuity.
Evidence failure affecting a mandatory stage blocks acceptance or promotion according to risk. An end-of-process receipt shall not compensate for missing material decisions earlier in the flow.

Cryptographic changes require evidence for approved algorithm and protocol, parameter, key usage, randomness, certificate validation, downgrade resistance, interoperability, rotation, revocation, failure, and lifecycle. The gate shall bind the exact cryptographic profile and implementation scope.

Key-management evidence shall cover generation or import, custody, access, activation, versioning, overlap, rotation, backup, recovery, revocation, compromise, destruction, and audit. Test keys shall remain separate from production keys.
The gate shall fail when cryptographic service unavailability causes plaintext fallback, unapproved algorithm use, signature bypass, stale key use beyond policy, or loss of required evidence.

Role and applicability shall be determined per processing purpose. The gate shall not assume that the customer is always controller or that ILATEN is always processor. Where competent legal or privacy review is required, engineering evidence cannot substitute for it.

The gate shall detect new collection, inference, logging, indexing, evidence capture, provider transmission, backup, or retention not represented in the approved data flow. A field removed from the primary interface may still exist in derived or operational systems.

Evidence retention shall follow an approved record-class-specific schedule that reconciles legal, contractual, certification, support, incident, defense, privacy, and minimization requirements. Retention is not indefinite by default.

Schema changes shall be evaluated for backward and forward compatibility, defaults, nullability, range, semantics, consumer behavior, privacy classification, indexing, and rollback or forward-recovery implications. Syntactic compatibility does not prove semantic compatibility.
The gate shall prevent promotion when reconciliation is incomplete, the migration tool is unverified, the source of truth is ambiguous, or rollback is promised without a safe supported path.

Reasoning evaluation gates assess the AI Reasoning and Recommendation Engine as a probabilistic advisory capability. They shall use versioned representative evaluation sets, prohibited and high-risk scenarios, defined rubrics, repeated trials, uncertainty, drift analysis, and competent human review where needed.

Gate thresholds shall be established before observing the release result and shall identify use profile, provider and model revision where available, configuration, language, sample, and known limitations. A single successful demonstration or fluent response is not evidence of dependable behavior.

The gate shall separately report proposal quality and surrounding deterministic control effectiveness. A harmful proposal correctly denied is a reasoning failure and a control success. A sound proposal executed without required policy or approval is a critical system failure.

Provider substitution shall pass functional, security, privacy, contractual, residency, performance, availability, and output-quality criteria for the defined use profile. Connectivity alone does not establish replaceability.
Fallback shall remain within the eligible provider set and shall not weaken policy or data restrictions. When no eligible provider exists, the approved failure behavior shall apply.

The gate shall re-evaluate on provider model update, endpoint change, retention-term change, regional change, incident, deprecation, or observed drift. Provider labels that resolve to mutable underlying models require controlled version and behavior monitoring.

Results shall identify version, artifact, architecture, deployment, region, data, dependency, concurrency, duration, percentile, errors, warm-up, and exclusions. Average response time alone is not an adequate gate basis.

The gate shall assess behavior near and beyond saturation, backpressure, rate controls, degraded dependencies, and recovery after load. It shall reject optimization that bypasses policy, encryption, validation, audit, evidence, or tenant isolation.

The gate shall consume fault-injection, endurance, backup restore, disaster-recovery, and operational-exercise evidence appropriate to risk. It shall compare measured recovery time and recovery point outcomes with approved objectives.

Unavailable identity, policy, approval, key, validation, or evidence-critical dependencies shall not produce unauthorized availability. A system that remains online by dropping required control fails the gate.
Unresolved restore inconsistency, unproven key recovery, unknown evidence continuity, or untested failback shall remain visible and may block release or promotion.

Alerts shall be proven through controlled triggering and routing. Runbooks shall be exercised proportionate to risk. A document or dashboard that has never been validated does not establish operational readiness.
Telemetry shall correlate material stages without exposing prohibited data. Sampling, aggregation, redaction, and retention shall preserve audit and evidence obligations.

The gate shall distinguish expected policy denial from system failure and shall provide visibility into reasoning, provider, execution, validation, evidence, and dependency conditions without transferring authority to observability tooling.

Generated Word, PDF, HTML, portal, package, and customer outputs shall be traceable to the controlled source revision and publication profile. Internal authoring controls, reviewer notes, secrets, restricted metadata, and unreconciled drafts shall be excluded from public output.

The gate shall validate links, terminology, numbering, examples, diagram sources, claims, accessibility, classification, redaction, and supersession as applicable. Documentation volume is not a pass criterion.

Accessibility gates evaluate the delivered product and documentation formats against the approved accessibility profile and declared conformance target. Automated checks shall be supplemented by manual and assistive-technology evaluation where required.

The gate shall address keyboard operation, focus, semantics, names and labels, contrast, text alternatives, reflow, timing, error identification, status communication, media alternatives, understandable approval, and equivalent access to evidence and recovery workflows.
A scanner score does not establish accessibility conformance. Defects shall be assessed by affected task and user impact, not only numerical count.

Any exception shall provide an accessible alternative, owner, reason, affected audience, remediation, and expiry where permitted. A contractual or legal accessibility requirement cannot be waived by engineering convenience.

The gate shall distinguish legal requirement, contractual control, internal policy, certification criterion, framework guidance, draft instrument, and voluntary practice. Reference to a framework does not establish compliance, certification, authorization, or readiness.
Customer-specific commitments shall not silently become universal product claims, and global documentation shall not erase deployment-specific limitations. Shared responsibilities shall be explicit.

Public, procurement, investor, and grant materials shall pass claim review when they describe security, privacy, performance, maturity, availability, roadmap, certification, or measured results. Aspirational or planned capabilities shall not be presented as released.

The gate shall verify environment identity, tenant and region scope, dependencies, capacity, compatibility, backup, restore, communication, approval, and change authority. Configuration shall be resolved and validated rather than inferred from a template.
The artifact approved for deployment shall be the artifact that passed the Artifact and Release Gates. Rebuilding after approval creates a different artifact and requires appropriate re-evaluation.

The gate shall review product acceptance, open defects, security and privacy findings, test evidence, artifact provenance, support readiness, documentation, migration, known limitations, legal and commercial conditions, and residual risk.
Conditional release shall identify limitations, eligible audience, monitoring, feature restrictions, support, expiry, and promotion criteria. It shall not be marketed as a higher maturity state.

Promotion authorizes an exact approved artifact and configuration to move into a defined environment or customer scope. Each promotion shall verify source environment, target identity, region, tenant, policy, secrets, keys, data, capacity, compatibility, approvals, and deployment plan.

Promotion shall be monotonic in assurance: movement toward a more sensitive or broadly exposed environment cannot rely on weaker evidence. Artifact identity shall remain unchanged unless the target profile explicitly requires a controlled transformation with new provenance.

The gate shall support staged rollout, canary, ring, tenant cohort, region, feature control, and hold points according to risk. These controls limit exposure but do not waive correctness or security requirements.
Cross-environment copying through personal workstations, mutable file shares, or unregistered registries is prohibited.

Post-deployment verification confirms that the intended artifact and configuration are active, health and control paths operate, migrations reconciled, telemetry and evidence are present, no prohibited exposure occurred, and service objectives remain within defined limits.

The gate shall use bounded smoke tests, synthetic transactions, configuration attestation, artifact digest verification, control-path checks, and operational telemetry as applicable. It shall not invoke uncontrolled customer side effects.
Production observation cannot retroactively justify bypassing a pre-deployment mandatory gate. Post-deployment gates add operational evidence; they do not replace prior assurance.

Customer-controlled, hybrid, and isolated deployments shall preserve the same canonical trust and quality invariants while recognizing different shared responsibilities and available services. The gate profile shall identify which evidence ILATEN produces, which evidence the customer produces, and who accepts residual risk.

The gate shall validate customer infrastructure prerequisites, identity integration, key and secret ownership, network boundaries, data residency, update path, evidence export, support access, backup, recovery, observability, and incident coordination.

Offline or isolated evidence shall remain attributable and reconcilable without weakening integrity or indefinite retention. Synchronization after reconnection shall address duplication, ordering, conflict, and tenant scope.

Public technical publications shall pass a dedicated gate for technical accuracy, source traceability, security disclosure, privacy, customer confidentiality, licensing, accessibility, legal claims, branding, and publication rights.

The gate shall bind the rendered artifact to the approved canonical source and verify that internal authoring controls, temporary comments, hidden objects, revision history, metadata, and recoverable redactions are absent.

Claims such as compliant, certified, secure, deterministic, auditable, tamper-proof, autonomous, available, supported, or guaranteed require precise approved scope and evidence. Unsupported absolute claims shall fail.

Manual gates are required where meaning, legal interpretation, risk acceptance, architecture judgment, customer context, usability, or executive authority cannot be established mechanically. They shall use a structured decision record rather than an informal message or meeting recollection.

The decision authority shall receive the required evidence, unresolved findings, limitations, alternatives, and recommendation. The decision shall record identity, role, scope, time, outcome, rationale, conditions, expiry, and evidence references.

Manual gates shall not become rubber-stamp queues. Approval without review is a control failure. Conversely, manual review shall not be inserted where objective automation can provide faster and more consistent enforcement without loss of judgment.

Automated gates shall be deterministic for the same controlled inputs, rule version, configuration, and environment state unless the Gate Definition explicitly governs statistical evaluation. They shall emit machine-readable result, reason, evaluated criteria, evidence references, and failure diagnostics.

Automation shall use least privilege and shall not possess unrelated repository, registry, environment, or release authority. Gate credentials, signing keys, approval identities, and deployment capabilities shall be separated according to role.

Rule configuration and gate code are governed production assets. Changes require review, testing, versioning, controlled rollout, and evidence. An author shall not modify the gate in the same unreviewed change that the gate evaluates.
Platform success status shall not be trusted without semantic mapping to the approved Gate Definition. An executed workflow with skipped mandatory jobs is not a pass.
A Composite Gate combines subordinate gate results for a defined transition. Aggregation logic shall be explicit, versioned, and fail closed for missing mandatory results.

Critical failures shall not be averaged away by numerous low-risk passes. Scores may support prioritization but shall not replace mandatory criteria. A weighted score is acceptable only where the Quality Profile defines why compensating strength in one area can offset weakness in another.
Contradictory evidence shall produce Blocked or Inconclusive status until resolved. The newest result does not automatically supersede a result with different scope, authority, or artifact binding.
The Composite Gate shall expose subordinate results and waivers. A green summary without accessible decision basis is insufficient for enterprise assurance.

Thresholds shall be established from product objectives, risk tolerance, historical evidence, standards, customer obligations, and validated capacity rather than arbitrary industry numbers. They shall identify measurement method, population, period, units, precision, and margin.

Baselines shall be controlled and shall not be updated automatically after regression. A change in expected behavior requires approved requirements, test, and risk review. `No worse than baseline` is insufficient when the baseline is already non-conformant.
Threshold adjustment after observing a failed result is prohibited unless handled as a separate governed rule change with transparent rationale and independent approval.

Gate definitions, thresholds, rule sets, profiles, mappings, exceptions, and automation are controlled changes. Each modification shall identify the reason, affected risks and repositories, compatibility, migration, validation, rollout, fallback, owner, and effective date.

Rule changes shall be tested against known pass, fail, boundary, and historical cases. A new rule may use an observation period to assess false positives and operational impact, but mandatory risk shall not remain advisory indefinitely without explicit treatment.
Weakening a gate requires risk and authority at least equivalent to the original rule. A local repository shall not weaken an enterprise gate without an authorized profile or exception.
Historical results shall retain the rule version used. Re-evaluation under a new rule shall create a new result rather than rewrite prior decisions.

Gate infrastructure is part of the trusted software delivery system and shall be protected accordingly. Controls include workload identity, least privilege, separation of duties, immutable or reviewed configuration, protected secrets, isolated execution, trusted dependencies, logging, monitoring, backup, recovery, and change control.

Untrusted change content shall not obtain gate credentials or alter the authoritative result. Pull-request or external-contributor workflows shall not expose production secrets, signing keys, deployment authority, or privileged network access.

The gate platform shall protect against result forgery, log deletion, artifact substitution, cache poisoning, unauthorized rerun, approval impersonation, and configuration downgrade. Administrative access shall be restricted and audited.

Changes from external contributors, customer repositories, mirrors, or forks shall be treated as untrusted until admitted through the canonical repository process. Their code, workflows, artifacts, test results, and attestations do not inherit ILATEN authority.

Pre-admission checks shall run without privileged secrets or deployment capabilities. Maintainer approval and trusted-context re-execution are required before authoritative integration or artifact production.

Post-event review shall reconcile source, documentation, tests, artifacts, releases, gate results, and incident evidence. Repeated emergency use indicates planning or platform failure.

A waiver authorizes a specific deviation from a gate criterion for a bounded transition. It is not a pass and shall remain visible in composite results, release records, customer scope where relevant, and residual-risk reporting.

Every material gate evaluation shall produce a Gate Decision Record containing Gate ID and version, evaluated scope, input identities, checks, evidence references, result, reason, decision authority, conditions, waivers, timestamps, validity, and downstream transition.

Evidence shall be structured and machine-readable where practical, with human-readable interpretation for material decisions. Raw tool output may be retained as supporting evidence but shall not be the only record when semantic mapping or risk judgment is required.
Retention shall follow the approved record-class-specific schedule. Sensitive source, customer data, exploit detail, credentials, and personal data shall be minimized and access-controlled.
The gate system shall be able to determine whether all mandatory evidence expected for a transition was received. A list of successful checks is insufficient if an expected check never reported.

Completeness mechanisms may include declared manifests, required-result sets, sequence or correlation records, independent workflow state, artifact attestations, and reconciliation. The chosen mechanism shall address events lost before durable admission and result substitution.

Late, duplicate, reordered, or conflicting evidence shall be handled deterministically. A duplicate pass shall not erase a failure. A result for an older artifact shall not satisfy the current transition.
Evidence-reconciliation failure produces Blocked or Inconclusive status according to the Gate Definition and shall not default to success.

Gate operation shall be monitored for disabled rules, skipped checks, unusual pass rates, increased waivers, stale profiles, long blocks, excessive retries, suppressed findings, changed tool versions, environment drift, and authorization anomalies.
Drift detection shall compare approved Gate Definitions with deployed workflow configuration and repository-level overrides. Unapproved divergence is a control finding even if current changes pass.

Monitoring shall identify repositories, environments, or teams that consistently bypass, postpone, or reclassify failures. Patterns may indicate incentives, capacity, training, tool, or governance defects.
Operational monitoring of the gate system shall itself be tested and included in continuity and incident procedures.
Quality Gate metrics shall evaluate decision integrity and risk control. Relevant indicators include:
- required gates not executed or lacking exact scope binding;
- manual approvals without required review evidence;

Number of gates, check count, workflow duration, aggregate pass rate, and low waiver count are not maturity measures alone. Teams shall not suppress findings, split gates, narrow scope, or avoid recording waivers to improve metrics.

Every material gate shall be reviewed periodically and after a serious escaped defect, incident, false pass, repeated waiver, major architecture change, platform compromise, or external-obligation change.

Review shall assess whether the gate addresses the intended risk, uses valid evidence, detects known failure classes, maintains appropriate independence, operates at the correct lifecycle point, and creates proportionate engineering cost.
Historical defects and incidents shall be replayed against the gate where feasible. A gate that would still pass a known unacceptable failure requires redesign, a new control, or explicit limitation.
- every required gate has a stable identity, approved definition, owner, authority, scope, evidence, outcomes, and lifecycle position;
- high-impact gate decisions preserve competent human accountability and required independence;
- one critical failure cannot be averaged away by numerous low-risk passes;
- threshold, baseline, rule, profile, test, expected-result, or suppression changes are governed and cannot be altered opportunistically to obtain success;

An engineering, delivery, or governance process is non-conformant if it treats a missing or skipped mandatory check as successful; attaches a pass from one commit, artifact, configuration, environment, tenant, or release to another; uses a mutable tag as the sole release identity; lets a workflow platform or probabilistic model approve its own authority; weakens a threshold or updates a baseline after observing failure without separate governance; deletes failed results after a rerun; averages a critical authorization, tenant, evidence, or security failure into a passing score; permits direct external action outside the Tool Gateway; accepts execution without independent Validation Pipeline evidence; tests audit or evidence only after completion; treats a signature, hash, scan, test count, coverage score, provenance statement, or supplier certificate as proof beyond its scope; allows untrusted change content to access signing, deployment, or production credentials; admits an artifact built from unregistered source or untrusted instructions; rebuilds an artifact after release approval and deploys the new bytes under the old decision; grants an indefinite waiver; uses the emergency profile for schedule or commercial convenience; marks a Draft or unreleased capability as publicly available; promotes to production while mandatory gates are Blocked, Inconclusive, Expired, or Cancelled; or uses gate volume and aggregate green status as a substitute for evidence-based enterprise assurance.

Continuous Integration and Continuous Delivery provide the controlled automation system through which ILATEN changes are integrated, verified, built, packaged, evidenced, approved, and made eligible for deployment. The system shall shorten reliable feedback cycles while preserving architecture, security, privacy, tenant isolation, human accountability, artifact integrity, and release authority.

CI/CD is a critical enterprise production capability even when it runs outside the ILATEN customer runtime. It can modify source, invoke privileged build systems, access sensitive environments, sign artifacts, publish packages, change infrastructure, migrate data, and deploy services. It shall therefore receive security, resilience, audit, recovery, and governance rigor proportionate to that authority.

A successful CI workflow does not create a release. A successful build does not authorize deployment. A deployable artifact does not authorize production promotion. A production deployment does not establish acceptance unless the required post-deployment and release decisions are complete.
