The engine shall be tested under the Engineering Standards and applicable Secure Software Development Lifecycle. Testing shall include deterministic contract tests and empirical behavior evaluation.
The minimum evaluation portfolio shall address, as applicable:
- required-field, invalid-field, tenant, identity, classification, and expiry behavior;

Evaluation data shall have documented provenance, purpose, representativeness, quality, rights, privacy treatment, version, limitations, and retention. Production customer data shall not be copied into evaluation merely because it is available. Synthetic data may reduce exposure but shall not be assumed representative without validation.

Qualified external review shall be completed before an affected high-impact reasoning capability or profile influences a Stable release, production environment, customer-controlled production deployment, or Enterprise operating profile; otherwise it shall remain blocked, prerelease, non-production, advisory-only, or constrained. Where true independence is unavailable during a registered bootstrap phase, the absence shall be recorded and shall not be represented as independent evaluation.

A reasoning-engine change shall not progress to a higher maturity, broader audience, production use, or Enterprise profile unless the applicable Quality Gates pass. Gates shall cover code and configuration integrity, schema compatibility, security, privacy, tenant isolation, provenance, grounding, evaluation, calibration, provider behavior, observability, rollback, documentation, and operational readiness.

A gate decision shall bind to the exact versions of relevant code, reasoning policy, model route, retrieval profile, prompt or instruction package, context schema, output schema, evaluation set, threshold configuration, and deployment profile. A material change invalidates prior eligibility to the extent defined by policy.

Gate failure shall block progression unless a formally permitted exception exists. Exceptions shall be specific, time-bound, owned, evidenced, monitored, and incapable of waiving non-waivable security, privacy, tenant-isolation, authorization, audit, evidence, safety, or human-accountability controls.

Operational monitoring shall provide sufficient visibility to identify degradation, misuse, cost anomaly, provider drift, quality regression, latency, failure, security events, privacy events, tenant anomalies, and control bypass attempts without indiscriminately collecting protected content.

Metrics are signals, not proof. High completion, low refusal, high user satisfaction, or low observed incident rate does not establish safety or correctness. Monitoring definitions, denominators, exclusions, retention, access, and known limitations shall be controlled.

Alert thresholds shall be risk-based and profile-specific. Material anomalies shall trigger investigation, restriction, rollback, provider isolation, capability suspension, incident response, customer notification assessment, or other controlled action as applicable.
The engine shall fail safely. Degraded operation shall have explicit entry criteria, allowed capabilities, data restrictions, output limitations, monitoring, expiry, and recovery conditions.
- inability to preserve required residency or confidentiality;
- inability to create required audit or evidence records;

The engine shall not conceal degraded assurance behind an ordinary Completed status. If a bounded result is still permitted, it shall use Completed with Limitations and disclose the material constraint. If the constraint affects a non-waivable control, output generation or downstream progression shall be blocked.

Retries shall be bounded and governed. A retry shall not silently alter tenant, purpose, provider assurance, region, data scope, retrieval source, output contract, or authority. Repeated failure shall escalate rather than create an indefinite automated loop.

Material configuration shall be versioned, reviewable, attributable, tested, approved, deployable through controlled channels, and recoverable. Hidden provider-side changes shall be monitored to the extent contractually and technically possible. When a provider change cannot be adequately characterized, affected use cases shall be re-evaluated or constrained.

Configuration shall not be edited through uncontrolled production interfaces. Emergency changes follow the approved emergency process and create retrospective validation, documentation, and expiry obligations. Temporary experiments shall not become permanent production behavior through inaction.

Changes to reasoning behavior shall follow Sections 4 and 5. A change record shall identify the intended outcome, affected profiles, sources, models, providers, schemas, controls, customers, risks, evaluation plan, rollout, observation, rollback, and evidence requirements.

Rollout shall be bounded by approved tenants, cohorts, regions, purposes, data classes, and use cases. Observation shall compare outcome quality, policy behavior, validation results, incidents, refusals, human overrides, latency, cost, and guardrails against the approved baseline.

Rollback shall restore a known approved reasoning profile without reviving revoked providers, sources, secrets, policies, or capabilities. Stored recommendations generated under a withdrawn profile shall be assessed for continued validity; rollback of configuration does not automatically invalidate or validate prior business decisions.
Governance shall assign accountable roles for:

One person may hold multiple roles during a registered Single-Maintainer Bootstrap Profile, but records shall not claim independent review, dual control, or Enterprise separation of duties when these did not occur. Qualified external review shall be completed before an affected high-impact reasoning capability or profile influences a Stable release, production environment, customer-controlled production deployment, or Enterprise operating profile; otherwise it shall remain blocked, prerelease, non-production, advisory-only, or constrained.

Providers, tools, frameworks, automated evaluations, model-generated recommendations, sales commitments, or customer preference cannot unilaterally interpret or waive canonical controls. Conflicts shall be escalated through the applicable architecture, legal, contractual, risk, security, privacy, and governance processes.
The bootstrap profile shall maintain:

The bootstrap profile shall not be represented as two-person continuity, independent validation, dual control, mature Enterprise governance, or completed separation of duties. Where lack of independence creates unacceptable risk, the capability shall remain disabled, prerelease, non-production, or limited to synthetic and non-sensitive data.
The following behaviors are prohibited:
- releasing a high-impact reasoning profile without the required evaluation and accountable approval; or
- conceal the use, limitations, or change of a model or provider where disclosure is required; or
- every material invocation is bound to a verified tenant and Immutable Context;
- every output is a versioned Recommendation Envelope with a registered status;
- facts, supplied assertions, retrieved statements, assumptions, inferences, estimates, and recommendations remain distinguishable where material;
- the engine grants no authority and initiates no controlled execution;
- proposed actions remain inert until deterministic policy, risk, approval, capability, and Tool Gateway controls complete;
- tenant isolation, purpose limitation, least privilege, and data minimization apply to context, retrieval, output, telemetry, and records;
- provider and model selection remains within the approved abstraction and deployment profile;
- fallback cannot weaken security, privacy, residency, tenant, contract, or output requirements;
- material sources and configurations are traceable and governed;
- uncertainty and confidence are expressed without becoming authority;
- high-impact recommendations receive the required human review;
- validation remains independent from recommendation generation and execution;
- audit and Evidence Chain records cover all material lifecycle events continuously;
- failures, refusals, limitations, revisions, and supersession remain visible;
- changes follow the approved Engineering, Release, and Change Management standards;
- bootstrap limitations are explicit, constrained, time-bound, and not represented as Enterprise independence; and
- retention follows approved record-class-specific schedules and is not indefinite by default.
The following invariants are binding:
- the component is named the AI Reasoning and Recommendation Engine because it recommends and does not decide;
- the engine belongs to the Intelligence Plane and not the deterministic Control Plane;
- the Policy Engine remains a deterministic Core Module under Section 2.3;
- the engine cannot authenticate, authorize, approve, waive, execute, validate, accept, or close on its own authority;
- a Recommendation Envelope is not an approval, capability, tool command, validation result, or Evidence Chain proof;
- models and providers remain replaceable and non-authoritative;
- every material invocation is tenant-bound, purpose-bound, context-bound, attributable, versioned, and auditable;
- context access follows least privilege and shall not expand through inference;
- retrieved content is treated as data and cannot override canonical control instructions;
- facts, assertions, assumptions, inferences, estimates, and recommendations are not silently conflated;
- confidence influences review and routing only through approved policy and never grants permission;
- Policy Engine evaluation occurs after recommendation generation and before any capability issuance;
- required human approval remains explicit, attributable, bounded, revocable, and tied to the exact proposal;
- controlled execution occurs only through the Tool Gateway under a separately issued capability;
- the Validation Pipeline independently assesses results against pre-established criteria;
- Audit Engine and Evidence Chain controls operate continuously across request, context, reasoning, policy, approval, execution, validation, acceptance, and closure;

- security, privacy, safety, tenant isolation, evidence, and human-accountability controls are non-waivable through model output, provider behavior, customer preference, sales commitment, or engineering convenience;

- qualified external review is completed before an affected high-impact reasoning capability or profile influences a Stable release, production environment, customer-controlled production deployment, or Enterprise operating profile; otherwise it remains blocked, prerelease, non-production, advisory-only, or constrained;
- bootstrap operation remains honest, constrained, temporary, and subject to dated exit criteria;
- data and evidence retention are purpose-bound and not indefinite by default; and
- architecture-changing recommendations require an authorized ADR and cannot redesign the system by their own force.

An AI Reasoning and Recommendation Engine implementation is non-conformant if it presents itself as the decision authority; grants or expands a capability; triggers controlled execution directly; treats natural-language certainty or confidence as permission; impersonates a human approver; determines legal or compliance status without competent authority; bypasses the Policy Engine, Approval Engine, Tool Gateway, Validation Pipeline, Audit Engine, or Evidence Chain; changes tenant, purpose, provider, region, data, source, tool, or capability scope without authorization; uses retrieved instructions to override canonical controls; commingles tenant information; hides material assumptions, conflicts, uncertainty, or adverse evidence; fabricates provenance, citations, validation, approval, or evidence; validates its own execution as the sole assurance source; retries with weaker controls; retains protected content indefinitely; silently learns from customer data; releases high-impact behavior without required evaluation; represents bootstrap self-review as independent assurance; or rewrites prior records to conceal changed reasoning, failure, rejection, or supersession.

Model Orchestration and Provider Abstraction provides the governed boundary through which ILATEN selects, configures, invokes, observes, changes, and retires approved reasoning models and model-service providers. It allows Intelligence Plane capabilities to use appropriate model capabilities without binding the canonical architecture, customer workflows, control records, or reasoning contracts to a specific provider, model family, deployment product, or commercial interface.

The component standardizes access to model capabilities while preserving material differences in assurance, behavior, data handling, regional availability, output semantics, reliability, cost, and lifecycle. Abstraction shall not erase differences that affect security, privacy, tenant isolation, contractual commitments, legal obligations, evaluation validity, or customer outcomes. Provider independence means that ILATEN controls its internal contracts and can change an underlying implementation through a governed process; it does not mean that every provider or model is interchangeable without qualification.

Model orchestration is a bounded technical and operational function. It may select among models and routes that have already been made eligible for the exact request profile. It shall not determine that prohibited processing is permissible, grant data access, issue a capability, accept risk, approve a provider, waive residency constraints, override a customer restriction, authorize execution, validate business results, or replace accountable human and deterministic control-plane decisions.

Model Orchestration and Provider Abstraction is an Intelligence Plane support component. It serves the AI Reasoning and Recommendation Engine, Confidence Scoring, Knowledge Graph, Repository Intelligence, Context Engine, and Planning Engine through controlled interfaces. It does not own their business semantics and shall not convert a provider-specific feature into canonical product authority.

The deterministic Policy Engine remains a Core Module under Section 2.3. Policy and authorization controls determine which providers, model classes, deployment profiles, regions, purposes, data classes, and capabilities are eligible before orchestration optimizes among them. The orchestrator shall not reinterpret a denial, omit policy-relevant attributes, or select a route that is ineligible merely because the route is cheaper, faster, more capable, or available.
The component shall:

The component shall not optimize for an abstract best model. It shall select a conformant route for a defined request under controlled criteria. Suitability is contextual and may vary by tenant, purpose, language, data classification, assurance profile, jurisdiction, latency objective, cost limit, and validated capability.
The orchestration domain shall distinguish the following objects:

These objects shall not be collapsed. A provider is not a model. A model family is not an exact model version. A model version is not an endpoint. An endpoint is not an approved route. Technical availability is not eligibility. Eligibility is not selection. Selection is not business authorization. A successful invocation is not a validated recommendation. A provider contract is not proof of operational conformance.

The internal abstraction shall define stable, implementation-independent contracts for capabilities required by ILATEN. The contract may cover input content, structured context, output schema, streaming, usage accounting, cancellation, timeout, error classification, integrity metadata, and supported inference controls. Provider-specific interfaces shall be isolated within governed adapters.
An adapter shall:
- preserve tenant, correlation, classification, region, and request-integrity metadata where supported and required;

The abstraction shall use the least common necessary contract, not the weakest common denominator. Capabilities that are materially provider-specific may be represented through explicit optional profiles, but customer or product logic shall not assume their availability without a governed dependency and fallback strategy.

Provider-specific extensions shall not alter the Product Constitution, canonical operational flow, policy placement, approval requirements, Tool Gateway boundary, Validation Pipeline independence, Audit Engine, Evidence Chain, tenant isolation, or human accountability. If an extension changes architecture, an authorized ADR is required before adoption.
Every orchestration request shall be typed and bound to the originating controlled context. The Model Access Request shall contain or reference, as applicable:
- required model capabilities and prohibited capability classes;
- required language, modality, context capacity, and structured-output behavior;

Narrative text shall not override typed constraints. If a prompt or retrieved document requests a different provider, region, data treatment, retention policy, model, tool, or capability, the orchestrator shall ignore the instruction unless the controlled request and policy permit it.

An invalid, incomplete, expired, unverifiable, or internally conflicting request shall not be routed. The orchestrator shall return a controlled failure, clarification, or policy-referral outcome with sufficient reason metadata for the authorized caller.

Eligibility shall be resolved before route optimization. The orchestrator shall derive an Eligibility Set using approved deterministic constraints and the current registered state of candidate routes.
- data classification and prohibited data classes;

A candidate route failing any mandatory criterion shall be excluded before scoring or preference optimization. The orchestrator shall not compensate for a failed mandatory requirement with higher performance, lower cost, greater capacity, or stronger results in another category.

The Eligibility Set and exclusion reason codes shall be recorded. Sensitive commercial, security, or provider details may be access-controlled, but authorized reviewers shall be able to determine why a route was eligible or excluded.

Selection rules shall be versioned, deterministic for their controlled inputs where required, attributable, testable, and protected from unauthorized modification. Where selection uses measured or predicted performance, the source, freshness, scope, confidence, and limits of the measurement shall be controlled.

The Route Decision Record shall identify the Eligibility Set, selected route, routing-policy version, material decision inputs, exclusions, conditions, fallback plan, time, and outcome. It shall not include unrestricted protected provider information in customer-visible records unless disclosure is authorized.

A route may not be selected solely because it is the default in a provider library, the newest available model, the model preferred by a developer, the option promoted by a vendor, or the option previously used for another tenant.
Routing policy shall define:

Dynamic routing may react to current health, capacity, latency, or validated quality indicators. It shall not react by weakening data, tenant, security, privacy, region, contract, or assurance controls. When telemetry is absent, stale, contradictory, or suspected of manipulation, routing shall use the approved conservative behavior.

The orchestrator shall prevent feedback loops in which routing sends most traffic to a route, the resulting volume makes that route appear more successful, and the apparent success further entrenches the route without controlled comparison. Evaluation and traffic allocation shall account for selection bias, cohort differences, and changing workloads.

Each profile shall define ownership and responsibility for provider contracting, identity, network boundary, credentials, keys, isolation, scaling, patching, model updates, logging, monitoring, retention, deletion, incident response, continuity, support, evaluation, and exit.

Where a deployment cannot provide a required assurance property, the limitation shall be explicit. The affected use case shall use compensating controls, a lower maturity claim, a constrained audience, or remain unsupported.

A provider shall not become eligible through technical integration alone. Provider onboarding shall include a documented applicability, risk, security, privacy, legal, contractual, operational, financial, continuity, support, and exit assessment proportionate to the intended use.
The Provider Profile shall address, as applicable:

Qualification shall produce an approved scope, not a universal approval. A provider may be approved for public non-sensitive summarization but not for confidential repository analysis, regulated personal data, high-impact decisions, production signing, or a restricted region.

Provider claims, marketing material, self-attestations, benchmark results, certifications, or contractual promises shall be treated as inputs to assessment, not automatic proof of ILATEN conformance. Material controls shall be independently verified where proportionate and feasible.
Provider approval does not approve every model, version, endpoint, or configuration. Each Model Route shall be qualified for its intended reasoning profiles and deployment scope.
Qualification shall consider:
- privacy and prohibited data-use behavior;
- release maturity and required human review.

Qualification shall bind to a versioned route and Invocation Profile. An unannounced provider-side change, model alias movement, endpoint migration, safety-policy change, context-limit change, response-format change, or data-handling change may invalidate qualification or trigger re-evaluation.

Aliases such as latest, recommended, standard, premium, or stable shall not be treated as immutable model identities. Where a provider does not expose an immutable identity, ILATEN shall record the best available provider version evidence, increase monitoring, define change-detection controls, and restrict use according to uncertainty.
The orchestrator shall maintain a controlled Model Capability Registry. The registry shall identify, for each approved route:
- approved data classifications and prohibited content classes;
- known defects, limitations, required warnings, and human-review conditions; and

Registry entries shall be versioned and attributable. Runtime discovery shall not automatically grant eligibility. A newly visible model or endpoint remains unavailable until qualification and approval complete.

The registry shall distinguish claimed capabilities, tested capabilities, approved capabilities, and currently available capabilities. A provider claim shall not be presented as a validated ILATEN capability.

Transformation shall preserve semantic intent and controlled constraints. It shall not remove tenant, data, purpose, authority, or safety information because a provider interface lacks a direct field. If a required constraint cannot be represented or enforced, the route is incompatible for that request.

Context truncation shall be governed. The orchestrator shall not silently remove policy-relevant, risk-relevant, tenant, purpose, instruction, source, or output-contract information to fit a model limit. Approved strategies may summarize low-priority context through a controlled process, retrieve narrower context, split analysis into bounded stages, select a larger eligible route, request clarification, or fail safely.

Inference parameters shall be treated as controlled configuration. Parameters affecting variability, determinism, creativity, length, safety, or tool behavior shall be selected by the approved reasoning profile, not arbitrary runtime input.

Provider output shall be normalized into the canonical response contract before it is consumed by the reasoning engine or downstream services. Normalization shall validate schema, types, size, encoding, content boundaries, status, usage, and integrity metadata.

Normalization shall not manufacture equivalence. If a provider cannot produce a required field, the field shall be marked unavailable or the response rejected according to contract. The adapter shall not invent provenance, confidence, citations, tool results, policy decisions, or completion status.

Unstructured provider text shall not be interpreted as a capability grant, approval, executable command, or authoritative control record. Structured fields supplied by a provider remain untrusted until validated against the canonical schema and policy.

Provider error codes shall map into a controlled error taxonomy such as invalid request, authentication failure, authorization failure, policy refusal, quota exceeded, rate limited, timeout, capacity unavailable, model unavailable, schema failure, content rejection, dependency failure, provider incident, or unknown failure. Unknown failures shall not be treated as retryable by default.

Composition shall not create circular self-validation. Multiple outputs from the same provider, model lineage, context, or reasoning method may improve robustness but shall not be represented as independent assurance without a justified independence analysis.

Every sub-invocation shall have a defined purpose, tenant binding, data scope, route, resource budget, status, and evidence link. Intermediate outputs remain non-authoritative and shall not escape their approved audience or retention class.

Aggregation rules shall be controlled and shall preserve disagreement. The orchestrator shall not select the answer that appears most confident or favorable without an approved method. Material disagreement shall trigger clarification, additional evidence, qualified review, or a bounded inconclusive result.
Multi-model operation shall not multiply data disclosure beyond necessity. Each route shall receive only the minimum context required for its assigned function.
Retry and fallback shall be explicit components of the Route Plan. They shall not be improvised after failure.
A retry policy shall define:

Fallback may occur only to a route that independently satisfies all mandatory eligibility constraints for the request. Fallback shall not change tenant, region, provider-use terms, retention, data classification, assurance, output schema, or approved purpose without renewed control-plane evaluation.

When fallback changes material model behavior, evaluation level, latency, cost, or expected quality, the outcome shall disclose the route change to downstream controls and, where required, the human reviewer. A degraded route shall not be represented as equivalent to the primary route if qualification differs.

Circuit breakers shall isolate routes exhibiting elevated failure, latency, schema, security, privacy, tenant, or quality anomalies. Breaker state shall be tenant-aware where appropriate, protected against manipulation, observable, and subject to controlled reset. Manual override shall be authorized, time-bound, attributable, and unable to waive non-waivable controls.

The orchestrator shall enforce approved resource boundaries. Cost governance is necessary for operational sustainability but remains subordinate to security, privacy, quality, and contractual requirements.

Budget exhaustion shall not cause silent routing to an ineligible provider, unqualified model, weaker assurance tier, or unapproved region. Approved responses include delay, queueing, narrowed scope, lower-cost eligible route, clarification, customer-authorized change, or refusal.

Usage and cost records shall be attributable to the tenant, purpose, route, and request while minimizing protected content. Commercial billing records shall remain distinct from technical usage estimates and provider invoices. A provider-reported token or cost count shall not be the sole authoritative billing record without reconciliation controls.

Model context capacity is a constrained resource, not permission to disclose more information. The orchestrator shall not maximize context by default. Context selection remains governed by the Context Engine, purpose limitation, data minimization, tenant isolation, and the reasoning contract.
- rejecting a request whose necessary context cannot be processed safely.

Any compression or summarization that may remove material facts, qualifications, policy attributes, or evidence shall be recorded and exposed as a limitation. A derived summary shall not replace the authoritative source for decisions that require the source.

The orchestration layer is a high-value boundary because it controls provider credentials, model routes, data movement, configuration, and fallback. It shall operate under Zero Trust and least privilege.

Controls shall include authenticated service identity, network restrictions, endpoint allowlisting, protected configuration, signed or integrity-checked artifacts where applicable, secret isolation, key rotation, least-privilege provider credentials, short-lived access where supported, strict schemas, egress control, request and response limits, route integrity checks, dependency governance, monitoring, circuit breaking, and independent validation.

Provider credentials shall not be included in prompts, Recommendation Envelopes, customer-visible logs, or model outputs. A model shall not receive authority to modify provider configuration, route policy, credentials, or its own monitoring.

Material provider compromise shall trigger incident response, route suspension, credential revocation, evidence preservation, customer-impact assessment, fallback evaluation, and controlled recovery. Restoration requires requalification proportionate to the incident.

Every Model Route shall have explicit data-handling terms and technical controls. The orchestrator shall enforce the approved combination of processing purpose, data categories, provider, region, retention, deletion, training use, human access, and disclosure.
The Provider Profile shall distinguish whether data may be:

Unclear provider terms shall not be interpreted in favor of broader processing. If required restrictions cannot be contractually and technically supported, the route is ineligible for the affected data or purpose.

Data minimization shall apply separately to each invocation. A provider approved for a tenant does not need all tenant context. Sensitive fields shall be removed, tokenized, pseudonymized, redacted, or kept within an approved private boundary where the use case permits and the transformation preserves required meaning.

Personal data and protected customer content shall follow approved record-class-specific retention. Provider retention shall be reconciled with ILATEN and customer obligations. Retention is not indefinite by default.

The orchestrator shall maintain tenant binding across eligibility, routing, queueing, invocation, caching, normalization, usage accounting, monitoring, audit, and deletion. Tenant identity shall derive from verified platform context and shall not be accepted from prompt text.
Isolation controls shall cover:

Shared infrastructure shall not permit one tenant's load, error, model output, provider metadata, or context to become visible to another. Cache keys shall include tenant and all material request dimensions, and protected reasoning output shall not be cached unless the purpose, expiry, invalidation, and access model are approved.

Customer-dedicated routing may be required by contract or assurance profile. Dedicated infrastructure shall not be represented as independent isolation without evidence of configuration, identity, network, key, data, monitoring, and operational separation.
A suspected cross-tenant route or data event shall block affected output and initiate security and privacy incident procedures.

The orchestrator shall select only deployment endpoints that satisfy the approved geographic processing and storage constraints. Region labels supplied by providers shall be mapped to controlled ILATEN region definitions and verified against data-flow, backup, logging, support, and subprocessor behavior.

Residency assessment shall consider more than primary inference location. It may include request routing, temporary processing, provider logs, abuse monitoring, support access, backups, telemetry, failover, subprocessors, and key management.

Fallback across regions is prohibited unless the controlled request and applicable assessment authorize it. An incident or capacity shortage does not automatically permit cross-border transfer. Where no eligible in-region route exists, the orchestrator shall fail safely or use an approved customer-controlled alternative.
The orchestrator shall preserve evidence of the selected region, route, provider commitment, and known limitations without claiming legal compliance solely from a technical region label.

Provider API credentials, service identities, client certificates, encryption keys, signing keys, and endpoint secrets shall be governed under Sections 3.4 and 3.5. Orchestration shall consume credentials through approved secret and key boundaries and shall not persist them in configuration files, prompts, logs, traces, model output, or Recommendation Envelopes.

Credentials shall be scoped by provider, environment, tenant or service boundary where required, allowed operations, network source, region, and lifetime. Shared unrestricted credentials are prohibited where narrower scope is supported or necessary.

Rotation and revocation shall be testable without uncontrolled outage or loss of evidence. Emergency credentials shall be separately governed, monitored, short-lived, and subject to post-event review. Provider offboarding requires credential revocation and independent verification that obsolete access paths are closed.
The orchestration layer shall define service objectives appropriate to each deployment and reasoning profile. Availability shall not be achieved through unsafe fallback.

The system shall distinguish provider availability, endpoint reachability, model responsiveness, schema-valid output, acceptable quality, and business-service availability. A route returning technically successful but invalid or degraded output is not healthy for the affected profile.

Availability metrics shall be segmented by route, profile, region, tenant class, and outcome where necessary. Aggregate availability shall not conceal repeated failure for a protected cohort or high-impact workload.

Observability shall support operational control without becoming an uncontrolled copy of customer prompts and outputs. Telemetry shall be minimized, classified, access-controlled, retained under schedule, and tenant-bound.

Sensitive request or response content shall be captured only through an approved diagnostic profile with purpose, access, redaction, retention, customer, and incident controls. Debug mode shall not be a permanent production state.
Provider telemetry shall be treated as an external signal. Critical measures such as usage, route identity, failure, and deletion may require independent corroboration.

Model behavior can change because of explicit versions, alias movement, provider configuration, safety policies, retrieval changes, adapter changes, infrastructure changes, or stochastic variation. The orchestrator shall monitor for material drift.

ilaten_requirement: Every Provider Profile, Model Route, Deployment Profile, Adapter, and Invocation Profile shall have a controlled lifecycle. The minimum model-route lifecycle may include Proposed, Under Assessment, Qualified for Limited Evaluation, Approved for Defined Use, Active, Restricted, Suspended, Deprecated, Withdrawn, and Retired.

Lifecycle state shall not compete with the product Release Lifecycle in Section 5.3. It governs internal route eligibility. Product release maturity remains Alpha, Beta, Release Candidate, or Stable under Section 4.10, and Long-Term Support remains a support designation.

State transitions shall identify the exact object, prior state, new state, scope, actor, authority, reason, conditions, effective time, affected profiles, and evidence. A mutable provider dashboard shall not be the sole authoritative lifecycle record.

Deprecation shall provide a migration path, impact assessment, customer and product communication, validation plan, and deadline. Withdrawal may be immediate when security, privacy, tenant, legal, contractual, quality, or continuity risk requires it. Retirement requires credential closure, route removal, record disposition, provider deletion evidence where applicable, and residual obligation ownership.
ILATEN shall prefer immutable or otherwise identifiable model versions. Where only a mutable alias is available, the route shall carry increased uncertainty and monitoring.
Alias governance shall define:
Changing a route from one model version to another is a controlled engineering and release event when behavior may materially change. It shall not be treated as ordinary infrastructure scaling.

Provider, model, adapter, route, configuration, schema, evaluation, fallback, and deployment changes shall follow Sections 4 and 5. The change record shall identify affected tenants, profiles, data, regions, capabilities, contracts, evaluation baselines, known risks, rollout, observation, rollback, support, and evidence.

Use within a Stable release shall bind to exact approved orchestration artifacts. A model or provider can be generally available while its ILATEN integration remains eligible only for an Alpha or Beta release, or while the applicable route remains Restricted, Suspended, or otherwise unsupported under its internal route lifecycle.

Rollout shall support bounded cohorts and route pinning. Moving a tenant to a new route shall preserve contract, region, data, assurance, and output semantics. Material differences require customer or competent authority involvement where applicable.

Rollback shall restore a qualified route and shall not reactivate revoked credentials, expired contracts, withdrawn models, or unsafe configurations. If no safe route remains, service restriction is preferable to uncontrolled substitution.
The orchestrator shall support:

Incident response shall not route protected work to an ineligible provider merely to restore availability. Recovery requires validation of current provider state, credentials, configuration, data handling, and route qualification.
Supply-chain controls shall include:
An adapter dependency shall not gain access to broader tenant data or credentials than necessary. Provider client software shall be treated as untrusted until reviewed and constrained.

Model provenance may be incomplete for externally supplied models. The limitation shall affect assurance, use-case eligibility, monitoring, and claims. ILATEN shall not claim knowledge of training data, safety properties, intellectual-property status, or model lineage that it cannot substantiate.

Provider independence requires operational exit capability, not merely an interface wrapper. Every material provider relationship shall have a Provider Exit Plan proportionate to concentration and business impact.
The plan shall address:
- customer consent, notification, or configuration where required;
Portability shall be tested. A theoretical adapter is insufficient if replacement cannot meet required quality, region, security, privacy, capacity, latency, or contract conditions.
Exit shall preserve the historical identity of prior routes and invocations. Migration does not rewrite the provider that processed an earlier request or the limitations applicable at that time.

Concentration risk arises when critical profiles depend on one provider, model family, region, identity system, network, or commercial relationship. The approved continuity strategy shall identify where concentration is accepted, mitigated, transferred, or prohibited.

Continuity testing shall not expose protected customer data or bypass normal control boundaries. Failover exercises shall validate policy eligibility, credentials, schemas, output quality, telemetry, audit, evidence, and rollback.

Enterprise customers may require control over provider allowlists, prohibited providers, dedicated endpoints, data regions, model families, retention, cost ceilings, or route transparency. Such controls shall be represented through approved tenant policy and configuration, not informal prompt instructions.
Transparency shall not disclose another tenant's information, provider confidential information, security-sensitive routing detail, secrets, or exploitable control configuration.
Governance shall assign accountable ownership for:

Separation of duties shall be proportionate to impact. High-impact provider onboarding, route approval, credential custody, production configuration, release, exception, and incident recovery shall not depend on one unreviewed action under the Enterprise Profile.

A registered Single-Maintainer Bootstrap Profile may temporarily combine provider research, adapter implementation, evaluation, configuration, and operational roles. The temporary state shall not be represented as independent provider assessment, two-person administration, dual control, or Enterprise separation of duties.
The bootstrap profile shall maintain:

Where lack of independent provider assurance, credential custody, route review, or continuity creates unacceptable risk, the affected route shall remain disabled, prerelease, non-production, or limited to synthetic and non-sensitive data.
Continued single-maintainer operation shall not become permanent through inaction. Enterprise Profile applicability requires the defined separation and continuity controls.
The following behaviors are prohibited:
- all model access passes through the governed abstraction;
- every route is represented by a versioned Provider Profile, Model Route, Deployment Profile, Adapter, Invocation Profile, and applicable Evaluation Baseline;
- eligibility is resolved before optimization;

The following invariants are binding:
- models and providers are replaceable implementation components, not architectural authorities;
- provider abstraction preserves material differences and does not manufacture equivalence;
- the deterministic Policy Engine controls route eligibility and remains outside the Intelligence Layer;
- orchestration selects only among already eligible routes and grants no business authority;
- technical availability never establishes eligibility, approval, validation, or acceptance;
- every Model Invocation is tenant-bound, purpose-bound, route-bound, versioned, attributable, resource-bounded, and auditable;
- provider-specific interfaces remain behind governed adapters;
- unverified prompt or retrieved content cannot select a provider, region, data policy, or credential path;
- mandatory security, privacy, tenant, region, contract, capability, and quality constraints are filters, not tradeable scores;
- cost and latency optimization occur only after mandatory constraints pass;
- fallback and retry never silently weaken assurance or expand data use;
- provider aliases and defaults do not become immutable ILATEN decisions;
- customer data is not used for unrelated training, evaluation, or provider improvement without approved governance and authority;
- tenant isolation applies across request, route, queue, cache, output, telemetry, evaluation, evidence, and deletion;
- provider and model changes follow controlled engineering, evaluation, change, and release processes;
- a provider contract, certification, or benchmark does not prove ILATEN product conformance;
- the Tool Gateway remains the controlled execution boundary;
- the Validation Pipeline remains independent from provider output and routing success;
- Audit Engine and Evidence Chain controls operate continuously across eligibility, selection, invocation, fallback, normalization, failure, incident, change, and retirement;
- provider exit capability is a required part of provider independence;
- bootstrap operation remains honest, constrained, temporary, and subject to dated exit criteria; and
- no model, provider, adapter, orchestrator, framework, customer preference, or sales commitment may weaken the Product Constitution, canonical architecture, or non-waivable controls.

A Model Orchestration and Provider Abstraction implementation is non-conformant if it integrates providers directly around the governed boundary; selects routes before deterministic eligibility; treats provider availability, price, latency, popularity, marketing, certification, or benchmark score as approval; permits a failed mandatory control to be offset by another score; silently routes protected data across providers, regions, tenants, or assurance profiles; accepts routing instructions from untrusted content; exposes provider credentials; uses mutable aliases without governance; allows fallback to weaken restrictions; hides semantic loss during normalization; treats correlated model outputs as independent validation; lets a model change routing, credentials, thresholds, or monitoring; adopts provider-side changes without assessment; uses customer data for unrelated training or evaluation; retains protected content indefinitely; bypasses tenant isolation; suppresses route or incident evidence; allows a temporary route to become permanent through inaction; represents integration as ready for inclusion in a Stable release without the required assurance; lacks a tested provider-exit path; or gives any model, provider, adapter, or orchestrator policy, approval, execution, validation, acceptance, or architectural authority.

Confidence is decision-support metadata. It is not truth, probability by default, permission, risk acceptance, approval, validation, compliance, correctness, execution authority, or evidence completeness. A high confidence result can be wrong, prohibited, harmful, stale, or outside authority. A low confidence result can still identify a serious risk, valid prohibition, or necessary escalation. Confidence shall therefore be interpreted only through its approved semantics and applicability profile.

Confidence Scoring shall not convert probabilistic output into deterministic authority. It shall make uncertainty more visible while preserving the canonical boundaries of the Policy Engine, Risk Classification Engine, Approval Engine, Tool Gateway, Validation Pipeline, Audit Engine, Evidence Chain, and accountable human authority.
The component shall not:

The deterministic Policy Engine may consume a confidence assessment only when policy defines the assessment type, scope, version, threshold semantics, freshness, and failure behavior. Policy may use a bounded advisory signal to require clarification, additional sources, stronger validation, human review, reduced capability, narrower scope, or denial. Confidence shall never independently create permission or waive a mandatory control.

These concepts shall not be collapsed. High confidence does not imply low risk. Low confidence does not imply high risk. A high-risk action may be supported by strong evidence and still require explicit approval, constrained capability, isolation, independent validation, and rollback. A low-risk informational output may have weak support and require qualification rather than prohibition.

Validation status is not an average of confidence dimensions. One failed mandatory validation rule cannot be offset by strong source quality, model consistency, or high historical performance. Confidence may inform which validation is required, but it cannot determine its own validation result.

Risk Classification may consume confidence as one bounded signal, especially where uncertainty increases exposure or review need. The Risk Classification Engine remains deterministic for its controlled inputs and cannot allow a favorable confidence score to reduce a non-waivable risk treatment.
Confidence Scoring shall:
The confidence domain shall distinguish the following objects:
- **Confidence Assessment Request:** the typed request defining subject, purpose, context, dimensions, profile, and required output;

These objects shall not be collapsed. A signal is not evidence merely because it is available. Evidence is not proof of correctness merely because it is recorded. A dimension is not a composite. A composite is not probability unless calibrated for that meaning. A threshold is not permission. A qualitative label is not portable across profiles unless the underlying semantics are equivalent.

Confidence shall attach to a clearly identified subject. An unrestricted score for an entire response is insufficient when the response contains materially different claims, assumptions, recommendations, and plan elements.
The system shall assess at the lowest granularity necessary for accountable use. Examples include:

Artifact-level confidence may summarize claim-level assessments only through an approved aggregation rule. It shall expose when one critical claim has materially weaker support than the aggregate. A high average shall not conceal a low-confidence prerequisite, safety condition, tenant boundary, legal assumption, or irreversible action.

The assessed subject shall be immutable or version-addressable. If the claim, recommendation, plan, source set, model route, context, or assessment method changes materially, a new Confidence Assessment is required.
Every material assessment shall begin with a typed Confidence Assessment Request containing or referencing, as applicable:
- required confidence dimensions;
- required output schema and explanation profile;
Narrative content shall not change the assessment profile, weights, threshold, scope, or downstream authority. An invalid or unverifiable request shall be rejected or returned for correction.

The assessment request grants no additional data access. Signals shall be obtained only through existing authorized context and data boundaries. Confidence Scoring shall not broaden retrieval merely to increase a score.
An approved assessment profile shall use dimensions appropriate to the subject and consequence. Potential dimensions include:
- **Context Completeness:** whether the authorized context contains the information required for the claim, including known gaps;
- **Source Integrity:** whether source authenticity, version, and integrity were verified to the required level;

No universal dimension set shall be forced onto every use case. Profiles shall select the dimensions that are material and shall explain exclusions. A dimension that cannot be assessed shall be marked unavailable, unknown, not applicable, or insufficient according to controlled semantics; it shall not silently receive a neutral or favorable score.
Every signal shall have a defined source, meaning, type, scope, time, provenance, reliability, and permitted use. Signals may originate from:

Provider-generated confidence, token probability, ranking score, self-evaluation, response consistency, or verbal certainty is one potential signal and shall not be treated as authoritative confidence by itself. Model self-confidence is particularly vulnerable to miscalibration and persuasive presentation.

Signals shall not be reused outside their validated scope. A model's strong performance in one language, domain, task, cohort, or output format shall not automatically transfer to another. A repository analyzer's deterministic result may strongly support a code fact but may be irrelevant to a legal conclusion or customer-impact estimate.

Duplicated signals shall not be counted as independent support. Multiple retrieved copies of the same source, multiple outputs derived from one provider lineage, or multiple metrics computed from one underlying observation require correlation treatment.
Confidence assessment shall consider supporting evidence and counterevidence. The system shall not select only sources favorable to the recommendation.
The Evidence Basis shall identify:

Material counterevidence shall reduce confidence, make the assessment inconclusive, or invalidate the profile according to controlled rules. It shall not be hidden through weighting, truncation, summarization, or selective retrieval.

The existence of an Evidence Chain record proves neither correctness nor completeness. Confidence assessment may consume chain-integrity status as one signal, but it shall independently consider whether relevant events and sources were captured.

ilaten_requirement: Confidence may be represented through a dimension vector, bounded numeric values, ordered categories, intervals, distributions, qualitative labels, or a combination appropriate to the use case. The representation shall have documented semantics.
A numeric value shall define:
- prohibited interpretations.

A number between zero and one shall not be called probability unless calibration and statistical interpretation support that claim. A percentage display shall not be used merely for visual familiarity.

A Composite Confidence value may be produced when a defined downstream process requires one bounded summary. The composite shall not replace its dimensions or evidence basis.
Aggregation rules shall:

Confidence communication shall be understandable to the intended audience without overstating certainty. Every displayed label shall be accompanied, directly or through an accessible detail view, by:
- prohibited interpretations;
- required review or validation; and

Interfaces shall not use color, placement, animation, or wording that manipulates reviewers into accepting a recommendation. A high score shall not be displayed as Approved, Safe, Compliant, Verified, or Guaranteed. A low score shall not be displayed as False unless the underlying evidence establishes falsity through an authoritative process.
Where a simplified interface is necessary, material limitations shall remain visible before approval. Disclosure after execution is insufficient.
A Calibration Profile shall identify:

Observed agreement between high confidence and successful outcomes may support calibration, but success definitions shall be independent of the score. The system shall not define success as acceptance of the recommendation if reviewers were influenced by the confidence display.
Calibration shall distinguish factual correctness, recommendation usefulness, plan feasibility, validation success, policy compliance, and business outcome. These are not interchangeable targets.
When adequate outcome data is unavailable, the system shall disclose that the score is heuristic, ordinal, or otherwise limited. It shall not imply probability.

Calibration evaluation shall use appropriate measures for the representation and consequence. It may examine reliability across score bands, overconfidence, underconfidence, discrimination, interval coverage, error costs, cohort differences, and stability over time.
Evaluation shall include:

Aggregate calibration shall not conceal a materially miscalibrated subgroup, language, task class, or high-impact scenario. Where performance differs, separate profiles, thresholds, warnings, or restrictions shall be used.

Calibration results shall not be optimized against the same hidden evaluation data repeatedly without controls against overfitting. Evaluation governance shall preserve dataset purpose, access, integrity, version, and independence.
Confidence thresholds are policy inputs that trigger defined treatment. They are not universal constants and shall not be chosen solely for convenience or automation rate.
A threshold record shall specify:
- required evidence and validation;

A threshold shall not grant permission. Passing a confidence threshold only satisfies the confidence condition defined by policy. All other policy, approval, capability, security, privacy, validation, and acceptance conditions remain required.

Threshold changes are controlled changes. Lowering a threshold to increase throughput, customer conversion, or automation requires evidence, risk review, authorization, testing, and monitoring. A temporary threshold shall expire and shall not become permanent through inaction.
The Policy Engine may consume a Confidence Assessment through a typed, versioned interface. The policy input shall include:

Policy shall reject an assessment that is stale, out of profile, bound to a different subject version, produced under an unapproved method, missing mandatory dimensions, or lacking required integrity.
Policy logic shall use explicit semantics. It shall not parse a natural-language explanation to infer a score or threshold result. Confidence output shall not include executable policy instructions.

The policy decision shall record whether confidence influenced routing, review, validation, denial, or capability restriction. This supports later calibration and governance without turning the confidence component into a policy authority.
Section 6.1 may request confidence assessment for material claims and recommendations. The reasoning engine shall not set its own authoritative confidence through verbal certainty or self-rating.

Context completeness means completeness for the defined subject and purpose, not possession of all potentially relevant data. Data minimization remains binding.

Knowledge Graph edges and nodes may carry provenance, confidence, temporal validity, and resolution state. Confidence Scoring shall distinguish verified graph facts, deterministic derivations, imported assertions, probabilistic relationships, and unresolved candidates.

Graph density, repeated paths, or number of supporting edges shall not automatically establish confidence. Multiple paths may depend on one source or circular inference. Assessment shall account for source independence and derivation lineage.

When a graph fact is corrected, revoked, merged, split, or expired, dependent Confidence Assessments shall be identified for review. The graph shall not rewrite historical assessments; it shall preserve temporal and version relationships.

Repository Intelligence produces facts and inferences about code, symbols, dependencies, ownership, change, tests, and evidence. Confidence Scoring shall preserve the distinction between deterministic analyzer results and probabilistic interpretation.
Repository state shall be bound to a commit, tree, artifact, or equivalent immutable identity. A score derived from one revision shall not be applied silently to another.

Missing language support, generated code, dynamic behavior, incomplete build context, ignored files, inaccessible dependencies, and parser errors shall reduce or invalidate affected dimensions rather than disappear from the aggregate.

Plan aggregation shall not hide a critical low-confidence dependency behind many routine high-confidence steps. Critical-path and irreversible elements may require minimum dimension thresholds or explicit human acknowledgment.

If execution or validation produces new evidence, the plan and affected Confidence Assessments shall be versioned. Historical scores shall not be rewritten to make the original plan appear better supported.

The Validation Pipeline may produce authoritative rule results that become signals for later Confidence Assessments. Confidence Scoring cannot determine the Validation Pipeline's pass, fail, blocked, error, waived, or inconclusive status.

Validation criteria shall not be derived after observing a favorable confidence score. A high score cannot waive a failed mandatory rule. A low score cannot convert a passing validation into failure unless policy separately defines a confidence-related requirement.
Outcome data from independent validation may support calibration. The calibration process shall preserve whether validation covered the exact claim, artifact, environment, and consequence.
The component used to generate a recommendation shall not be the sole source used to validate the confidence of that recommendation. Independence requirements shall be proportionate to consequence.
An override shall record:
- required follow-up and monitoring; and

Controls shall include typed inputs, subject digests, source provenance, integrity checks, profile versioning, access control, separation of duties, immutable or equivalently protected records, signal deduplication, correlation analysis, threshold protection, evaluation governance, change control, anomaly detection, and independent validation.

Calibration data shall not become an uncontrolled secondary-use dataset. Production outcomes may be used only under approved governance, contracts, privacy terms, minimization, access, and retention.

Where confidence contributes to qualifying automated decision-making or another legally protected process, applicable human intervention, explanation, contestation, and review safeguards shall be supported. Confidence Scoring does not determine legal applicability.

The Context Engine assembles the minimum authorized, relevant, attributable, and time-appropriate information required by an Intelligence Plane capability to perform a bounded task. It converts approved source records and the authoritative Immutable Context into a purpose-specific Context Package while preserving tenant, identity, scope, classification, source authority, provenance, temporal validity, confidence, and downstream-use restrictions.

The Context Engine is not the Immutable Context Manager. The Immutable Context is the authoritative task-level basis for policy, risk, approval, capability, execution, validation, and accountability. The Context Engine consumes that immutable basis and produces a governed projection for analysis. It shall not mutate, expand, reinterpret, or replace the authoritative context.

Context assembly is not unrestricted retrieval. The engine shall not maximize the amount of information presented to a model or downstream component. - **Untrusted Content Item:** source data that may be relevant but cannot modify instruction or control semantics;
- **Context Gap:** required information that is missing, unavailable, withheld, conflicted, stale, unsupported, or outside authority;

A cached item is not current merely because it exists. A summary is not the authoritative source. A Context Package is not an execution capability.

- permitted and prohibited source classes;

- Audit Engine and Evidence Chain controls operate continuously across request, basis, construction, revision, policy, risk, approval, capability, execution, validation, acceptance, delivery, closure, and review;
- bootstrap operation remains honest, constrained, temporary, and subject to dated exit criteria; and
- architecture-changing plan proposals require an authorized ADR and cannot modify canonical controls by their own force.

A Planning Engine implementation is non-conformant if it owns or advances authoritative task state; treats a plan as approval, capability, tool command, validation, acceptance, or release authority; mutates Immutable Context; expands tenant, target, repository, environment, destination, data, or capability scope; hides destructive or irreversible effects; embeds credentials or unrestricted commands; splits steps or uses branches, retries, fallbacks, compensation, or emergency labels to evade controls; changes approved material plan content without a new digest and reassessment; declares its own changes non-material; executes tools directly; removes mandatory validation; defines success after results; equates completion with acceptance; reuses template authority; creates indefinite replanning loops; bypasses Policy Engine, Risk Classification, Approval Engine, Identity and Capability Manager, Tool Gateway, Validation Pipeline, Audit Engine, Evidence Chain, privacy, security, tenant isolation, or human accountability; represents bootstrap self-review as independent assurance; retains protected data indefinitely; or gives any model, provider, framework, template, customer preference, sales commitment, or engineering convenience architectural authority.

ILATEN distinguishes learning from ordinary inference, context use, retrieval, memory, analytics, configuration, policy administration, software change, and release management. These mechanisms can affect future behavior in different ways, carry different risks, and require different controls. Describing all adaptation as learning would hide material changes in authority, data use, reversibility, validation, and accountability. Every learning mechanism shall therefore have an explicit type, purpose, scope, owner, data basis, assurance profile, release path, and rollback method.

The default production posture is no autonomous learning. A production request, response, approval, rejection, execution outcome, validation result, correction, customer comment, operator action, incident, or metric shall not automatically modify model weights, prompts, routing logic, confidence thresholds, retrieval sources, graph assertions, persistent memory, policies, capabilities, approval rules, validation requirements, or executable behavior. Any such modification is a governed change and must enter the applicable data, privacy, security, engineering, validation, change, and release processes.

Learning Boundaries do not create a new execution authority. They do not displace the Product Constitution, canonical architecture, deterministic Policy Engine, Approval Engine, Risk Classification Engine, Identity and Capability Manager, Tool Gateway, Validation Pipeline, Audit Engine, Evidence Chain, or accountable human decision-maker. Learning may propose improvement; it cannot authorize itself, deploy itself, validate itself, or declare itself safe.

The deterministic Policy Engine shall not learn policy from observed behavior. Policy is an approved, versioned, attributable, testable, reviewable, and auditable control artifact. A recurring approval, common operator choice, historical exception, model recommendation, customer preference, or successful execution does not become policy through repetition. Policy changes shall follow the applicable governance and change process, and an authorized Architecture Decision Record is required where the accepted change modifies architecture.

The Approval Engine shall not infer standing approval from prior approvals. The Identity and Capability Manager shall not expand authority because a capability was frequently requested or previously issued. The Tool Gateway shall not make a tool, action, destination, or parameter eligible because prior invocations succeeded. The Validation Pipeline shall not reduce mandatory checks because earlier outcomes passed. Audit and evidence controls shall not be sampled away merely because a pattern appears low risk.

No model, provider, dataset, training process, evaluation framework, optimization objective, learning metric, tool, customer instruction, sales commitment, or engineering preference has authority to supersede non-waivable controls. Applicable law and competent-authority requirements remain binding. Contracts are binding only within their lawful and formally approved scope and do not silently weaken the Product Constitution, canonical architecture, tenant isolation, security, privacy, safety, authorization, validation, audit, evidence, or human-accountability controls.

Learning Signals are advisory inputs. They shall not authorize or directly apply any change to a model, prompt, template, routing policy, context source, ranking method, Knowledge Graph, Repository Intelligence rule, Confidence Scoring method, Planning Profile, policy, capability, tool, validation rule, or production configuration. Every proposed learning change shall enter the applicable Development Lifecycle, Code Review Process, Quality Gates, Release Lifecycle, and Change Management process and shall receive deterministic policy evaluation, required human approval, independent validation, Audit Engine coverage, and Evidence Chain evidence before controlled promotion.
The Learning Boundaries shall:

**Learning Dataset.** A Learning Dataset is a governed collection of records approved for a stated learning purpose. It has defined provenance, ownership, lawful basis or other applicable authorization, tenant scope, permitted uses, exclusions, classification, retention, quality criteria, and access controls. A convenient collection of logs, prompts, responses, tickets, repository content, or telemetry is not a Learning Dataset until it has passed the required assessment.

**Evaluation Baseline.** An Evaluation Baseline is the approved reference against which a Candidate Artifact is assessed. It includes functional, safety, security, privacy, fairness, tenant-isolation, performance, reliability, explainability, evidence, and operational criteria appropriate to the use case. The baseline is versioned and cannot be changed after seeing candidate results merely to make the candidate pass.

**Correction and Unlearning Record.** A Correction and Unlearning Record tracks data correction, restriction, deletion, exclusion, re-indexing, re-training, artifact retirement, or another required remediation. It distinguishes deletion from source systems, exclusion from future datasets, removal from retrieval, invalidation of derived artifacts, and any technically substantiated model-unlearning action.

Every mechanism that can alter future output or behavior shall be classified before use. The classification determines data, validation, approval, release, monitoring, and rollback requirements. At minimum, ILATEN distinguishes:

Classification shall reflect actual effect rather than marketing terminology. Calling a persistent update memory, personalization, optimization, caching, tuning, or analytics does not avoid learning controls if the update can materially influence later behavior. Conversely, using retrieved authoritative data during a request does not mean that a model has learned that data.

Production learning is disabled by default. Runtime systems may capture approved Learning Signals and produce Learning Proposals, but they shall not autonomously change production behavior. The separation between observation and modification is a canonical safety boundary.

An automatic loop from production outcome to production behavior is prohibited unless a specifically approved learning profile defines the bounded mechanism, eligible data, safety envelope, rate limits, evaluation, monitoring, rollback, ownership, and release authority. Even under such a profile, the mechanism shall not modify policy, approval conditions, identity, capability, tenant scope, tool eligibility, validation obligations, evidence requirements, or human-accountability controls.

ILATEN shall not autonomously rewrite its Product Constitution, canonical architecture, policy, approval rules, capability semantics, tool permissions, validation criteria, Evidence Chain behavior, security controls, prompts, model routes, context rules, graph ontology, repository-analysis rules, confidence thresholds, or planning profiles. Observed outcomes may create an attributable Learning Proposal only. The proposal remains inert until it passes the applicable architecture, development, review, testing, release, and change-governance processes.

The absence of a detected incident does not establish that autonomous learning is safe. Historical success does not create approval for future adaptation. A model or metric that predicts improvement does not authorize a change. Operational urgency, cost pressure, provider deprecation, customer preference, or competitive pressure does not remove the required controls.

Feedback shall enter through approved channels that preserve attribution, tenant, purpose, integrity, and data classification. Free-form comments, support tickets, operator edits, acceptance decisions, validation results, and implicit behavior may have different meanings and shall not be collapsed into one undifferentiated reward signal.

Feedback normalization shall preserve source meaning. Positive and negative labels shall not be inferred from ambiguous behavior without documented semantics and validation. Aggregation shall not erase material minority outcomes, high-impact failures, protected-group effects, or tenant-specific differences. Duplicate, coordinated, automated, or anomalous feedback shall be detected and treated according to risk.

Feedback affecting safety, security, privacy, legal rights, tenant isolation, authorization, evidence, release, or production controls requires qualified review. Popularity, frequency, average rating, or short-term completion rate shall not override a severe but infrequent failure.

Where authoritative truth is unavailable, the record shall remain an attributed assertion or unresolved observation. Conflicting feedback shall remain visible until resolved or explicitly accepted as uncertainty. The system shall not silently choose the majority position where the minority may reveal safety, legal, privacy, security, accessibility, or tenant harm.

Human feedback is subject to expertise limits, inconsistency, bias, fatigue, incentives, and abuse. Automated feedback is subject to instrumentation errors, circular evaluation, distribution shift, and shared failure modes. Model-generated labels or synthetic examples are derivative evidence and shall be identified as such. A model shall not validate its own outputs using materially equivalent reasoning and then treat the result as independent truth.

Data shall be used for learning only when the use is authorized for the defined purpose and compatible with applicable law, contract, tenant configuration, notice, consent where required, and ILATEN policy. Access to data for service delivery does not automatically authorize use for training, provider improvement, benchmarking, generalized product improvement, or another tenant.

Customer, personal, employee, repository, prompt, output, telemetry, feedback, incident, and operational data shall not be reused for training, fine-tuning, evaluation, personalization, benchmarking, provider improvement, or cross-tenant learning merely because ILATEN processed it. Every use requires a defined purpose, documented role and applicability assessment, lawful and contractual authority, tenant scope, minimization, provenance, access control, retention and deletion treatment, security review, and customer control or consent where applicable.
The eligibility assessment shall identify:
- lawful basis, contractual authority, consent, notice, or other required authorization;

Ineligible records shall be excluded before a Learning Run. Redaction, masking, pseudonymization, anonymization, aggregation, or de-identification shall not be assumed sufficient merely because direct identifiers were removed. Linkability, rare combinations, model memorization, reconstruction, membership inference, and contextual re-identification shall be assessed.

Every material Learning Dataset shall have an accountable owner and a documented dataset specification. The specification defines intended use, prohibited use, source classes, tenant scope, temporal coverage, label semantics, sampling, exclusions, quality thresholds, known gaps, protected attributes where lawful and necessary for assessment, retention, refresh cadence, access, and disposition.

Dataset construction shall be reproducible. Selection queries, filters, transformations, redactions, label-generation methods, deduplication, sampling, split logic, and manual interventions shall be versioned and attributable. Undocumented spreadsheets, local exports, personal copies, support dumps, copied prompts, ad hoc log collections, or provider-held histories shall not serve as authoritative training data.

Training, validation, calibration, test, challenge, and holdout sets shall be separated according to the evaluation design. Leakage between these sets shall be assessed. Repeated evaluation against a fixed holdout can indirectly train the development process and shall trigger renewal or additional protected evaluation. Synthetic data shall be labeled, generated under approved conditions, and assessed for inherited bias, privacy leakage, implausibility, and reduced coverage of rare events.

Dataset quality shall be measured across completeness, accuracy, consistency, timeliness, provenance, duplication, label agreement, class balance, subgroup representation, contamination, and known error. Quality scores do not remove the need for risk-specific judgment. A large dataset is not necessarily representative, lawful, current, or safe.

Learning lineage shall connect the original source, Feedback Event, eligibility decision, transformation, Dataset Snapshot, Learning Run, Candidate Artifact, evaluation, approval, release, deployment, monitoring, rollback, and retirement records. Where lineage is incomplete, the limitation shall constrain use and claims.

Every derived artifact shall identify the source versions and processing steps that materially influenced it. Hashes and signatures can support integrity and identity but do not prove truth, lawful use, completeness, representativeness, or absence of manipulation. Provenance claims shall distinguish verified facts from provider declarations, operator assertions, inferred relationships, and unavailable information.

Provider-supplied models or datasets may have incomplete training lineage. ILATEN shall not claim knowledge of sources, rights, safety, bias, privacy properties, or deletion capability that it cannot substantiate. Unknown provenance shall affect eligibility, assurance, routing, customer disclosure, monitoring, and residual-risk acceptance.

Learning controls shall preserve tenant isolation across signals, datasets, prompts, responses, embeddings, indexes, graph assertions, memories, models, adapters, evaluations, telemetry, caches, artifacts, operators, and evidence. A tenant identifier in metadata is insufficient if storage, retrieval, training, batching, logging, or evaluation can mix content improperly.

Customer and tenant data shall not be used to improve a shared model, provider service, generalized feature, cross-tenant index, benchmark, or another tenant by default. Such use requires an explicit approved product profile, applicable legal and contractual authority, purpose transparency, tenant controls where required, data minimization, isolation analysis, re-identification assessment, security review, and documented accountability.

An opt-in shall be specific enough to identify the proposed use and consequences. Service acceptance, general terms, silence, historical participation, or a user interface default shall not be treated as universal permission. An opt-out mechanism does not cure a use that requires affirmative authorization under the applicable role or law.

Tenant-specific adaptation shall remain tenant-bound. Shared base models, libraries, or infrastructure shall not receive tenant-specific parameters or derived artifacts unless the approved architecture preserves isolation. A tenant-specific adapter shall not be selected for another tenant. Evaluation and observability shall test for cross-tenant retrieval, memorization, inference, and contamination.

Learning involving personal data or protected information shall follow privacy by design, data minimization, purpose limitation, access limitation, storage limitation, security, and accountability requirements. The processing role shall be determined for each purpose rather than assumed globally.
