ilaten_requirement: Code suggestions, review outcomes, defect history, incident lessons, test results, and operational metrics may inform Learning Proposals. They shall not create a loop that rewards changes merely because they are easy to merge, reduce visible alerts, increase throughput, or match historical patterns. Security, privacy, evidence, maintainability, and long-term risk shall remain represented in evaluation.

Repository content can include secrets, personal data, proprietary code, third-party material, licenses, vulnerabilities, and customer-specific configuration. Eligibility for service delivery does not establish eligibility for training. Generated code and synthetic tests shall preserve provenance and shall not be treated as independently authored or independently validated.

Calibration datasets shall match the intended domain and shall preserve subgroup, tenant, task, model, provider, language, and temporal distinctions where material. A global average can conceal severe local miscalibration. Calibration changes shall be evaluated for false confidence, under-confidence, selective abstention, escalation load, downstream behavior, and distribution shift.

Policy, approval, capability, validation, or acceptance shall not be weakened merely because a calibrated score improved. A threshold change that affects control behavior is a controlled configuration or policy change, not a harmless statistical update. The Confidence Scoring component shall not use its own score as the sole evidence that recalibration succeeded.

Planning outcomes may identify useful patterns in decomposition, dependency ordering, validation placement, rollback design, estimation, and failure handling. Those patterns can inform template or heuristic candidates but cannot become standing approval or executable authority.

A successful plan does not prove that every step was necessary, safe, efficient, or causally responsible for success. A failed plan does not prove that its planning approach was wrong if execution, tools, data, or external conditions failed. Learning analysis shall preserve these causal limitations.

Planning templates remain inert. Historical approval of a similar plan does not approve a new plan. A learned heuristic shall not omit identity, context, policy, risk, approval, capability, Tool Gateway, Validation Pipeline, Audit Engine, or Evidence Chain stages. It shall not hide destructive effects, split actions to evade thresholds, or classify its own changes as non-material.

Model adaptation includes parameter training, fine-tuning, adapters, preference optimization, distillation, prompt tuning, embedding changes, or any process that materially changes model behavior through learned parameters. Each adaptation shall begin with an approved Learning Proposal and shall produce a new versioned Candidate Artifact.

The proposal shall define the intended behavior, prohibited behavior, eligible domains, training sources, evaluation baseline, safety constraints, expected limitations, computational environment, reproducibility requirements, rollback, monitoring, and retirement. It shall identify whether the artifact can memorize sensitive content, reproduce training examples, change language or subgroup performance, alter refusal behavior, or increase harmful capability.

Training completion, loss reduction, benchmark improvement, user preference, or provider recommendation does not establish release readiness. Candidate Artifacts shall pass independent or organizationally separated evaluation appropriate to risk. Qualified external review shall be completed before an affected high-impact Candidate Artifact influences a Stable release, production environment, customer-controlled production deployment, or Enterprise operating profile; otherwise it shall remain blocked, prerelease, non-production, advisory-only, or constrained through formal risk treatment.

Adaptation shall not silently change the assurance profile. If a model is modified, previous provider certifications, evaluations, safety claims, or compatibility results may no longer apply. The changed artifact shall be re-evaluated for its actual scope. A fine-tuned model remains replaceable and shall not become an architectural dependency merely because substantial training investment has occurred.

Online or continual learning introduces elevated risk because operational data can alter future behavior before complete offline evaluation. It is prohibited by default for production decision, action, policy, approval, capability, security, privacy, tenant, evidence, and safety functions.
Where an approved product requirement justifies a bounded online-learning mechanism, the profile shall define:

Online adaptation shall not learn from an event that it caused without accounting for feedback-loop and selection effects. It shall not optimize solely for engagement, acceptance, completion, cost, latency, or another proxy that can be improved by hiding uncertainty, avoiding escalation, weakening validation, or selecting easier tasks.

If safe suspension or rollback cannot be demonstrated, the mechanism is ineligible for production. Where individual updates cannot be attributed and reproduced, the system shall not claim enterprise-grade controlled learning.

An optimization objective is a design choice, not an objective truth. Every reward, preference, ranking, or success metric shall have an owner, rationale, scope, known proxies, prohibited trade-offs, and review cadence.

Learning shall be assessed for reward hacking, specification gaming, shortcut learning, hidden-state exploitation, evaluator manipulation, sycophancy, approval seeking, alert suppression, selective reporting, and other behavior that improves a measured objective without improving the intended outcome. A system shall not receive favorable reward for bypassing controls, reducing audit detail, avoiding difficult cases, overstating confidence, or persuading reviewers to accept unsafe output.

Composite objectives shall preserve non-waivable constraints. Security, privacy, tenant isolation, authorization, validation, evidence, and human accountability are not ordinary weighted preferences that may be traded away for aggregate score improvement. A candidate that violates a protected control fails regardless of average performance.

Learning processes expand the attack surface across feedback channels, data ingestion, labeling, transformation, training, evaluation, artifact storage, provider interfaces, deployment, and monitoring. Threat modeling shall include poisoning, backdoors, trigger insertion, label manipulation, gradient or parameter attacks where applicable, model extraction, membership inference, inversion, data exfiltration, supply-chain compromise, evaluation contamination, provenance forgery, and insider misuse.

Data sources shall have trust classification and integrity controls. High-volume or privileged sources shall not be assumed trustworthy. Rate limits, anomaly detection, source diversity, sampling review, quarantine, provenance verification, and challenge datasets shall be applied according to risk. A single customer, operator, provider, or automated source shall not be able to dominate a shared learning process silently.

Learning environments shall be isolated from production authority. Training code, dependencies, images, datasets, artifacts, credentials, and provider endpoints shall follow secure supply-chain and secrets-management standards. A Learning Run shall receive only the minimum access and time-bound capability required. Candidate Artifacts shall be scanned, signed or otherwise integrity-protected, registered, and promoted through controlled paths.

Security findings in a candidate, dataset, or learning system shall trigger containment and the applicable Defect, Incident, Change, and Release processes. A suspected poisoning event shall preserve evidence and may require invalidating downstream artifacts, not merely deleting the suspected source record.

Evaluation shall test the intended benefit and plausible harm. It shall include representative normal cases, difficult cases, boundary cases, adversarial cases, rare high-impact events, unavailable dependencies, ambiguous input, conflicting context, stale data, and attempts to bypass controls.

Evaluation dimensions shall be selected according to the use case and can include correctness, groundedness, completeness, calibration, abstention, security, privacy, safety, fairness, accessibility, robustness, reproducibility, latency, cost, reliability, tenant isolation, evidence quality, explainability, operator workload, and recovery. No single aggregate metric proves suitability.

The evaluator shall be sufficiently independent of the candidate and its optimization loop. Using the same model family, prompt, provider, data, or reasoning path for generation and judgment can create correlated failure and shall be disclosed. Automated evaluation supports scale but does not eliminate qualified human or domain review where impact requires it.

Acceptance criteria and regression limits shall be defined before final candidate results are inspected. Post hoc changes require documented justification and renewed review. Passing an evaluation establishes only that the candidate met the defined criteria under the evaluated conditions. It does not prove universal safety, legal compliance, absence of bias, or future performance.

Approved artifacts shall be monitored for data drift, concept drift, model drift, provider change, calibration drift, retrieval drift, ontology drift, behavior regression, subgroup harm, security abuse, privacy leakage, tenant contamination, and operational degradation. Monitoring shall distinguish input distribution change from output quality change and infrastructure failure from model behavior.

Thresholds shall trigger investigation, restriction, fallback, suspension, rollback, re-evaluation, or retirement according to risk. A monitoring threshold is not a silent permission to retrain or relax controls. Unknown drift shall reduce assurance rather than be normalized as expected behavior.

Provider model updates, undocumented provider changes, new regions, changed moderation behavior, changed retention terms, new tool integrations, dependency updates, and material context-source changes can invalidate prior evaluation. The Model Orchestration and Provider Abstraction component shall detect or receive such changes where feasible and route them through change and requalification processes.

The change record shall identify affected models, prompts, policies, thresholds, routes, indexes, graphs, memories, datasets, tenants, environments, interfaces, controls, evaluations, evidence, rollback, and customer commitments. If the change affects canonical architecture, an authorized ADR is required before implementation proceeds.

Alpha, Beta, Release Candidate, and Stable remain release-maturity attributes. Long-Term Support is a support designation applied to a qualifying Stable release or support line, not a learning maturity. Experimental improvement shall not be represented as eligible for inclusion in a Stable release or as Enterprise-ready without the required assurance.

Promotion shall be explicit and environment-bound. A candidate approved for offline evaluation is not approved for shadow use, limited tenant use, production, general availability, or provider training. Shadow evaluation still processes real data and requires data, privacy, tenant, security, and operational authorization.

Every material learning-derived artifact shall have a tested rollback or safe-disable mechanism appropriate to impact. Rollback shall restore the prior artifact and its compatible configuration, routing, index, schema, thresholds, and dependencies. Restoring model weights while retaining an incompatible prompt, index, or calibration does not constitute complete rollback.

Reproducibility requirements shall be proportionate to risk. The organization shall retain enough approved metadata, code, configuration, dataset references, seeds where relevant, provider version information, environment details, and evidence to explain how a candidate was produced and evaluated. Where a provider prevents exact reproduction, the limitation shall be recorded and shall affect assurance and eligibility.

Artifacts shall have suspension and retirement states. Retirement includes removal from routing, revocation of deployment eligibility, disposition of copies, preservation of required evidence, update of dependent references, and customer or operator communication where applicable. An artifact shall not remain selectable merely because deleting it is operationally inconvenient.

Data correction or deletion shall propagate through governed source, dataset, index, graph, memory, cache, evaluation, and artifact lineage according to the applicable role and obligation. The response shall distinguish what has actually been corrected, deleted, excluded, invalidated, retired, retrained, or made inaccessible.

Deleting a source record does not necessarily remove its influence from an already trained model. ILATEN shall not claim complete machine unlearning unless the method, scope, verification, and residual limitations are substantiated. Where exact unlearning is unavailable or unreliable, the response may require dataset exclusion, artifact retirement, retraining from an eligible snapshot, output filtering, use restriction, tenant-specific replacement, or another approved risk treatment.

Correction and deletion requests shall not be rejected solely because lineage is operationally complex. The architecture shall maintain sufficient lineage to support reasonable action. Conflicting legal holds, evidence preservation, security investigation, and privacy requirements shall be resolved through authorized, documented, narrowly scoped decisions.

Named accountable roles shall govern learning purpose, data, security, privacy, domain validity, evaluation, release, and operation. One role may perform multiple activities only where the approved operating profile permits it and the absence of independence is recorded.

Human review shall focus on decision quality, not ceremonial approval. Reviewers shall receive the proposal, data basis, provenance, evaluation design, results, failures, subgroup effects, limitations, residual risk, rollback, monitoring, and dissent necessary to decide. Material information shall not be hidden behind an aggregate score or model-generated summary.

Approval is scope-bound, version-bound, environment-bound, tenant-bound where applicable, time-bound where required, and revocable. Approval of a dataset does not approve every future use. Approval of a Learning Run does not approve its Candidate Artifact. Approval of a candidate for testing does not approve release. Prior approval does not transfer automatically to a new model, provider, dataset, purpose, tenant, or jurisdiction.

The bootstrap profile shall not be represented as independent data review, independent model validation, two-person control, Enterprise segregation of duties, or external assurance. Qualified external review shall be completed before an affected high-impact learning-derived artifact influences a Stable release, production environment, customer-controlled production deployment, or Enterprise operating profile; otherwise it shall remain blocked, prerelease, non-production, advisory-only, or constrained through formal risk treatment.

The profile cannot waive tenant isolation, data eligibility, privacy, security, authorization, Tool Gateway, Validation Pipeline, Audit Engine, Evidence Chain, rollback, or non-autonomous-learning controls. Highest-risk data or adaptation activities shall use independently governed services or remain outside the bootstrap scope where one-person operation would create unacceptable risk.

The exit plan shall identify the second competent administrator or reviewer capabilities, separation of duties, external review requirements, access transition, recovery, evidence, and target date. Continued single-maintainer operation shall not become permanent through inaction.

Material evidence shall cover signal capture, feedback attribution, data eligibility, consent or other authorization where applicable, dataset construction, transformations, access, labeling, snapshot creation, proposal, risk assessment, Learning Run, artifact registration, evaluation, approval, release, deployment, monitoring, incident, rollback, correction, deletion, unlearning action, and retirement.

Evidence shall preserve event identity, tenant, actor, service identity, time, version, purpose, affected objects, input and output references, decision, authority, reason, policy version, risk classification, approval, integrity state, and relationship to preceding and succeeding events. Sensitive evidence shall follow classification, minimization, access, retention, and disclosure controls.

Cryptographic linkage can support tamper evidence but does not prove that every required event was captured, that source data was true, that consent was valid, or that an evaluation was independent. Evidence completeness, semantic validity, coverage, and custody shall be validated separately.

A governed learning initiative shall use explicit states sufficient to distinguish at least proposed, data assessment, blocked, approved for preparation, dataset prepared, run authorized, run completed, evaluation, rejected, approved for constrained testing, release candidate, deployed under observation, accepted, suspended, rolled back, superseded, and retired. Display labels may differ only when an approved mapping preserves state and transition semantics.

Failure shall be fail-safe. Missing provenance, unresolved tenant scope, ineligible data, invalid approval, failed integrity, incomplete evaluation, absent rollback, unknown provider change, material regression, suspected poisoning, or evidence gap shall block progression or reduce the candidate to an explicitly constrained state.

Retries shall not create duplicate labels, conflicting dataset snapshots, uncontrolled provider disclosure, repeated charging without limits, or multiple artifacts with ambiguous identity. Partial runs and failed artifacts shall be quarantined and shall not become eligible through a later successful step without a complete, attributable decision.

Emergency processes may suspend, disable, roll back, or constrain a harmful artifact. They shall not establish a permanent shortcut for training, evaluation, approval, or release. Deferred analysis, evidence completion, correction, and preventive action remain required.
Learning-related Quality Gates shall be defined according to risk and can include:
- approved purpose, owner, and Learning Proposal;
- complete role, legal, contractual, privacy, tenant, and data-eligibility assessment;
- reproducible Dataset Snapshot and lineage;
- secrets, sensitive-data, licensing, and contamination checks;
- threat model and poisoning controls;
- approved evaluation baseline and protected holdout;
- functional, safety, security, privacy, fairness, robustness, calibration, and tenant-isolation evaluation;
- independent review appropriate to impact;
- signed or integrity-protected Candidate Artifact and registry record;
- tested rollback and safe-disable path;
- approved release, deployment, monitoring, and incident plan;
- complete audit and evidence coverage; and
- explicit residual-risk acceptance by competent authority.

A gate shall fail when its evidence is missing, stale, mismatched, unverifiable, or outside scope. A model-generated explanation, provider benchmark, customer request, schedule deadline, or successful demonstration shall not substitute for a required gate.
The following practices are prohibited:
- autonomous production learning without an explicitly approved bounded profile;
- treating feedback, approval, repetition, popularity, or model output as verified truth;
- learning policy, authority, capability, approval, validation, or evidence requirements from observed behavior;
- using customer or tenant data for shared improvement by default;
- cross-tenant training, retrieval, memory, indexing, graph propagation, or adapter selection without explicit lawful governance;
- provider training or retention outside the approved data-destination profile;
- training on secrets, active credentials, private keys, capabilities, or unsanitized restricted security data;
- using undocumented logs, exports, tickets, copied prompts, or local files as an authoritative dataset;
- changing evaluation criteria after results solely to obtain a pass;
- evaluating a candidate only with materially equivalent models, data, prompts, or reasoning while claiming independence;
- optimizing a proxy in a manner that weakens protected controls or hides harm;
- silently changing model, provider, route, prompt, threshold, index, graph, memory, or learned parameter in production;
- deploying a candidate because training completed or an aggregate metric improved;
- representing deletion from a source or index as verified model unlearning;
- retaining learning data indefinitely by default;
- using historical approval as standing approval for new learning scope;
- allowing an online learner to alter its own safety envelope, monitoring, rollback, or suspension criteria;
- allowing learning components to invoke tools outside the Tool Gateway;
- allowing learning results to self-validate, self-approve, self-release, or self-accept;
- representing bootstrap self-review as independent assurance; and
- giving a model, provider, framework, dataset, metric, customer preference, sales commitment, or engineering convenience architectural authority.

Learning Boundaries do not require ILATEN to train a proprietary foundation model, retain customer interactions for improvement, implement online learning, maintain universal memory, create a shared cross-tenant dataset, or promise complete unlearning where it cannot be substantiated.

They do not define domain truth, replace qualified legal or privacy assessment, certify fairness, eliminate the need for human accountability, or make probabilistic behavior deterministic. They do not treat every software configuration change as model training, and they do not prohibit controlled improvement that follows the required governance.
- production operates with no autonomous learning by default;
- every mechanism affecting future behavior has an explicit classification and control profile;
- Learning Signals, Feedback Events, Ground Truth, Learning Proposals, datasets, runs, artifacts, evaluations, approvals, releases, and acceptance remain distinct;
- feedback is attributed and is not treated automatically as truth;
- data use is purpose-bound, role-aware, lawful, contractually authorized, tenant-scoped, minimized, and retention-controlled;
- customer data is not used for provider, shared-model, or cross-tenant improvement by default;
- dataset construction and transformations are reproducible and evidence-bearing;
- model, provider, prompt, route, threshold, index, graph, memory, and parameter changes are versioned and governed;
- the deterministic Policy Engine does not learn policy from operational behavior;
- prior approval does not become standing authorization;
- learning cannot expand tenant, data, identity, capability, tool, destination, or execution scope;
- evaluation is defined before final result inspection and is sufficiently independent for the risk;
- protected controls cannot be traded away for aggregate metric improvement;

- qualified external review is completed before an affected high-impact Candidate Artifact influences a Stable release, production environment, customer-controlled production deployment, or Enterprise operating profile, with the artifact otherwise remaining blocked, prerelease, non-production, advisory-only, or constrained;
- online or continual learning, if approved, is bounded, reversible, monitored, attributable, and isolated from authority;
- Tool Gateway remains the only controlled execution path;
- Validation Pipeline remains independent of the learning candidate;
- rollback, safe disable, correction, deletion, and retirement are operationally defined;
- unlearning claims are limited to technically substantiated scope;
- bootstrap limitations remain explicit, temporary, constrained, and subject to dated exit criteria;
- Audit Engine and Evidence Chain controls operate continuously across all material learning events; and
- learning-derived architecture changes require authorized ADR governance.
The following invariants are binding:
- operational experience does not silently modify production behavior;
- feedback is an assertion or observation until verified under an appropriate authority model;
- learning may propose change but cannot authorize, execute, validate, release, or accept itself;
- policy is deterministic, versioned, approved, and never learned automatically from behavior;
- prior approval, successful execution, or repeated use does not create standing authority;
- customer and tenant data are not shared learning material by default;
- tenant isolation applies to signals, datasets, models, adapters, indexes, graphs, memories, evaluation, telemetry, artifacts, and evidence;
- access for service delivery is not authorization for training or generalized improvement;
- removing data from retrieval is not proof of model unlearning;
- aggregate performance cannot override security, privacy, safety, tenant isolation, authorization, validation, evidence, or human accountability;
- every material learning-derived artifact is versioned, evaluated, reviewable, releasable through controlled paths, reversible, and retireable;
- online learning is prohibited by default and, where exceptionally approved, cannot alter its own boundaries or authoritative controls;
- model and provider outputs remain non-authoritative;
- Tool Gateway remains the controlled execution boundary;
- Validation Pipeline remains independent;
- Audit Engine and Evidence Chain operate continuously from signal capture through correction, rollback, and retirement;
- retention follows approved record-class-specific schedules and is not indefinite by default;
- bootstrap operation does not imply independent assurance and cannot waive non-waivable controls; and
- architecture-changing learning proposals require an authorized ADR and cannot modify canonical architecture by their own force.

A Learning Boundaries implementation is non-conformant if it allows production interactions or feedback to change behavior without governed classification, evidence, evaluation, approval, versioning, and rollback; treats feedback, popularity, model confidence, or historical approval as truth or authority; learns policy, permissions, capabilities, approvals, validation requirements, or tenant scope from behavior; uses customer data for provider, shared, or cross-tenant improvement by default; mixes tenant signals, datasets, memories, indexes, graphs, models, adapters, telemetry, or evidence; trains on secrets or ineligible protected information; permits poisoning or provenance gaps to pass silently; changes evaluation criteria to fit results; deploys because a metric improved; allows an artifact to validate, approve, release, or accept itself; uses online learning without a bounded approved profile; allows an online learner to modify its own safety envelope; makes unsupported unlearning or privacy claims; executes tools outside the Tool Gateway; bypasses the deterministic Policy Engine, Approval Engine, Risk Classification Engine, Identity and Capability Manager, Validation Pipeline, Audit Engine, Evidence Chain, tenant isolation, security, privacy, or human accountability; represents bootstrap self-review as independent assurance; retains protected learning data indefinitely; or gives any model, provider, framework, dataset, metric, customer preference, sales commitment, or engineering convenience architectural authority.

The cloud architecture exists to provide a secure and resilient substrate for ILATEN. It does not create a new source of policy, approval, capability, execution, validation, acceptance, audit, evidence, or architectural authority. Infrastructure may enforce canonical decisions, isolate workloads, preserve state, and expose verified operating conditions. It shall not decide that a business action is permitted merely because a resource can execute it.

Every supported cloud implementation shall preserve the canonical operational flow: verified request intake; identity, tenant, and integrity validation; Immutable Context creation; preparation of a non-authoritative plan or recommendation; deterministic policy and capability evaluation; risk classification; explicit human approval where required; issuance of constrained execution authority; isolated execution through the Tool Gateway; independent assessment by the Validation Pipeline; acceptance or rejection; and controlled delivery, closure, and review. Audit Engine and Evidence Chain controls operate continuously across all material stages.

This section defines the common cloud architecture. Section 7.2 defines supported Deployment Models and their shared-responsibility profiles. Sections 7.3 and 7.4 define container orchestration and container strategy where those mechanisms are used. Sections 7.5 through 7.10 define storage, networking, scalability, observability, monitoring, and logging in greater detail. Those sections may specialize this architecture but shall not create a competing trust model.

ILATEN adopts a deployment-neutral and technology-agnostic cloud posture. Logical responsibilities are stable; physical products and placement may vary. The architecture shall support provider substitution and deployment evolution where product scope justifies them, but portability shall be demonstrated rather than assumed.

The architecture does not require every supported environment to use identical provider-native mechanisms. It requires equivalent canonical outcomes and documented differences. A control demonstrated in an ILATEN-managed hosted environment shall not be assumed effective in a customer-controlled, hybrid, isolated, or differently regulated environment.
The Cloud Architecture shall:

**Control Domain.** The set of components and records that participate in a particular canonical authority function, such as policy, approval, capability, execution mediation, validation, or evidence. A Control Domain may cross physical services but shall preserve single semantic ownership.
Cloud placement shall preserve the logical planes defined in Section 2. Physical consolidation does not merge authority, and physical distribution does not create a new authority path.

The Experience Layer provides controlled user, operator, reviewer, and integration surfaces. It shall connect through the Secure Access Layer and shall not receive direct administrative, execution, data-store, or Trust Core authority merely because it is hosted within the same cloud environment.

The Control Plane owns authoritative task progression, Immutable Context, deterministic policy, risk treatment, accountable approval, capability issuance, Model Gateway access, and Tool Gateway mediation. Control Plane state shall have explicit ownership, consistency, durability, and failover semantics. Infrastructure controllers shall not mutate business authority directly.

The Execution Plane performs only separately authorized operations in restricted workers. Execution placement shall minimize access, isolate tenants and tasks according to risk, prevent direct Control Plane mutation, and return results through controlled channels. Workers shall not possess standing authority merely because they are part of an approved cluster or account.

The Validation Pipeline independently assesses results against pre-established criteria. It shall not depend solely on the execution worker, deployment system, model, or component under validation to declare success. Shared infrastructure may be used only when logical and access separation preserve independence appropriate to the risk.

The Trust and Evidence Plane records and binds material events across the lifecycle. Its availability, ordering, integrity, custody, retention, and recovery requirements shall reflect the assurance profile. It is not replaced by provider activity logs or general observability telemetry.

The Cloud Estate shall use explicit organizational and administrative boundaries. Accounts, subscriptions, projects, folders, resource groups, namespaces, or equivalent constructs shall be assigned stable identity, owner, purpose, environment, tenant scope, region, lifecycle, billing responsibility, and security profile.

Production, non-production, security, evidence, recovery, and shared-service responsibilities shall be separated according to risk. Naming alone does not establish separation. Effective identity, network, key, storage, deployment, logging, recovery, and administrator boundaries shall be verified.

Administrative access shall be least-privilege, strongly authenticated, attributable, time-bound where appropriate, and logged. Ordinary administration shall use individual human identities or verified workload identities rather than shared accounts. Privileged actions shall use controlled elevation, approval where required, session limitation, monitoring, and post-action review.

Break-glass administration shall be separately governed. It requires protected recovery factors, explicit activation criteria, short validity, narrow scope, monitoring, evidence, and mandatory retrospective review. Emergency access does not provide a standing bypass around policy, evidence, customer, privacy, or change requirements.

Provider root, owner, billing, domain, and recovery identities require enhanced protection. They shall not be used for ordinary operation. Account recovery and organizational ownership shall remain recoverable without creating an undocumented personal dependency.

Every Environment shall have a stable identity and an approved specification. The specification identifies purpose, owner, permitted release maturity, tenants, data classes, region, network, dependencies, model routes, tools, capabilities, configuration source, keys, secrets, observation, support, recovery, and retirement.

Development, test, evaluation, staging, recovery, and production environments shall be separated according to risk. Data, identity, keys, capabilities, endpoints, domains, provider accounts, and administrative paths shall not cross environments silently. Production credentials and customer data shall not be copied into non-production merely for convenience.

Environment promotion is not a file copy. It is a controlled authorization decision binding an exact artifact set, configuration, policy, schema, infrastructure definition, region, tenant cohort, change record, validation evidence, and rollback plan to a target environment.

Long-lived shared environments shall not become an uncontrolled accumulation of exceptions. Temporary resources, experiments, previews, and diagnostic modes require owner, expiry, allowed data, access, cost, monitoring, and cleanup. Expiry shall be enforced or escalated rather than left to informal memory.

A tenant identifier attached to a shared record is insufficient if authorization, encryption, routing, caching, query construction, operational access, recovery, or deletion can cross the boundary. Isolation shall be enforced at multiple appropriate layers and tested under normal, failure, migration, support, backup, restore, and incident conditions.

The architecture may support shared and dedicated infrastructure patterns where the Deployment Model permits them. Shared infrastructure shall maintain logical isolation, capacity fairness, noisy-neighbor protection, cryptographic separation where required, tenant-aware observability, and tenant-scoped recovery and deletion. Dedicated infrastructure shall not be represented as secure merely because resources are physically separate; identity, configuration, keys, management access, monitoring, and support paths remain material.

Tenant creation, suspension, migration, export, deletion, and closure are governed lifecycle events. Resource cleanup shall address live data, replicas, caches, indexes, queues, backups, temporary workers, provider-held data, telemetry, support artifacts, and evidence according to applicable retention and legal obligations.

Cross-tenant analytics or shared operational views shall use minimized, approved dimensions and shall not expose protected content, sensitive counts, timing, error differences, or identifiers. Aggregate visibility shall not create a covert cross-tenant inference channel.

Cloud identity shall follow Zero Trust principles. Network address, account membership, cluster membership, workload location, provider-managed status, or prior successful access does not establish current authority.

Human identities shall be federated with approved enterprise identity sources where supported and shall preserve tenant, role, authentication assurance, session, device, and risk context. Local identities shall be constrained, inventoried, justified, and reviewed.

Workload identities shall be unique to the service, environment, and purpose at an appropriate granularity. Short-lived credentials and identity-based access are preferred over embedded or broadly reusable secrets. Identity issuance, rotation, revocation, audience, subject, scope, and proof shall be verifiable.

Service-to-service communication shall authenticate both endpoints where risk requires it and shall authorize the specific action and resource. Mutual authentication does not replace business policy or capability validation. A service identity permitted to connect is not automatically permitted to perform every exposed operation.

Identity failure shall fail safely. When identity, federation, revocation, time, or authorization dependencies are unavailable or inconsistent, protected operation shall be denied, delayed, or constrained according to policy. Cached identity state shall have explicit freshness and revocation semantics.

Cloud networking shall implement explicit trust zones and controlled flows. Public, user-facing, administrative, Control Plane, intelligence, execution, validation, data, evidence, build, recovery, and provider-integration paths shall be separated according to risk.

Network policy shall be deny-by-default or equivalently restrictive for protected paths. Permitted flows shall define source identity, destination identity, protocol, port or interface, purpose, environment, tenant or service scope, data class, direction, inspection, logging, and expiry where appropriate.

Outbound access is a security and data-governance boundary. Workloads shall reach only approved model providers, tools, repositories, package sources, enterprise systems, update services, and operational destinations. Domain or address allowlisting alone may be insufficient where provider infrastructure is shared or mutable; destination identity and data-use eligibility shall be evaluated.

Inbound administrative access shall use controlled management paths rather than exposing ordinary workload interfaces. Remote support and customer access shall be tenant-bound, time-bound, attributable, monitored, and restricted to approved purposes.

Network segmentation is defense in depth, not the sole authorization mechanism. A component inside a private network shall still validate identity, tenant, request integrity, capability, schema, and current authority. An internet-accessible endpoint is not inherently non-conformant when equivalent controls and approved exposure exist.

Compute shall be selected and configured according to workload type, trust boundary, state, latency, scale, isolation, recovery, and operational responsibility. ILATEN may use long-running services, event-driven workers, scheduled processes, restricted execution workers, device-bound components, or other qualified compute forms without changing canonical semantics.

Services shall have explicit ownership, interface, identity, dependency, resource limits, scaling policy, lifecycle, health model, data access, failure behavior, observability, support, and retirement. A provider service shall not become a canonical component merely because implementation is convenient.

Control Plane services require predictable state and failure semantics. Horizontal replication or distribution shall not create competing authority, duplicate approvals, duplicate capability issuance, or conflicting task progression. Coordination shall preserve idempotency, ordering, fencing, lease, version, or equivalent controls appropriate to the state transition.

Statelessness shall not be claimed when material state exists in queues, caches, provider sessions, local files, model conversations, deployment controllers, or external systems. State ownership and recovery shall be explicit even when compute instances are disposable.

Containerized and orchestrated compute may be used, but this section does not mandate it. Container orchestration and container-image controls are defined in Sections 7.3 and 7.4. Equivalent controls are required for non-container compute.

Execution is isolated from reasoning, approval, and validation. Every governed tool action shall enter through the Tool Gateway with an active, task-bound, tenant-bound, target-bound, least-privilege, time-bound capability. Cloud infrastructure shall not create an alternate execution path.

Restricted workers shall receive only the approved code, input, filesystem paths, network destinations, tools, environment values, compute resources, credentials, and duration. They shall not receive cloud administrative credentials, unrestricted tenant access, general model-provider secrets, signing keys, evidence-control authority, or direct business-state mutation rights.

Worker isolation shall be proportionate to consequence. High-risk, untrusted, customer-supplied, model-generated, repository, browser, build, or external-integration workloads may require ephemeral workers, stronger process or virtual-machine isolation, dedicated network boundaries, read-only source mounts, output quarantine, and post-task destruction.

Execution results are untrusted until validated. A successful process exit, provider response, API status, deployment status, or tool message does not establish business correctness or acceptance. Results shall be correlated to task, capability, invocation, worker, artifact, time, and target before the Validation Pipeline evaluates them.

Worker reuse requires demonstrated cleanup. Where reliable cleanup cannot be proven, the worker shall be destroyed or returned to a verified base state. Residual files, processes, credentials, network sessions, caches, logs, or tenant content shall not survive into an unauthorized task.

Model access shall occur through the governed Model Gateway and Model Orchestration and Provider Abstraction. Direct provider integration by product components is prohibited where it bypasses routing, data destination, credential isolation, tenant, region, schema, provenance, timeout, cost, or evidence controls.

Provider and model eligibility is determined before orchestration selects a route. Availability, benchmark, cost, latency, popularity, provider certification, or customer preference does not create policy permission. Fallback shall select only among currently eligible routes and shall not weaken data, region, tenant, security, privacy, output, or assurance constraints.

Model endpoints can be external, private, customer-controlled, or locally hosted according to the approved Deployment Profile. Location does not create authority. Each route shall preserve provider, model or best available revision, endpoint, region, configuration, input classification, retention, data-use terms, invocation identity, output provenance, and limitations.

Protected data shall be minimized before disclosure. Secrets, keys, active capabilities, and unrestricted internal context are excluded. Provider-side logging, training, retention, human review, subcontractor access, and abuse monitoring shall match the approved profile.

Cloud data architecture shall preserve semantic ownership. Task state, policy, approval, capability, execution, validation, audit, evidence, configuration, tenant, model, graph, repository, context, and operational records remain distinct even when they share physical infrastructure.

Each data class shall define owner, authoritative source, schema, tenant, purpose, classification, region, consistency, durability, access, encryption, retention, correction, deletion, backup, recovery, export, and evidence requirements. Convenience joins or shared databases shall not erase component boundaries.

Direct cross-component database mutation is prohibited unless the canonical architecture explicitly assigns shared ownership. Components shall interact through governed interfaces, events, or controlled data products that preserve schema, authorization, provenance, and failure semantics.

Derived indexes, caches, search structures, graph projections, analytics, and replicas shall not become undocumented sources of truth. They shall retain source linkage, freshness, invalidation, tenant, deletion, and rebuild semantics. Authorization shall not depend on stale derived state without an explicit fail-safe policy.

Queues and event streams may decouple workloads and improve resilience, but they shall not weaken authority or evidence. Every material message shall have a defined producer, consumer, schema, tenant, correlation, classification, integrity expectation, ordering need, retry rule, expiry, dead-letter treatment, and idempotency model.

Delivery acknowledgement is not business acceptance. At-least-once delivery requires duplicate-safe consumers. At-most-once behavior requires explicit loss treatment. Ordered workflows shall define the scope of ordering and the response to gaps, late events, duplicates, replay, and partition.

Messages shall not carry unrestricted credentials or capabilities beyond their required lifetime and audience. A capability that expires, is revoked, is consumed, or no longer matches current context shall not become valid through queued delivery.

Dead-letter and quarantine stores contain potentially sensitive failed data. They require ownership, restricted access, alerting, retention, correction, replay authorization, and deletion. Manual replay is a controlled action and shall not bypass current policy or validation.

The Cloud Architecture shall protect the continuous Audit Engine and Evidence Chain path. Audit collection begins with request intake and continues through identity, context, reasoning, policy, risk, approval, capability, execution, validation, acceptance, delivery, closure, incident, recovery, and review.
