ilaten_requirement: The Validation Pipeline shall independently assess the container-specific assertions required by the applicable gate. Validation may verify digest, media type, platform, provenance, signer, SBOM, composition, vulnerability disposition, secrets, malware, privilege, filesystem, process, configuration, health contract, and runtime compatibility.

The builder, scanner, registry, signer, deployment system, or running workload shall not be the sole validator of its own success. Tool results may be consumed as evidence, but acceptance requires deterministic interpretation under the approved validation profile.

Validation shall distinguish artifact integrity, supply-chain provenance, policy eligibility, functional correctness, runtime security, deployment readiness, and business result. Success in one category shall not be generalized to the others.
Validation failure, unavailable required evidence, identity ambiguity, digest mismatch, or revoked trust shall block promotion or trigger the exact approved constrained response.

The threat model shall include malicious or compromised source, dependency, base image, package repository, builder, cache, registry, signing identity, scanner, plugin, runtime, maintainer account, mirror, and customer-supplied artifact.

Response shall be able to identify every affected source revision, build, digest, index, tag, signature, registry, environment, cluster, tenant, customer delivery, cache, backup, and derivative artifact.

Containment may suspend builds, quarantine repositories, revoke signatures, block digests, disable promotion, rotate credentials, isolate workloads, restrict egress, or withdraw releases. The chosen action shall preserve evidence and avoid uncontrolled duplicate effects.

Changes to image format, Build Profile, builder trust model, base-image family, dependency source, registry, signing system, provenance schema, SBOM format, admission expectation, Runtime Profile, platform matrix, or customer-delivery model shall follow Section 5.7.

Section 5.3 remains the canonical Release Lifecycle. Container build and promotion states shall map to it and shall not create a competing release state machine. A signed or published image is not automatically an Approved, Published, Accepted, or Supported ILATEN release.

Exceptions shall be exact, time-bound, owned, monitored, and reviewed. A customer request, sales commitment, provider default, tool limitation, or engineering preference shall not silently waive non-waivable controls.

One actor or system may perform multiple functions only where the approved operating profile permits it. Role combination shall not erase the distinction between source authoring, build, verification, promotion, deployment, validation, and release acceptance.

During a registered Single-Maintainer Bootstrap Profile, one authorized maintainer may temporarily perform multiple container-lifecycle roles when independent personnel are unavailable. This state shall be recorded and shall not be represented as independent review, dual control, or Enterprise separation of duties.

The bootstrap profile shall require exact source and artifact attribution, protected organizational ownership, mandatory automated Quality Gates, immutable or equivalently protected provenance and evidence, explicit self-review, least privilege, separately protected recovery factors, administrative-event logging, periodic access review, constrained release maturity, and a dated exit plan.

High-impact builder, signing, registry, base-image, privilege, restricted-execution, tenant, production, or release changes shall receive qualified external review before they affect a Stable release, production environment, or Enterprise operating profile; otherwise the affected capability shall remain blocked or constrained through formal risk treatment.

The bootstrap profile shall not waive controls where one-person compromise would create unacceptable platform, tenant, signing, evidence, release, recovery, or customer risk. External managed custody, protected build services, independent verification mechanisms, or reduced scope shall be used where required. Continued single-maintainer operation shall not become permanent through inaction.
Before a container artifact becomes eligible for its target scope, the applicable gates shall verify:
- accepted source, review, and change identity;
- version-controlled Build Definition and minimal Build Context;
- approved builder identity, isolation, and configuration;
- immutable and verified base images and dependencies;
- absence of embedded secrets and prohibited material;
- artifact format, manifest, index, platform, and digest integrity;
- provenance completeness and authenticity for the required assurance target;
- SBOM generation, identity binding, and adequacy;
- vulnerability, malware, license, secret, and composition disposition;
- required signatures, attestations, trust roots, scope, and revocation status;
- runtime user, privilege, capabilities, filesystem, process, configuration, network, health, and resource conformance;
- functional, integration, security, tenant-isolation, shutdown, recovery, and compatibility testing appropriate to risk;
- registry namespace, immutability, promotion, retention, and recovery controls;
- release state, approval, target Deployment Profile, and support eligibility;
- independent Validation Pipeline outcome;
- Audit Engine and Evidence Chain completeness for the defined gate; and
- exception ownership, expiry, monitoring, and residual-risk acceptance.
No single tool result shall satisfy the complete gate. A gate shall fail safely when mandatory identity, evidence, verification, or policy state is missing or ambiguous.
The following practices are prohibited unless an explicitly defined canonical exception applies:
- using a mutable tag as the sole production artifact identity;
- using `latest` as a controlled release reference;
- building production images from unaccepted source or a developer workstation without an approved constrained profile;
- allowing unpinned remote content to enter a release build without exact capture and verification;
- embedding secrets, private keys, credentials, customer data, or tenant state in images or layers;
- passing secrets through persistent build arguments, logs, labels, annotations, history, provenance, SBOMs, or caches;
- giving build workloads unrestricted network, host, runtime-socket, cluster-administrator, signing-key, or production access;
- treating a valid digest, signature, SBOM, scan result, registry location, or successful startup as complete approval;
- admitting an unverified platform variant through a trusted multi-architecture index;
- using unsupported, unowned, unlicensed, or unpatchable base images without bounded risk treatment;
- installing packages or changing application binaries inside running production containers;
- committing a running container as a production artifact;
- running as root or privileged by default;
- adding broad kernel capabilities, host namespaces, device access, host mounts, or runtime sockets for convenience;
- storing durable business state in undocumented writable container layers;
- downloading and executing unverified code at startup;
- allowing direct governed external action outside the Tool Gateway;
- allowing restricted workers to change policy, approval, capability, validation, audit, or evidence authority;
- rebuilding during promotion without treating the result as a new artifact;
- reassigning an immutable published release reference to different content;
- suppressing findings globally or indefinitely;
- deleting evidence or active artifacts through uncontrolled garbage collection;
- treating registry replication, runtime pull, rollout, or health as independent validation;
- representing bootstrap self-review as independent Enterprise assurance; or
- giving any container engine, build system, registry, scanner, signer, format, provider, customer commitment, or engineering convenience architectural authority.
- containers are used through an approved Container Profile and not treated as mandatory universal architecture;
- container format, builder, registry, runtime, and provider remain replaceable within the approved portability boundary;
- accepted source, build definitions, inputs, builders, outputs, and release records are attributable;
- production artifacts are immutable and referenced by exact digest;
- base images and dependencies are approved, traceable, supported, and updateable;
- build secrets and signing material are protected and absent from image content and persistent metadata;
- provenance and SBOMs bind to the exact artifact and meet the profile's assurance target;
- signatures and attestations are verified against identity, scope, policy, time, and revocation state;
- multi-platform variants receive platform-specific assurance;
- images use minimal runtime content, least privilege, bounded writable state, and explicit process and configuration contracts;
- runtime secrets, network dependencies, health, shutdown, resources, and specialized hardware assumptions are governed;
- restricted execution preserves Policy Engine, Approval Engine, capability, Tool Gateway, Validation Pipeline, Audit Engine, Evidence Chain, tenant, and human-accountability boundaries;
- third-party and customer-provided images do not bypass non-waivable controls;
- registries preserve ownership, access, immutability, integrity, promotion, recovery, and evidence;
- promotion uses an already verified immutable artifact and does not conceal a rebuild;
- vulnerability, malware, secret, license, and support findings receive documented disposition;
- patching produces a new verified artifact rather than mutable production repair;
- deployed artifact identity and material runtime drift are detectable;
- isolated delivery preserves integrity, provenance, trust, revocation, and support constraints;
- Audit Engine and Evidence Chain controls operate continuously across material events;
- the Validation Pipeline remains independent;
- bootstrap limitations remain explicit, temporary, constrained, and subject to dated exit criteria; and
- architecture-significant container decisions require an authorized ADR.
The following invariants are binding:
- a container image is a deployable artifact, not business authority;
- a digest establishes exact content identity under the accepted algorithm, not safety or approval;
- a signature authenticates according to its trust policy, not functional correctness or release acceptance;
- an SBOM is an inventory, not proof of completeness, security, or license compliance;
- a scanner result is a decision input, not deterministic truth;
- source acceptance, build, verification, signing, promotion, deployment, validation, and business acceptance remain distinct;
- production artifacts are immutable and promotion does not silently rebuild them;
- production runtime modification is replaced by rebuild and controlled rollout;
- container isolation is one defense layer and not a complete tenant or security boundary;
- least privilege, non-root execution, minimal content, read-only filesystems, bounded writable state, and constrained network are defaults subject to exact justified profiles;
- secrets, private keys, customer data, and tenant state are not embedded in images;
- artifact provenance, SBOM, signature, scan, release, and deployment records bind to exact digests;
- the deterministic Policy Engine remains within the ILATEN Control Plane;
- the Approval Engine and human accountability remain independent of container tooling;
- every governed external action remains mediated by the Tool Gateway under constrained capability;
- restricted execution cannot mutate its authority or accept its own output;
- the Validation Pipeline remains independent;
- Audit Engine and Evidence Chain controls operate continuously and are not replaced by build, registry, scanner, or runtime logs;
- third-party, customer, managed-service, and offline artifacts remain subject to the applicable non-waivable controls;
- bootstrap operation does not imply independent Enterprise assurance; and
- architecture-significant container decisions require an authorized ADR.

A Container Strategy implementation is non-conformant if it treats containers as mandatory without an authorized architecture decision; uses mutable references as sole production identity; permits untrusted or untraceable build inputs; exposes secrets or signing material; relies on developer workstations as ordinary release builders; accepts unsupported base images or dependencies without bounded treatment; promotes artifacts without exact digest, provenance, SBOM, required signatures, assessment, release state, and independent validation; conflates a digest, signature, scan, registry, startup, rollout, or health result with approval; hides unapproved platform variants in an image index; runs unnecessarily privileged or mutable workloads; embeds customer or tenant state; permits governed external action outside the Tool Gateway; lets restricted workers change or validate their own authority; mutates production containers instead of rebuilding; loses active artifacts or evidence through registry operations; misrepresents offline, customer-provided, third-party, or bootstrap limitations; or gives any image format, container engine, builder, registry, scanner, signer, provider, tool, customer preference, sales commitment, or engineering convenience architectural authority.

Possession of a storage credential, database role, volume attachment, object URL, encryption key reference, network path, replica, snapshot, or backup does not create ILATEN business permission. Storage-layer controls are mandatory defense-in-depth controls, but they shall not replace tenant policy, task capability, purpose limitation, approval, validation, or human accountability.

Section 3.4 governs secrets, Section 3.5 governs cryptographic keys, Section 3.6 governs encryption, Section 3.10 governs Backup and Recovery, Section 3.11 governs Disaster Recovery, and Section 3.12 governs compliance applicability, privacy roles, retention, and legal requirements. Section 7.3 governs orchestration storage integration; Section 7.4 prohibits durable reliance on container-writable layers. This section defines the storage architecture those controls shall preserve.

ILATEN shall select storage technologies through approved Storage Profiles based on data semantics, assurance, availability, performance, scale, recovery, residency, portability, operational capability, and cost. No database engine, query language, persistence framework, cloud service, replication product, file system, object protocol, search technology, graph implementation, or volume interface is canonical by default.

A customer or product profile may require a specific technology only through an authorized decision within lawful and formally approved scope. Provider marketing, sales commitment, developer preference, benchmark result, or model-generated recommendation shall not silently redefine canonical storage semantics.
Storage Architecture shall:
- support controlled schema evolution and reversible migration where required;
**Snapshot.** A point-in-time storage representation created by a storage system. Snapshot consistency, independence, retention, and restorability shall be established rather than assumed.
ILATEN storage shall be organized into explicit domains. A domain may share physical infrastructure only where logical and cryptographic controls preserve its accepted boundary.

**Platform Configuration State** includes versioned service configuration, feature configuration, deployment references, schema state, and operational policy references. It shall not become an undocumented substitute for source-controlled configuration or canonical policy.

**Operational State** includes queues, leases, locks, checkpoints, idempotency records, schedules, and workflow coordination. Its failure semantics shall be explicit because seemingly temporary data may protect against duplicate or unauthorized effects.

Every persistent data asset shall have an owner, purpose, classification, tenant scope, data-subject relevance where applicable, residency constraints, authoritative source, retention class, encryption profile, access profile, backup profile, recovery objective, and disposal method.

Classification shall account for confidentiality, integrity, availability, legal, contractual, privacy, safety, security, intellectual-property, evidence, and operational impact. A data asset may require high integrity even when it is not confidential.

Classification metadata shall be protected against unauthorized downgrading. Absence of a classification shall default to the most restrictive applicable handling profile until resolved; it shall not default to unrestricted use.

Labels, database names, bucket names, schemas, paths, and tags may assist governance but shall not be the sole control. Effective enforcement shall occur through identity, authorization, encryption, network, query, lifecycle, and validation controls.
Each material fact shall have one declared authoritative source or an explicitly governed multi-authority reconciliation model. Duplicate writable sources without conflict semantics are prohibited.

Indexes, search stores, knowledge graphs, embeddings, analytical stores, caches, reports, and materialized views shall be treated as derived unless architecture explicitly assigns authority. Derived state shall preserve lineage to the authoritative source, transformation version, tenant, time, and rebuild conditions.

Loss or corruption of derived state should be recoverable by controlled rebuild. A rebuild shall not overwrite authoritative source, cross tenant boundaries, expand purpose, or silently accept stale or unverified inputs.

Every data asset shall have an accountable business owner and an operational steward. Ownership shall define permitted purposes, quality expectations, access approval, retention, disclosure, recovery priority, migration, and retirement.

Custody by ILATEN, a provider, a customer, or a subcontractor does not by itself determine legal role or ownership. Controller, joint-controller, processor, and other legally recognized roles shall be established per processing purpose through Section 3.12.

Service owners shall not create new persistent copies, exports, indexes, or caches without assigning purpose, classification, lineage, access, retention, and deletion behavior. Convenience copies are governed data assets when they contain governed information.
Stewardship shall include periodic review of access, schema, quality, residency, retention, backup, recovery, support state, and unused data.

Authoritative data structures shall use versioned schemas or equivalently controlled contracts. Schemas shall define identity, tenant, ownership, field meaning, type, nullability, constraints, classification, relationships, lifecycle, and compatibility.

Semantic meaning shall not depend solely on undocumented application behavior. Enumerations, units, time zones, precision, ordering, state transitions, and deletion markers shall be explicit where material.

Schema validation shall occur at trusted boundaries. Storage acceptance does not prove semantic validity, authority, or business acceptance. Invalid, unknown, ambiguous, out-of-range, or cross-tenant references shall fail safely according to the data contract.
Schema ownership and approval shall be defined. A persistence framework's generated migration or inferred model is an implementation artifact, not an architectural decision.

Human, workload, service, node, provider, customer, backup, recovery, replication, migration, and emergency identities shall remain distinct. Shared database or storage credentials are prohibited for ordinary operation.

Workload access shall use a verified workload identity bound to environment, service, tenant scope where applicable, purpose, audience, and lifecycle. Credentials should be short-lived and automatically rotated where supported.

Storage systems shall strongly authenticate administrative access. Privileged human access should use phishing-resistant authentication where the approved Deployment Profile supports it and shall follow Section 3.2.
Recovery and break-glass identities shall be separately governed, protected, monitored, time-bounded, and reviewed. They shall not become routine application credentials.

Storage authorization shall enforce least privilege across control-plane administration, data-plane read, write, append, delete, schema, backup, restore, replication, export, key use, retention override, and audit access.

Application identities shall receive only the operations, data domains, tenants, schemas, tables, collections, objects, prefixes, or paths required for their purpose. Administrative ownership shall not be granted for convenience.

The deterministic Policy Engine decides ILATEN business authorization. Storage authorization enforces technical access to storage resources. Neither shall be represented as the other. A permitted database query does not authorize the business purpose, and a business capability does not automatically grant direct database access.

Highly sensitive operations—including bulk export, cross-tenant access, retention override, destructive schema change, backup deletion, evidence deletion, key reassignment, and recovery—shall require elevated, attributable, and independently controlled authorization according to risk.

Tenant identity shall be present and validated at every material storage boundary. Tenant isolation shall cover connection, identity, authorization, schema or namespace, row or object ownership, query construction, cache keys, indexes, encryption, backup, restore, export, telemetry, support, and deletion.

A database, schema, table, collection, bucket, prefix, volume, namespace, account, or cluster name is not a complete tenant boundary by itself. The Storage Profile shall document the combined enforcement model and its failure modes.

Cross-tenant queries, joins, exports, analytics, support actions, and migrations shall be denied by default. Authorized aggregation shall use an explicit purpose, scope, privacy treatment, output control, and evidence.
Tenant deletion, restore, and migration shall preserve isolation. Restoring one tenant shall not overwrite, expose, revert, or resurrect another tenant's data.

ILATEN shall collect and persist only information necessary for a defined product, security, operational, contractual, or lawful purpose. Potential future usefulness is not a sufficient retention purpose.

Fields, payloads, prompts, outputs, attachments, traces, logs, support bundles, and derived features shall be reviewed for minimization. Sensitive content should be referenced, transformed, tokenized, redacted, aggregated, or processed ephemerally when full persistence is unnecessary.

Purpose changes require an applicability and governance assessment. Data collected for one tenant or purpose shall not be reused for model improvement, analytics, benchmarking, product development, or another customer without the required lawful basis, contract, policy, and authorization.

Protected data shall be encrypted at rest and in transit according to Section 3.6. The Storage Profile shall define encryption boundaries, algorithms or approved suites, keys, rotation, revocation, backups, replicas, snapshots, exports, caches, temporary files, and metadata coverage.

ilaten_requirement: Every authoritative storage interaction shall have an explicit consistency model appropriate to its semantics. Strong, serializable, snapshot, causal, monotonic, read-after-write, bounded-staleness, or eventual behavior shall not be assumed from a product category.

Client behavior shall account for stale reads, concurrent updates, lost responses, retry, failover, replica lag, clock uncertainty, and partial commit. A read from a replica shall not be treated as current when the decision requires authoritative freshness.

Multi-step authoritative changes shall use a transactional boundary or a formally designed distributed workflow with compensation, idempotency, reconciliation, and evidence. Partial success shall not be hidden behind a generic success state.

Database commit, message publication, external action, evidence append, and notification often occur across different systems. The architecture shall define ordering and recovery, such as a transactional outbox, durable state machine, or equivalent pattern, without claiming unsupported atomicity.

State transitions shall validate current version, permitted predecessor state, actor, tenant, policy, approval, capability, and expiry where applicable. Blind overwrite of authoritative state is prohibited.
Rollback of data is not always a valid compensation for an external effect. The Tool Gateway and workflow state shall preserve exact reconciliation semantics.

Concurrent writers shall use explicit coordination such as version columns, compare-and-set, leases, locks, unique constraints, transactions, or single-writer ownership according to risk. Last-write-wins behavior shall not be used for high-integrity state unless its consequences are accepted.

Locks and leases shall have ownership, scope, timeout, renewal, fencing, release, and recovery semantics. Expired or partitioned holders shall not continue to create authoritative writes after a new holder is accepted.
Administrative repair and migration shall respect application concurrency. Maintenance mode, write fencing, traffic draining, dual-write transition, or reconciliation may be required.
Concurrency failures shall produce attributable conflict outcomes rather than silent data loss. Retries shall re-evaluate authorization and current state when those may have changed.

Every retriable authoritative command and governed external action shall have an idempotency or reconciliation design appropriate to its effect. Idempotency keys shall bind to tenant, operation, scope, parameters, authority, and validity period.

Duplicate detection state may be operationally small but is security-relevant when it prevents repeated payment, deletion, notification, deployment, provider call, or customer-system action. It shall receive durability, isolation, retention, and recovery appropriate to the protected effect.
Retries after ambiguous timeout shall not assume failure. The system shall determine whether the prior attempt committed, remained pending, or produced an external effect.
Idempotency shall not permit reuse of an old approval or capability for changed parameters. A duplicate request with materially different content is a new request or a conflict.
Stored timestamps shall use an unambiguous standard representation and preserve the source and assurance of time where material. Local display time shall not replace canonical event time.

Wall-clock time alone shall not establish distributed ordering. Sequence numbers, versions, causal identifiers, chain links, transaction positions, or trusted timestamps shall be used where ordering affects authorization, evidence, recovery, or reconciliation.

Clock skew, delayed delivery, backfill, restore, replay, and migration shall not silently reorder authoritative events. Late-arriving records shall preserve original occurrence time and ingestion time as distinct values.
Expiration of approval, capability, secret, lease, retention, or legal hold shall use the authoritative time source defined by the profile and shall fail safely under uncertainty.

Replication shall have a defined purpose, topology, consistency, lag, conflict, encryption, tenant, region, failover, recovery, monitoring, and capacity model. Synchronous and asynchronous replication create different durability and availability tradeoffs that shall be represented honestly.
Cross-region or cross-border replication shall comply with residency, transfer, customer, key, and contractual requirements. A provider's global service label shall not establish lawful placement.
Failover shall prevent two writable authorities from diverging unless an approved multi-writer conflict model exists. Fencing, quorum, recovery-point selection, and failback shall be tested.

Replica promotion shall verify integrity, lag, schema, keys, revocation, policy, identity, and dependent service state. Availability shall not be restored by accepting an untrusted or stale authority without explicit treatment.

Storage service-level objectives shall define acknowledgement semantics, tolerated loss window, replication, failure domains, maintenance, capacity, recovery, and measurement. Marketing durability figures shall not substitute for an ILATEN end-to-end assessment.

A write shall be considered durable only after the Storage Profile's required persistence boundary is met. Buffered, cached, asynchronous, or locally acknowledged writes shall disclose their loss window.

High availability shall address dependencies including identity, keys, network, DNS, control plane, storage metadata, replication, quota, and client failover. Redundant media without redundant access or key availability is not sufficient.

Backup requirements are defined in Section 3.10 and specialized here for storage implementation. Every authoritative and required evidentiary data asset shall map to an approved Backup Profile or have a documented reason why reconstruction is sufficient.

The Backup Profile shall define scope, frequency, recovery-point objective, consistency method, encryption, keys, isolation, immutability, retention, region, ownership, access, monitoring, restore testing, legal hold, and disposal.

Backups shall include the dependencies required for usable restoration: schemas, configuration, identity mappings, encryption keys or protected recovery paths, integrity metadata, manifests, sequence state, object references, and compatible application versions.

Application-consistent backup may require transaction coordination, quiescence, write ordering, checkpoints, logs, or group snapshots. Crash-consistent snapshots shall not be represented as application-consistent without evidence.

Backup administration and deletion shall be separated from ordinary production administration according to risk. At least one required recovery path should resist compromise or deletion by the primary production identity.

Snapshots may support backup, migration, testing, forensic preservation, rollback, or recovery. Their purpose, consistency, dependency, retention, encryption, access, region, and deletion shall be defined.

A snapshot that depends on the same control plane, account, encryption key, metadata service, or physical storage may not provide independent recovery. Copy-on-write behavior and provider lifecycle shall be understood.
Snapshots containing production or tenant data shall not be attached to development, analytics, or support environments without approved transformation, access, isolation, and purpose.

Snapshot creation success does not prove restorability. Restore testing shall verify data integrity, application compatibility, identity, keys, policy, revocation, tenant isolation, and evidence continuity.
Restore is a controlled state transition, not a file-copy operation. The selected Recovery Point shall be authorized, integrity-assessed, compatible, and appropriate to the incident or failure.

Restoration shall preserve current authorization, revocation, legal hold, security, tenant, key, and policy requirements. Restoring old data shall not reactivate revoked users, expired capabilities, deleted secrets, vulnerable configuration, withdrawn releases, or closed incidents.

Recovery shall reconcile writes and external actions occurring after the Recovery Point. Missing, duplicated, or ambiguous effects shall be resolved before normal operation or represented as constrained state.

The Validation Pipeline shall independently verify restored data and service behavior. A successful storage restore command is not acceptance. Production return requires defined integrity, consistency, functional, security, tenant, evidence, and business gates.
Recovery exercises shall produce measured RPO, RTO, completeness, error, dependency, and corrective-action evidence. Untested backup is not an accepted recovery capability.

Section 3.11 remains authoritative for Disaster Recovery. Storage Architecture shall provide recoverable data and state aligned to the approved failover, failback, regional, provider, and customer-responsibility model.

Disaster recovery shall identify which storage domains move together, which may tolerate different Recovery Points, and which require ordered restoration. Control Plane, Trust Core, tenant data, keys, artifacts, configuration, and derived indexes may have different recovery sequences.

Split-brain prevention, write fencing, region identity, DNS or route transition, key availability, replica lag, and external action reconciliation shall be coordinated. Two sites shall not both accept conflicting authoritative writes unless the architecture explicitly supports it.
Failback shall be governed as carefully as failover. Data accumulated during recovery shall be reconciled and validated before authority moves again.

Retention shall follow an approved, record-class-specific schedule that reconciles applicable legal, contractual, certification, product-support, incident, defense, privacy, evidence, and data-minimization requirements. Personal data and other protected information shall not be retained longer than necessary or lawfully required for the defined purpose. Retention is not indefinite by default.

The schedule shall define start event, duration, disposition, owner, review, archive behavior, backup treatment, derived-copy treatment, and exceptions. Creation time alone may be insufficient when retention begins at contract termination, case closure, consent withdrawal, release retirement, or another event.

Archival shall preserve identity, integrity, encryption, keys, format readability, metadata, access, legal hold, retrieval, and disposal. Moving information to lower-cost storage does not remove governance.

Conflicting requirements, legal holds, investigations, and justified extensions shall be documented, narrowly scoped, authorized, and periodically reviewed. Expired holds shall be released through an attributable process.

Deletion shall address authoritative stores, replicas, indexes, caches, search structures, embeddings, exports, queues, temporary files, snapshots, backups, archives, support bundles, and provider residuals according to the approved scope and technical feasibility.

Logical deletion, tombstoning, access revocation, cryptographic erasure, purge, overwrite, media sanitization, and physical destruction are distinct actions. The required outcome shall be selected according to data sensitivity, storage technology, reuse, legal obligations, and threat model.

Deletion requests shall verify identity, authority, tenant, scope, conflicts, legal hold, and downstream dependencies. Destructive operations shall be idempotent, attributable, reversible where required, and protected from accidental bulk impact.

Backup deletion may occur through scheduled expiry rather than immediate selective mutation when that approach is lawful and documented. Restored backups shall reapply current deletion and suppression records before ordinary use.

Media sanitization and provider disposal shall follow an approved program aligned to current authoritative guidance. A provider statement shall be evaluated for exact media, encryption, reuse, destruction, evidence, and shared-responsibility scope.

Each Storage Profile shall identify permitted and prohibited countries, regions, facilities, providers, support paths, replication locations, backup locations, key locations, metadata locations, and administrative access jurisdictions as applicable.

Cross-border transfer and remote access shall be governed through Section 3.12. Customer-selected residency shall not silently weaken security, recovery, support, or evidence controls; limitations shall be documented.
Migration between regions shall preserve tenant identity, encryption, integrity, retention, deletion, legal hold, lineage, and recovery. Source copies shall be retired according to the approved plan.

Storage design shall apply privacy by design through minimization, separation, pseudonymization, tokenization, encryption, aggregation, access restriction, purpose metadata, bounded retention, and controlled disclosure where appropriate.

Direct identifiers, sensitive attributes, free-text content, model inputs, outputs, embeddings, and linkage keys shall not be combined without a defined need and authorization. Pseudonymized data remains protected when re-identification is reasonably possible.

Indexes and embeddings may leak or reproduce protected information. They shall inherit appropriate classification, tenant, purpose, retention, deletion, access, and incident controls even when the original text is not directly stored.

Data-subject and customer requests shall be supported according to applicable law and ILATEN's processing role. Retrieval and deletion mechanisms shall avoid exposing another tenant or confirming protected data to an unauthorized requester.

Knowledge Graph, Repository Intelligence, Context Engine, Planning Engine, and retrieval stores shall preserve source lineage, tenant, repository, revision, extraction version, model or algorithm version, time, confidence, and staleness metadata.

Derived intelligence state shall not overwrite accepted source, canonical architecture, repository truth, policy, approval, audit, or evidence. A graph edge, embedding similarity, search rank, or model-generated summary is not business authority.

Repository deletion, branch change, permission change, tenant offboarding, and source correction shall propagate to indexes and caches according to a bounded freshness objective. Stale derived state shall not bypass current authorization.

Cross-tenant vector search, shared embeddings, or global retrieval indexes are prohibited unless an approved design demonstrates effective isolation, privacy treatment, purpose, output filtering, and evidence.

Caches shall have a declared source, key design, tenant scope, freshness, invalidation, consistency, capacity, encryption, access, failure, and rebuild model. A cache shall not silently become the only copy of authoritative state.

Cache keys shall include all material dimensions required to prevent cross-tenant, cross-user, cross-policy, cross-model, cross-region, or cross-version contamination. Secret values and protected raw content shall not appear in observable cache keys.

Cached authorization, policy, approval, revocation, capability, or identity state shall use bounded validity and invalidation sufficient to prevent stale permission. High-impact deny and revocation state shall fail safely.

Cache miss, eviction, corruption, poisoning, stampede, and provider outage shall not produce authorization bypass or unbounded load. Cache content shall follow retention and deletion requirements when it contains governed data.
Block storage provides device-like persistence and may support databases or filesystems. Attachment, multipath, encryption, snapshot, resize, fencing, and sanitization semantics shall be governed.
