ilaten_requirement: In Kubernetes profiles, PersistentVolumes, PersistentVolumeClaims, StorageClasses, Container Storage Interface drivers, snapshots, access modes, reclaim policies, topology, expansion, and attachment are orchestration constructs. They shall map to an approved Storage Profile.

A PersistentVolume lifecycle may outlive a Pod, but persistence alone does not establish backup, tenant isolation, encryption, recovery, or support. Dynamic provisioning shall enforce allowed classes, regions, encryption, topology, performance, reclaim, snapshot, and ownership controls.

Reclaim policies shall be explicit. Automatic deletion may cause data loss; automatic retention may leave protected orphaned data. Both require lifecycle, ownership, sanitization, and evidence controls.

Volume snapshots shall be treated according to their actual consistency and independence. Multi-volume applications may require coordinated or group-consistent capture, application quiescence, or transaction-log recovery.

Workloads shall not use host paths, node-local disks, shared volumes, or privileged storage drivers for durable or sensitive state unless an approved profile defines isolation, scheduling, backup, recovery, and compromise containment.

Customer-managed keys, databases, buckets, volumes, archives, or backup systems may be supported through an explicit Deployment Profile and shared-responsibility matrix. ILATEN shall document required capabilities, configurations, evidence, support boundaries, and failure behavior.

Customer ownership does not waive non-waivable tenant, security, privacy, authorization, validation, audit, evidence, or human-accountability controls. ILATEN shall not claim control over customer systems it cannot verify or operate.

Customer restrictions on region, provider, encryption, retention, export, or administration shall be evaluated before acceptance. Unsupported constraints shall result in scope restriction, contract correction, or non-acceptance rather than hidden degradation.

Recovery testing, incident access, legal hold, deletion, offboarding, and evidence export responsibilities shall be defined. Missing customer action shall not be represented as ILATEN-completed control.

Storage technology selection shall define an exit path for data, schema, metadata, identities, encryption, indexes, audit, evidence, retention, and deletion. Portability shall be evaluated through tested export and import, not inferred from a standard API label.

Exports shall preserve tenant boundaries, type, precision, ordering, identifiers, relationships, time, integrity, lineage, classification, retention, and required evidence. Lossy export shall be documented and approved.
Provider exit shall address keys, snapshots, replicas, backups, logs, support copies, residual media, contractual retrieval windows, verification, and deletion evidence.

Migration shall use controlled dual-run, freeze, capture, validation, reconciliation, cutover, rollback, and source retirement as appropriate. Dual-write periods shall have a declared authority and conflict model.

Schema and data migrations shall be version-controlled, attributable, tested, observable, recoverable, and compatible with the Release Lifecycle. Migration execution is a privileged Tool Gateway or controlled deployment action, not an ordinary application side effect.

Backward-compatible expansion should precede incompatible contraction where continuous service requires it. Application, schema, index, and rollback compatibility shall be defined for the deployment window.
Migrations shall validate tenant scope, expected source version, row or object counts, constraints, checksums or equivalent integrity, rejected data, duration, resource impact, and completion.

Destructive migration requires backup or an approved recovery path, explicit approval, bounded scope, and post-migration validation. Rollback claims shall account for irreversible transformation and external effects.
Failed or partial migration shall enter a controlled state. Automatic retry shall not repeat non-idempotent transformation without reconciliation.

Data quality rules shall define completeness, validity, uniqueness, consistency, timeliness, lineage, and accepted exceptions according to the data asset. Quality metrics shall not be generalized across unrelated purposes.

The system that writes data shall not be the sole validator of high-impact results. The Validation Pipeline shall independently assess required storage state, relationships, evidence, and side effects.
Repair shall preserve the original observation and correction history. Silent mutation of audit, evidence, approval, or accepted-result records is prohibited.

Storage capacity shall be planned by data domain, tenant, region, environment, growth, retention, replication, backup, snapshot, index, cache, and recovery needs. Logical capacity and physical consumed capacity shall be distinguished.

Quotas shall limit tenant, service, object, transaction, backup, snapshot, and export growth according to the profile. A quota failure shall produce a controlled error and shall not truncate an authoritative record or evidence while reporting success.
Capacity thresholds shall provide sufficient time for safe remediation. Emergency expansion, retention override, compression, tiering, or deletion shall remain governed.

Storage exhaustion shall be tested for critical paths. Audit and evidence capacity shall receive protected reservation or backpressure so ordinary workload growth cannot silently eliminate accountability.
Performance objectives shall define latency, throughput, concurrency, object size, query shape, consistency, freshness, and tail behavior for exact workloads. Average latency alone is insufficient.

Resource pools, connection limits, query limits, priorities, admission, indexes, partitions, compaction, and workload isolation shall prevent one tenant or analytical task from degrading authoritative control or evidence operations.

Optimization shall not bypass encryption, authorization, validation, audit, evidence, retention, or tenant isolation. Denormalization and materialization create governed copies with lineage and deletion obligations.
Benchmarks shall use representative scale, failure, concurrency, tenant, encryption, and recovery conditions. Provider benchmark claims are not ILATEN acceptance evidence.

Storage telemetry shall include availability, latency, errors, saturation, capacity, replication lag, consistency conflict, lock contention, transaction abort, queue depth, backup status, restore status, corruption, unauthorized access, privilege change, retention override, deletion, and key failure as applicable.
Telemetry shall distinguish tenant and environment without exposing protected content or high-cardinality sensitive identifiers. Detailed requirements are defined in Sections 7.8 through 7.10.

Monitoring shall detect both infrastructure failure and semantic risk, including stale replicas, stuck migrations, orphaned data, unexpected growth, missing backups, untested restores, expired holds, unsupported versions, and drift from the Storage Profile.

The threat model shall include credential compromise, unauthorized query, bulk export, cross-tenant access, injection, ransomware, corruption, deletion, rollback, replica poisoning, backup compromise, snapshot exposure, key loss, provider breach, insider misuse, and supply-chain compromise.
Response shall identify affected data assets, tenants, subjects, regions, stores, replicas, snapshots, backups, caches, exports, keys, identities, applications, and derived indexes.

Containment may revoke identities, isolate stores, block writes, fence replicas, rotate keys, preserve snapshots, disable exports, restrict Tool Gateway actions, or move the service into constrained operation. Containment shall preserve required evidence.

Recovery shall select a last known good Recovery Point, restore trustworthy infrastructure and keys, validate state, reconcile later events, reapply current revocations and deletions, and monitor for recurrence.
Notification timing and scope shall follow applicable law, role, contract, regulator, and Section 3.9 rather than a universal assumed deadline.

During a registered Single-Maintainer Bootstrap Profile, one authorized maintainer may temporarily perform multiple storage roles when independent personnel are unavailable. The absence of independent administration shall be recorded and shall not be represented as dual control or Enterprise separation of duties.

The bootstrap profile shall maintain organizational ownership, least privilege, strong authentication, separately protected recovery factors, encrypted storage and backups, mandatory automated Quality Gates, exact migration and administrative attribution, protected audit and evidence, periodic access review, restore testing, and a dated exit plan.

Highest-impact production data, keys, backup deletion, evidence retention, cross-tenant access, bulk export, and destructive migration shall use external managed controls, qualified review, constrained capability, or remain prerelease or blocked where one-person compromise would create unacceptable risk.

Qualified external review shall occur before high-impact storage architecture, migration, recovery, tenant, privacy, Trust Core, or production changes affect a Stable release, production environment, or Enterprise operating profile. Continued single-maintainer operation shall not become permanent through inaction.
Before a storage implementation or material change becomes eligible for its target scope, the applicable gates shall verify:
- approved Storage Profile, owner, purpose, classification, tenant, region, and lifecycle;
- declared authoritative and derived sources with complete lineage;
- versioned schema, constraints, compatibility, and migration plan;
- verified human and workload identity with least-privilege authorization;
- effective tenant isolation across primary, derived, cache, backup, restore, and support paths;
- data minimization and purpose limitation;
- encryption in transit and at rest, key separation, rotation, recovery, and revocation;
- integrity, authenticity, ordering, concurrency, transaction, idempotency, and failure semantics;
- Audit Engine and Evidence Chain append, durability, completeness, and verification controls;
- replication topology, lag, fencing, failover, and failback;
- backup scope, consistency, isolation, immutability, retention, and successful restore testing;
- disaster-recovery sequence, RPO, RTO, dependency, and reconciliation evidence;
- retention, legal hold, deletion, archival, and sanitization behavior;
- residency, transfer, customer-control, portability, and provider-exit requirements;
- capacity, quota, performance, observability, monitoring, and incident readiness;
- Kubernetes or equivalent volume lifecycle where applicable;
- independent Validation Pipeline outcome;
- required Audit Engine and Evidence Chain records; and
- exception ownership, expiry, monitoring, and residual-risk acceptance.
No single successful query, replica, snapshot, backup job, restore command, encryption setting, provider status, or migration completion shall satisfy the complete gate.
The following practices are prohibited unless an explicitly defined canonical exception applies:
- treating storage credentials, database roles, volume access, or network location as business authorization;
- assigning authority based on a technology's primary, leader, master, source, or system-of-record label without canonical designation;
- maintaining multiple writable authoritative copies without conflict and reconciliation semantics;
- using cross-tenant queries, shared caches, indexes, volumes, exports, or restores without effective isolation;
- embedding secrets, keys, customer data, or tenant state in container images or unmanaged files;
- using shared privileged storage credentials for ordinary applications;
- disabling encryption or certificate validation for convenience;
- treating encryption as proof of authorization, tenant isolation, integrity, or lawful processing;
- representing checksums or Evidence Chain hashes as proof of completeness;
- silently dropping Audit Engine or Evidence Chain records during backpressure or outage;
- acknowledging durability before the required persistence boundary is met;
- using eventual consistency for authority-sensitive decisions without bounded and safe semantics;
- retrying ambiguous writes or external actions without idempotency or reconciliation;
- representing replication or snapshots as backup without independent backup controls;
- restoring old authorization, secrets, capabilities, withdrawn releases, or deleted data without current-state reconciliation;
- treating backup completion as proof of successful recovery;
- retaining protected data indefinitely by default;
- using legal hold as an unreviewed blanket retention mechanism;
- treating deletion of a pointer, row, object name, or encryption key as complete erasure without validating all copies;
- attaching production snapshots to uncontrolled development or support environments;
- using container-writable layers, host paths, or node-local storage as undocumented durable state;
- running destructive migrations without approval, recovery, validation, and evidence;
- allowing storage exhaustion to truncate authoritative audit or evidence while reporting success;
- treating operational storage logs as the canonical Audit Engine or Evidence Chain;
- representing bootstrap self-review as independent Enterprise assurance; or
- giving any database, storage provider, replication system, volume driver, framework, customer preference, sales commitment, or engineering convenience architectural authority.
- every persistent data asset is governed by an approved Storage Profile;
- authoritative, evidentiary, derived, cached, ephemeral, replicated, backed-up, and archived state remain distinct;
- ownership, purpose, classification, tenant, region, schema, access, retention, recovery, and disposal are defined;
- technology selection preserves required semantics and an evidence-backed exit path;
- storage identity and authorization are least-privilege and remain distinct from ILATEN business authority;
- tenant isolation covers primary, derived, cache, backup, restore, export, telemetry, and support paths;
- minimization and purpose limitation govern raw and derived information;
- encryption, key separation, integrity, authenticity, and tamper evidence meet the exact risk profile;
- Audit Engine and Evidence Chain storage preserves append-only semantics, ordering, durability, completeness assessment, retention, and independent verification;
- consistency, transaction, concurrency, idempotency, time, and failure behavior are explicit;
- replication, availability, durability, backup, snapshot, restore, and Disaster Recovery remain separate governed capabilities;
- restore validates current authorization, revocation, deletion, keys, schema, tenant, evidence, and external effects;
- retention is record-class-specific and not indefinite by default;
- deletion and sanitization address all applicable copies and media;
- residency, transfer, customer control, provider exit, and migration are governed;
- knowledge, repository, embedding, cache, and search stores preserve lineage and non-authority;
- Kubernetes or equivalent storage constructs map to the approved Storage Profile;
- capacity, performance, monitoring, and incident controls protect critical state;
- the Validation Pipeline remains independent;
- Audit Engine and Evidence Chain controls operate continuously across material storage events;
- bootstrap limitations remain explicit, constrained, temporary, and subject to dated exit criteria; and
- architecture-significant storage decisions require an authorized ADR.
The following invariants are binding:
- storage persists state but does not create ILATEN business authority;
- possession of storage access does not grant tenant purpose, policy permission, approval, or capability;
- every material fact has a declared authoritative source or an explicit reconciliation model;
- derived state never silently becomes authoritative;
- tenant isolation is a full lifecycle property and no single schema, bucket, prefix, namespace, volume, or key is sufficient by itself;
- encryption does not replace authorization, minimization, integrity, validation, or lawful processing;
- the deterministic Policy Engine remains within the ILATEN Control Plane;
- the Approval Engine remains the accountable approval authority;
- every governed external action remains mediated by the Tool Gateway under constrained capability;
- the Validation Pipeline remains independent;
- Audit Engine and Evidence Chain controls operate continuously and are not replaced by database, provider, backup, or storage audit logs;
- Evidence Chain hashing does not prove event completeness or storage availability by itself;
- buffered audit persistence has explicit durability, ordering, backpressure, and failure semantics;
- replication is not backup, snapshot creation is not restore validation, and backup success is not recovery acceptance;
- restore re-applies current authorization, revocation, deletion, key, tenant, and policy state;
- retention follows approved record classes and is not indefinite by default;
- deletion, erasure, sanitization, archive expiry, and legal hold remain distinct governed actions;
- derived intelligence stores preserve lineage, tenant, purpose, and non-authority;
- container and orchestration storage constructs do not redefine durable data semantics;
- bootstrap operation does not imply independent Enterprise assurance; and
- architecture-significant storage decisions require an authorized ADR.

A Storage Architecture implementation is non-conformant if it treats storage access as business authority; allows an implementation label to define canonical truth; creates ambiguous multiple writers; permits cross-tenant leakage through primary data, indexes, caches, backups, restores, exports, logs, or support access; weakens encryption, key, privacy, retention, residency, integrity, or sanitization controls; loses audit or evidence under ungoverned buffering; acknowledges durability without meeting the declared boundary; uses stale state for authority-sensitive decisions; retries ambiguous operations without reconciliation; conflates replication, snapshot, backup, restore, and disaster recovery; restores revoked authority or deleted data without reconciliation; retains protected information indefinitely by default; relies on container layers or unmanaged host paths for durable state; performs destructive migration without recovery and validation; represents provider status or operational logs as independent validation or canonical evidence; misrepresents customer-controlled or bootstrap limitations; or gives any database, object store, file system, block device, cache, search store, graph store, vector store, volume provider, tool, contract, customer preference, sales commitment, or engineering convenience architectural authority.

Network reachability is not trust. An IP address, subnet, virtual network, security group, firewall rule, namespace, service name, tunnel, private link, virtual private network, device location, or successful Transport Layer Security session shall not by itself grant tenant access, policy permission, human approval, capability, Tool Gateway authority, validation, release acceptance, or architectural authority.

Section 3.1 defines Zero Trust, Sections 3.2 and 3.3 define authentication and authorization, Section 3.6 defines encryption, and Section 3.8 defines the Threat Model. Section 7.3 defines Kubernetes orchestration networking. Sections 7.7 through 7.10 define scalability, observability, monitoring, and logging in greater depth. This section establishes the network architecture those standards shall preserve.

ILATEN networking shall be technology-agnostic except where an approved Deployment Profile requires a specific capability. No cloud network, firewall, proxy, gateway, load balancer, service mesh, tunnel, software-defined network, container network, domain-name provider, content-delivery network, DDoS service, private-connectivity product, or telecommunications provider is canonical by default.

Equivalent products are interchangeable only when they preserve the required identity, policy enforcement, segmentation, encryption, tenant isolation, observability, failure, recovery, portability, and shared-responsibility outcomes. Similar product categories or configuration names are insufficient evidence.
The network architecture shall:

Every environment shall have an approved Network Profile before receiving production identities, customer traffic, protected data, provider credentials, Tool Gateway connectivity, or Enterprise support claims.
The Network Profile shall bind:

Authentication and authorization shall be explicit, resource-focused, context-aware, and continuously reassessed where risk requires it. Network session establishment and ILATEN business authorization remain separate decisions.

Continuous verification shall account for identity status, device or workload posture, service version, environment, tenant, destination, protocol, risk, certificate, policy, revocation, and observed behavior as applicable. Verification shall not silently expand access because telemetry is unavailable.
The Network Profile shall separate or explicitly govern communication among:

Physical separation is not mandatory for every boundary, but effective identity, authorization, encryption, routing, filtering, monitoring, and failure isolation shall match the risk. Naming two subnets differently is not evidence of separation.

Restricted execution shall not have direct network paths to Policy Engine mutation, Approval Engine authority, Evidence Chain mutation, signing keys, administrative interfaces, orchestration control planes, or unrelated tenant services.

Network design shall support the canonical operational flow without changing its authority sequence. Request intake enters through an approved ingress boundary. Identity, tenant, and integrity verification precede authority-sensitive processing. Immutable Context and authority scope are established before planning or action preparation.

The intelligence layer may reach approved model services through the Model Gateway. It grants no permission and initiates no governed external action. Policy and capability evaluation occur within the ILATEN Control Plane. Human approval is obtained where required.

Every protected service connection shall use a verified subject or workload identity appropriate to the risk. IP address, network interface, node, cluster, namespace, service name, or certificate possession alone shall not be treated as complete identity.

Workload identities shall bind to service, environment, Deployment Profile, audience, purpose, lifecycle, and tenant scope where applicable. Identity issuance, rotation, revocation, and recovery shall follow the applicable authentication and key controls.

Authorization shall evaluate the authenticated identity and requested resource or operation. A network enforcement point may apply an infrastructure access decision, but it shall not create ILATEN business permission.

Identity forwarding through gateways and proxies shall be integrity-protected and bounded. Untrusted clients shall not supply authoritative internal identity headers, tenant headers, approval claims, or capability claims.

Protected traffic shall be encrypted in transit according to Section 3.6. Encryption shall cover public, private, east–west, hybrid, provider, storage, backup, administrative, and recovery paths according to the Network Profile.

Transport protection shall authenticate the intended endpoint, use approved protocol versions and cryptographic suites, validate names or service identities, enforce revocation or short-lived identity semantics, and prevent unsafe downgrade.

Termination points shall be explicit. Traffic decrypted at an edge proxy, gateway, service mesh, load balancer, inspection device, or provider service remains protected information and shall be re-encrypted where the next boundary requires it.

Certificates and equivalent service credentials shall have defined issuers, subjects, audiences, names, usages, validity, algorithms, rotation, revocation, ownership, and recovery. Wildcard and broadly scoped certificates shall be minimized.
Private keys shall remain within approved cryptographic boundaries where required and shall not be embedded in images, repositories, configuration files, logs, or unprotected runtime volumes.

Automated issuance and renewal should be used with bounded identity and authorization. Automation shall not permit any workload to request arbitrary names, environments, tenants, or privileged usages.

Trust stores shall be versioned, distributed through controlled paths, monitored for expiry and compromise, and capable of staged rotation. Adding a private trust anchor shall require explicit authority and impact assessment.
Certificate validation shall not be disabled to resolve connectivity incidents. Emergency trust changes shall be time-bounded, attributable, evidenced, and reviewed.

Only intentionally public services shall receive public endpoints. Public exposure shall be recorded by service, domain, protocol, port, region, owner, purpose, data class, authentication, rate profile, protection, certificate, and support state.

Backend services, storage, orchestration APIs, node interfaces, key services, secret stores, administrative interfaces, build systems, registries, validation services, Audit Engine, and Evidence Chain endpoints shall not be publicly exposed unless an exact Deployment Profile authorizes and protects the path.

An API gateway or equivalent edge component may provide protocol normalization, authentication integration, request limits, routing, version handling, and telemetry. It shall not become the sole owner of canonical business policy or task state.

Gateway rules shall be version-controlled or equivalently governed, least-privilege, testable, reviewable, and attributable. Hidden console changes and provider defaults shall not define production behavior.

Identity, tenant, request integrity, replay protection, content type, size, timeout, and rate controls shall fail safely. Header rewriting and forwarding shall prevent spoofing, ambiguity, duplicate-header attacks, request smuggling, and trust of client-supplied internal metadata.

Inbound webhooks shall use authenticated origin, integrity protection, replay defense, bounded timestamp or nonce semantics, schema validation, size limits, rate limits, tenant binding, and idempotency appropriate to risk.
A webhook shall enter as an untrusted request. Provider ownership of the source address or successful signature verification does not automatically authorize the requested ILATEN action.

Outbound callbacks shall use approved destinations, authenticated transport, bounded retry, idempotency, secret rotation, response validation, timeout, and failure handling. Redirects shall not escape the approved destination scope.
Webhook secrets, verification keys, payloads, and delivery logs shall follow classification and retention controls. Failed deliveries shall not expose protected content through diagnostics.

Internal service communication shall be denied by default where the approved platform supports effective enforcement. Required flows shall be enumerated by source service identity, destination service identity, protocol, port, purpose, tenant behavior, and environment.
Service-to-service authentication shall use workload identity or an equivalent high-assurance mechanism. Network adjacency and DNS resolution are insufficient.

Authorization shall occur at the resource boundary and may be reinforced by service proxies, gateways, or network controls. Internal calls shall not bypass tenant, policy, approval, capability, or validation checks because they originate inside the platform.

Connection pooling, retries, multiplexing, proxies, and service discovery shall preserve attributable identity and tenant boundaries. A shared connection shall not permit response or request confusion across tenants.

Microsegmentation shall reduce the reachable set around exact services, workloads, data, and administrative functions. Segments shall follow trust and workload purpose rather than organizational convenience alone.
Enforcement may occur at workload, host, cluster, subnet, gateway, service proxy, application, or provider layer. Multiple layers may be required for defense in depth.

Rules shall default deny where feasible, explicitly allow required communication, and be validated from both permitted and prohibited perspectives. Declared segmentation without effective enforcement is non-conformant.

Segmentation shall account for IPv4, IPv6, host networking, node traffic, service translation, overlays, tunnels, sidecars, proxies, control-plane paths, metadata services, and provider-managed endpoints. Uncovered alternate paths shall not silently bypass the intended boundary.

Kubernetes NetworkPolicy or equivalent workload-network controls shall be used where the selected network implementation demonstrably enforces them. The presence of a NetworkPolicy object is not evidence that traffic is restricted.
Namespaces shall have default-deny ingress and egress or an approved equivalent baseline. Required DNS, identity, telemetry, storage, gateway, and control-plane flows shall be explicitly allowed.

Selectors, labels, namespace identity, service accounts, nodes, host networking, host ports, ingress controllers, egress gateways, and service-mesh paths shall be governed against bypass and unintended selection.

NetworkPolicy commonly governs defined layer-three and layer-four traffic; it may not provide name-based egress, application identity, layer-seven authorization, host protection, or provider-edge controls. The Network Profile shall fill those gaps.
The Kubernetes control plane, container network, service object, namespace, or Pod IP shall not become an ILATEN business authority. Section 7.3 remains authoritative for orchestration.
A service mesh or application proxy is optional and shall be adopted only when its identity, encryption, policy, telemetry, resilience, complexity, latency, and operational benefits justify the risk.
Mesh control planes, certificate authorities, sidecars, node proxies, gateways, policy components, and upgrade paths are privileged infrastructure and shall be governed accordingly.
Mesh policy may enforce service communication but shall not replace the deterministic ILATEN Policy Engine, Approval Engine, Tool Gateway capability checks, or application tenant authorization.

Fail-open behavior, sidecar bypass, host traffic, initialization ordering, certificate failure, proxy resource exhaustion, and incompatible protocol behavior shall be assessed. A mesh outage shall have a defined safe mode.

Workload egress shall be denied by default or constrained to the minimum approved destinations, protocols, ports, identities, and purposes supported by the profile. Unrestricted internet egress is prohibited for protected or restricted workloads.

Egress controls shall account for direct IP, DNS, redirects, proxies, tunnels, alternate ports, IPv6, cloud metadata, local networks, service discovery, content-delivery networks, and provider address changes.

Destination allowlisting by domain name alone may be vulnerable to rebinding, shared hosting, redirects, compromised DNS, and provider multiplexing. Identity-aware transport and application-level verification shall supplement network destination controls.
Egress gateways or proxies may centralize policy, identity, inspection, attribution, and rate control. They shall not receive universal unbounded credentials or become an unaudited bypass path.
Data classification and purpose shall govern outbound payloads. Network allow does not authorize disclosure.

The Tool Gateway is the only governed path for ILATEN-controlled external action. Its network paths shall be explicit by connector, destination, tenant, environment, protocol, identity, capability, data class, rate, timeout, and failure behavior.

Execution workers shall connect to the Tool Gateway through an authenticated and constrained channel. They shall not receive direct network access to customer systems, provider control planes, repositories, infrastructure, or operating-system administration when the action belongs behind the gateway.

The Tool Gateway shall validate destination scope and prevent confused-deputy use, server-side request forgery, redirect escape, DNS rebinding, protocol smuggling, credential misuse, and cross-tenant connector selection.
Outbound credentials shall be bound to the exact connector and purpose where feasible. Tool results and network success remain subject to the independent Validation Pipeline.

External model access shall traverse the Model Gateway or approved Model Orchestration boundary. Workloads shall not call model providers directly when doing so bypasses provider policy, tenant configuration, privacy, routing, cost, audit, or evidence controls.
Provider endpoints, regions, identities, encryption, data-use terms, retention, failover, rate, timeout, and supported models shall be bound to the Deployment Profile.
Fallback between providers shall not silently cross residency, privacy, customer, model, capability, cost, or support boundaries. Network failover requires policy-eligible provider selection.
Storage data paths, administrative paths, replication, backup, snapshot, archive, restore, and recovery traffic shall be separated or effectively governed according to Section 7.5.

Application workloads shall not receive storage-administration or backup-deletion network reachability. Backup systems should use protected paths and identities resistant to compromise of ordinary production services.

Cross-region replication and recovery traffic shall preserve encryption, residency, tenant, capacity, ordering, and integrity. Network restoration alone shall not establish storage recovery acceptance.
Recovery networks, emergency routes, and dormant failover endpoints shall be tested, monitored, and protected from becoming hidden persistent access paths.

Build systems shall use constrained access to approved source, dependency, base-image, registry, signing, and provenance services under Section 7.4. Release builds shall not have unrestricted production or customer network access.
Artifact registries shall expose only required pull, push, replication, signing, and administrative paths. Runtime identities shall not obtain registry administration or promotion access.
Dependency and package retrieval should use approved repositories, mirrors, or integrity-verified endpoints. Proxy and cache behavior shall not substitute unapproved content.

Build network activity shall be attributable and represented in provenance where required. Network isolation shall prevent untrusted build inputs from reaching signing keys, release authority, or production systems.

Administrative access shall use strongly authenticated, least-privilege, attributable, time-bound paths appropriate to risk. Private network membership or VPN connection alone shall not grant administration.

Direct inbound management access from the public internet is prohibited unless an exact emergency or customer-controlled profile provides equivalent assurance. Shared bastion accounts and unmanaged jump hosts are prohibited.

Support access to customer or tenant environments shall require purpose, authorization, scope, time limit, tenant awareness, monitoring, and evidence. Persistent support tunnels shall not be created for convenience.
Break-glass network paths shall be separately protected, narrowly scoped, exercised, monitored, and reviewed. They shall not become ordinary operations.

Customer APIs, private endpoints, peering, tunnels, dedicated circuits, allowlists, federation paths, webhooks, and connectors shall be defined through a customer-specific or profile-specific connectivity agreement.

The agreement shall identify endpoints, identities, routes, domains, protocols, encryption, certificates, address ownership, network translation, availability, monitoring, incident contacts, change windows, testing, and shared responsibilities.

Customer IP allowlists may reduce exposure but shall not replace authentication and authorization. Shared customer address space, network translation, overlapping ranges, remote users, and provider egress can limit identity value.

Customer-managed connectivity shall not be represented as ILATEN-controlled when ILATEN lacks the authority or telemetry to verify it. Unsupported customer constraints shall lead to scope restriction or contract correction rather than hidden control degradation.

Hybrid Deployment Profiles shall define trust boundaries between ILATEN-managed, customer-managed, provider-managed, on-premises, edge, and cloud networks. Each transition shall authenticate and authorize the exact service and purpose.
Routing domains, overlapping addresses, network translation, proxying, split DNS, inspection, certificate trust, latency, availability, bandwidth, and operational ownership shall be documented.

Loss of the hybrid link shall have defined behavior for task intake, execution, approval, validation, evidence, queued work, timeout, and recovery. Offline continuation shall occur only under an approved constrained profile.

An isolated Deployment Profile shall define which communication is absent, local, periodically transferred, or mediated through a controlled gateway. Isolation claims shall reflect all management, update, support, telemetry, time, licensing, and recovery paths.

Import and export gateways shall verify identity, content integrity, malware status, authorization, tenant, purpose, classification, and chain of custody. Removable media and one-way transfer mechanisms remain governed interfaces.
Offline certificate, trust-store, revocation, DNS, time, model, artifact, vulnerability, and policy updates shall have bounded procedures and support limitations.
DNS is a critical dependency and shall have approved ownership, authoritative zones, registrars, resolvers, records, access, change control, logging, redundancy, security, and recovery.

Production domains and records shall use organizational ownership and protected administrator identities. Personal registrar accounts, shared credentials, and unreviewed manual changes are prohibited.

Internal and external DNS views, search domains, split-horizon behavior, service discovery, caching, negative caching, and time-to-live values shall be documented where they affect routing or failover.

Resolvers shall be protected from spoofing, poisoning, unauthorized recursion, data exfiltration, and policy bypass. Encrypted DNS may be used according to the profile, but it shall not bypass organizational filtering or monitoring without authorization.
DNS resolution does not authenticate the destination. Transport identity and application verification remain required.

Service discovery shall provide current endpoint information without becoming an authorization mechanism. Registration, deregistration, health, ownership, environment, tenant behavior, and staleness shall be governed.
Only authorized services shall publish protected names or endpoints. Discovery poisoning, stale endpoints, cross-environment collision, and ambiguous naming shall be prevented or detected.
Clients shall validate service identity after discovery. A discovered endpoint shall not be trusted solely because it was returned by a registry or cluster service.
Failover and load balancing through discovery shall preserve region, tenant, release, data, policy, and support constraints.

Address spaces, subnets, prefixes, service ranges, Pod ranges, node ranges, customer ranges, public addresses, virtual addresses, and reserved ranges shall be inventoried and assigned through an approved process.
Overlapping ranges shall be avoided or explicitly handled because they can cause routing ambiguity, unintended translation, policy bypass, and hybrid integration failure.
Public IP allocation shall have an owner, purpose, endpoint, environment, protection profile, and lifecycle. Unused public addresses and stale DNS records shall be removed.
IPv4 and IPv6 shall be governed together. Security controls that cover only one protocol family are incomplete where the other is enabled or reachable.
Dynamic addresses shall not be used as durable workload identity. Address changes shall not invalidate audit attribution or policy semantics.
Routes shall be least-privilege, attributable, version-controlled or equivalently governed, and reviewed for destination, next hop, propagation, priority, translation, and failure behavior.

Default routes shall be intentional. Route propagation, peering, transitive connectivity, gateway sharing, and provider-managed routing can create paths beyond the apparent diagram and shall be verified.

Production routing changes shall use controlled rollout, pre-change validation, impact analysis, rollback, monitoring, and post-change verification. Emergency routes shall be time-bounded and removed after review.
Asymmetric routing, black holes, loops, path maximum transmission unit, fragmentation, and stateful-firewall behavior shall be considered for supported protocols.
Load balancers and proxies shall have explicit frontend, backend, health, protocol, timeout, connection, retry, certificate, identity, and observability configuration.

Source identity, client address, request identifiers, tenant context, and authenticated claims shall be forwarded only through integrity-protected and trusted mechanisms. Direct backend paths shall not permit spoofing of proxy-added metadata.
Retries shall be limited to operations whose semantics permit them. A proxy shall not repeat non-idempotent Tool Gateway or customer-system actions without end-to-end reconciliation.
Health-based removal and failover shall not route traffic to an incompatible release, tenant, region, or data authority. Load distribution success is not result validation.
Network address translation may obscure original endpoints and cause many subjects to share one address. IP-based controls shall account for this loss of identity.

ilaten_requirement: Cloud and platform metadata endpoints, node-local services, link-local addresses, control-plane proxies, and credential endpoints shall be denied to ordinary workloads unless explicitly required.
Access shall use the strongest supported identity, token, hop, audience, and path restrictions. Legacy unauthenticated metadata access is prohibited for protected workloads.
Server-side request forgery defenses shall block requests to local, private, metadata, administrative, and prohibited address ranges unless the exact connector authorizes them.
DNS resolution and redirects shall be re-evaluated throughout request processing so that an initially allowed name cannot redirect or rebind to a protected endpoint.
Every rule shall have an owner, purpose, source, destination, protocol, port, direction, environment, tenant behavior, creation record, review date, and expiry where temporary.
Rules shall be as narrow as operationally feasible. Broad address ranges, all-port access, wildcard destinations, any-to-any rules, and perpetual temporary exceptions require explicit risk treatment.
Rule changes shall be version-controlled or equivalently recorded, tested, peer-reviewed or bootstrap-reviewed, approved, deployed through controlled automation, and verified after enforcement.

Unused, shadowed, duplicate, conflicting, ineffective, and stale rules shall be detected and removed through governed change. Cleanup shall not remove required recovery or evidence paths without impact analysis.
Policy existence is not enforcement evidence. Tests shall demonstrate permitted flows succeed and prohibited flows fail.
Rate controls shall protect availability, cost, provider quotas, tenant fairness, and abuse boundaries without becoming the sole authorization mechanism.
Burst, sustained rate, concurrency, payload size, timeout, retry, queue, and backoff shall be coordinated end to end. A downstream provider limit shall not cause uncontrolled retry amplification.
Rate-limit responses shall avoid exposing sensitive thresholds or cross-tenant activity. Emergency limit changes shall be attributable, time-bounded, monitored, and reviewed.
The Network Profile shall identify volumetric, protocol, application, authentication, expensive-query, model, connector, and state-exhaustion denial-of-service risks.

Security, approval, validation, audit, and evidence controls shall not be disabled merely to preserve throughput. Load shedding shall prioritize safe rejection over unaudited or unauthorized processing.
Tenant-level abuse shall not exhaust shared resources without detection and containment. Critical control and evidence paths should have protected capacity.
DDoS failover shall preserve domain, certificate, identity, data, region, privacy, and support constraints.

Capacity planning shall cover bandwidth, packets, connections, flows, DNS queries, certificate operations, proxy resources, gateway limits, tunnel limits, NAT ports, load balancer rules, and provider quotas.
Objectives shall include latency, throughput, jitter, loss, connection setup, tail behavior, and availability for exact flows. Average response time alone is insufficient.
Capacity shall account for encryption, inspection, service proxies, replication, backup, model payloads, artifact transfer, telemetry, failover, and incident conditions.

Optimization shall not bypass segmentation, encryption, identity, validation, audit, evidence, or tenant isolation. Direct paths created for performance require the same authority and security controls.

Multi-region designs shall define active and standby regions, data authority, routing, health, failover, failback, DNS, anycast or equivalent mechanisms, certificates, identity, keys, provider dependencies, and customer connectivity.
Traffic shall not fail over into a region that violates residency, customer, model-provider, storage, release, or support constraints.
Health checks shall distinguish network reachability from application, data, policy, validation, and evidence readiness. A reachable region is not necessarily eligible to accept authoritative work.
Split-brain routing shall be prevented or reconciled with Section 7.5. Failback shall be controlled and evidence-backed.

Single points of failure shall be identified by flow and recovery objective. Redundant components that share one account, region, control plane, route, certificate, or administrative identity may not provide independent resilience.
Failover behavior shall be deterministic and tested. Automatic failover shall not select an unapproved provider, public path, region, endpoint, or tenant scope.
Maintenance and provider outages shall have customer communication, degraded-mode, queue, timeout, recovery, and validation plans appropriate to the service.

Reliable time is required for certificate validation, token expiry, capability expiry, approval validity, evidence ordering, incident reconstruction, rate windows, leases, and distributed coordination.
Approved time sources, hierarchy, authentication where supported, redundancy, drift limits, monitoring, and failure behavior shall be defined. Workloads shall not use arbitrary public time servers.

Clock uncertainty shall not silently extend approval, capability, certificate, token, retention, or lease validity. Authority-sensitive operations shall fail safely or enter a documented constrained mode.
Time synchronization traffic shall be protected from spoofing, redirection, and unauthorized configuration. Time correction events shall be observable and evidenced when material.

Network telemetry shall provide sufficient source, destination, identity where available, direction, protocol, port, bytes, outcome, time, enforcement point, environment, tenant-safe correlation, and rule context for operations and investigation.

Payload capture shall be exceptional, purpose-bound, authorized, minimized, encrypted, access-controlled, time-limited, and reviewed. Packet captures can contain credentials, personal data, customer content, model inputs, and secrets.
Telemetry gaps, sampling, aggregation, NAT, encryption, proxying, and provider limitations shall be documented. Absence of a log entry is not proof that traffic did not occur.

The Audit Engine shall record material network events including endpoint publication, certificate issuance and revocation, rule change, route change, gateway change, connectivity grant, privileged session, Tool Gateway connection, provider path selection, failover, isolation, emergency bypass, incident containment, and retirement.
