ilaten_requirement: Cloud, orchestration, container, node, runtime, storage, network, DNS, certificate, queue, registry, and load-balancer telemetry shall map to resource identity and Deployment Profile.
Provider-native signals shall be normalized where necessary while preserving original provider identity, semantics, collection delay, and limitations.
Kubernetes metrics, logs, and traces shall include cluster, namespace, workload, Pod, container, node, controller, and release context within cardinality and privacy budgets.
Infrastructure health does not establish application, tenant, policy, validation, or business health. Cross-layer correlation shall preserve the distinction.

Instrumentation shall be included as an engineering requirement rather than added only after incident. Service design shall identify critical operations, boundaries, dependencies, failure modes, and required signals.
Manual and automatic instrumentation may coexist. Automatically generated telemetry shall be reviewed for semantic accuracy, data exposure, cardinality, performance, and duplication.
Instrumentation libraries and runtime hooks are supply-chain dependencies under Section 3.7. They shall be versioned, supported, tested, and prevented from receiving unnecessary authority.
Instrumentation failure shall not corrupt business processing. Critical audit and evidence emission follows its own mandatory path and shall not be silently downgraded to best-effort telemetry.
Collectors shall use verified workload identity, least privilege, encrypted transport, bounded receivers, controlled processors, protected exporters, and explicit tenant routing.

Collection components shall not receive universal access to customer payloads, secrets, business databases, orchestration administration, or canonical authority merely because they observe many services.

Collector configuration shall be version-controlled or equivalently governed. Receivers, processors, filters, sampling, redaction, routing, retries, queues, and exporters shall be attributable and testable.
Processing may enrich, normalize, filter, redact, aggregate, sample, route, or transform signals. Each transformation shall have a defined semantic and privacy effect.
Enrichment shall use trusted resource metadata. Untrusted request attributes shall not become authoritative resource, tenant, release, environment, or security labels.

Redaction shall occur as close to the source as practical when sensitive data is not required downstream. Central redaction alone may leave protected data in local buffers, network paths, or failed exports.
Aggregation and transformation shall preserve units, time, cardinality, and interpretation. Lossy processing shall be disclosed and shall not be used for completeness claims.

Sampling shall be signal- and purpose-specific. Metrics commonly use aggregation rather than trace-style sampling; traces may use head, tail, probabilistic, rule-based, or adaptive sampling; logs and profiles require their own policies.

Sampling shall retain sufficient visibility for errors, high latency, security events, Tool Gateway actions, validation failures, rare states, and tenant-impacting incidents as required. A global fixed rate may miss material low-volume events.
Sampling decisions and effective rates shall be observable. Sampled data shall be represented as sampled and shall not support unsupported completeness claims.
Untrusted clients shall not force full sampling or suppress sampling through propagated flags. Security and audit requirements shall not depend solely on sampled operational telemetry.
Partial or late spans shall not cause incorrect classification. The profile shall define decision windows, incomplete-trace handling, capacity, and loss behavior.
Telemetry quality shall be evaluated across completeness, accuracy, timeliness, consistency, continuity, uniqueness, lineage, semantic correctness, and availability.
Every signal used for autoscaling, monitoring, incident response, contractual reporting, security decisions, or capacity claims shall have a quality objective and known limitations.
Quality defects shall be observable and enter the Defect Lifecycle. A dashboard shall not hide uncertain or incomplete data behind a normal status.
Telemetry shall record timestamps with an unambiguous representation and distinguish event time, start time, end time, observation time, and ingestion time where material.
Clock synchronization and uncertainty shall follow Section 7.6. Distributed traces may contain clock skew; duration and causal interpretation shall not rely blindly on wall-clock ordering.
Backfilled or delayed telemetry shall preserve original occurrence and ingestion context. It shall not rewrite historical dashboards without an attributable change in interpretation.
Telemetry shall be classified data. It can contain personal data, customer identifiers, repository paths, network topology, model usage, operational secrets, security events, and behavioral patterns.

Collection shall be limited to a defined purpose. Raw request and response bodies, prompts, model outputs, documents, secrets, credentials, tokens, headers, cookies, query strings, database statements, file paths, and stack variables shall be excluded by default or transformed through approved controls.
Tenant, user, and customer correlation shall use the minimum necessary protected reference. Human-readable personal or customer names shall not be used as general telemetry dimensions.
Debug or incident verbosity shall be time-bounded, authorized, monitored, and automatically returned to the approved baseline. Elevated collection shall not become permanent through inaction.

Tenant isolation shall cover instrumentation, context propagation, collection, buffers, processors, sampling, export, storage, query, dashboards, alerts, customer access, support access, deletion, and incident investigation.

Cross-tenant aggregation requires explicit purpose, authorization, privacy treatment, output control, and evidence. Aggregated metrics shall not permit re-identification or disclosure of another tenant's activity.

Telemetry from customer-controlled deployments shall not be exported to ILATEN unless the Deployment Profile, contract, role assessment, consent or other lawful basis where applicable, and network policy authorize it.
Telemetry endpoints shall authenticate producers and consumers, encrypt protected transport, validate schemas and sizes, enforce rates, and prevent arbitrary tenant or resource spoofing.

Collectors and backends are high-value targets because they aggregate operational and security information. Administrative access shall use strong authentication, least privilege, time-bound elevation, logging, and review.
Telemetry query, export, deletion, retention, redaction, sampling, and configuration privileges shall be separated according to risk.

Injection through log bodies, span attributes, metric labels, dashboard variables, query languages, links, or rendered content shall be prevented. Observability interfaces shall treat all telemetry as untrusted content.

Transport integrity and authenticated producer identity shall protect telemetry against spoofing and alteration. Provider-native and customer-provided signals shall retain source and assurance metadata.

Operational telemetry may be sampled, transformed, aggregated, or delayed and therefore shall not be represented as immutable truth. Integrity controls do not establish completeness or semantic correctness.
High-impact telemetry configuration changes, such as disabling export, changing sampling, removing redaction, or altering tenant routing, shall be audited and evidenced.
Where telemetry contributes to a security or contractual claim, the exact source, transformation, quality, retention, and verification shall be documented.
The Telemetry Pipeline shall define buffering, queue durability, retry, ordering, batching, rate, overflow, drop, shutdown, and recovery behavior.

Ordinary telemetry shall not cause the application to fail catastrophically through blocking, memory exhaustion, disk exhaustion, retry storms, or exporter latency. Bounded asynchronous export is preferred where appropriate.
Loss policy shall prioritize mandatory security and operational signals according to profile. Dropped telemetry shall be counted and reported; silent loss is prohibited.
Audit Engine and Evidence Chain emission follows separate mandatory durability semantics. It shall not be treated as optional telemetry when the observability path is overloaded.

Collection and storage shall have availability appropriate to the operational and incident needs of each signal. Critical services may require local buffering, multiple collectors, regional aggregation, or alternate export.
Redundant collectors that share one configuration, identity, route, provider, or backend may not provide independent resilience.

Telemetry outage shall not grant permission, accept results, disable policy, or hide current health. Services shall enter the profile's safe observability-degraded mode and raise an independently reachable indication where possible.
Recovery shall reconcile buffered data, disclose gaps, restore semantic configuration, and validate tenant routing before normal claims resume.

Telemetry storage shall follow an approved record-class-specific schedule based on operational, security, incident, contractual, privacy, and data-minimization requirements. Retention is not indefinite by default.

Deletion shall address primary storage, indexes, caches, replicas, archives, exports, and customer copies according to role and technical feasibility. Restored backups shall reapply current deletion requirements.

Observability Profiles shall identify collection, processing, storage, backup, support, and administrative locations. Provider region settings shall not be assumed to cover global control planes or support access.

Customer-controlled, hybrid, and isolated deployments may keep telemetry locally, export a reduced set, or provide customer-operated integration. The exact boundary and limitation shall be documented.
Cross-border telemetry transfer shall follow Section 3.12. Operational convenience shall not override customer, legal, privacy, or residency obligations.
When ILATEN lacks access to customer telemetry, support and service claims shall state the resulting limitation honestly.
Telemetry query access shall be least-privilege by service, environment, tenant, signal, time range, field, and purpose where the platform supports it.

Broad production access shall not be granted solely because a person is an engineer or support operator. Sensitive searches, exports, packet captures, profiles, and cross-tenant views require elevated authorization.
Saved queries, dashboards, notebooks, links, and exports are governed artifacts when they expose protected data. Sharing shall preserve access controls and expiry.
Query activity, administrative changes, bulk export, retention override, and customer-data access shall be logged and audited according to risk.
Dashboards shall state source, scope, environment, release, region, tenant-safe context, time range, freshness, sampling, and known limitations.
Visualization shall not convert correlation into causation or incomplete data into certainty. A green status shall not imply policy compliance, evidence completeness, or business acceptance.
Dashboards shall use governed definitions for shared enterprise metrics. Private exploratory dashboards shall not become official customer or investor claims without validation.
Dynamic variables and links shall be sanitized. Dashboard access shall not permit query injection or navigation into unauthorized tenant data.
Observability Profiles shall define ingestion, storage, query, export, sampling, cardinality, retention, and support cost budgets.

Costs shall be allocated by service, environment, signal, and privacy-safe tenant scope where feasible. A single high-cardinality field or verbose debug mode can create material cost and availability risk.
Cost controls shall prefer instrumentation correction, aggregation, bounded sampling, and retention alignment rather than deleting required security or diagnostic visibility.
Provider budget alarms and automatic limits shall not silently discard mandatory signals. Controlled degradation shall be explicit and observable.
Multi-region telemetry shall preserve region identity, time, release, tenant, provider, and failover context. Regional aggregation shall not hide localized failure or residency boundaries.
Centralized telemetry can simplify correlation but may create a global dependency, transfer obligation, and incident bottleneck. Regional and central responsibilities shall be explicit.
Failover shall preserve telemetry continuity or disclose gaps. The observability system shall identify which region was authoritative for the workload and data at each time.
Cross-region queries and exports shall follow access, privacy, residency, and cost controls.

Kubernetes observability shall include workload and relevant cluster metrics, logs, traces, events, resource state, controller outcomes, scheduling, node, network, storage, and autoscaling signals according to the profile.
Cluster, namespace, Pod, container, node, controller, and workload identities shall remain distinct. Ephemeral instance churn shall not erase service-level continuity.
Kubernetes system traces and telemetry may use OpenTelemetry-compatible export where supported. Feature maturity, component support, sampling, overhead, and security shall be recorded.

Kubernetes events are short-lived operational signals and shall not be treated as durable audit or evidence. Cluster observability does not replace application or ILATEN canonical-flow instrumentation.
Customer-facing telemetry shall use defined product contracts, tenant isolation, units, freshness, retention, completeness, and support status.
Customers shall receive only their authorized scope. Shared infrastructure, other tenants, internal security controls, provider details, and sensitive topology shall be protected.

Export interfaces shall provide versioned schemas, rate and size limits, authentication, encryption, replay behavior, and delivery guarantees. Export success is not proof that a customer consumed the data.
Customer-provided collectors or backends shall be governed through shared responsibility. ILATEN shall not claim completeness beyond the export boundary it controls.

Every deployment, configuration change, policy change, feature enablement, model change, connector change, infrastructure change, and failover shall emit an attributable change marker or equivalent correlation signal.
Change markers shall identify release, environment, region, scope, owner, change record, and rollout stage without exposing protected content.
Observability shall support comparison before, during, and after change. Correlation does not prove the change caused an observed effect; investigation and validation remain required.
Instrumentation and semantic changes are release changes and shall be tested for compatibility, cost, dashboards, monitoring, logging, and evidence impact.

Observability shall support detection triage, timeline reconstruction, dependency analysis, scope estimation, performance analysis, and recovery verification without replacing Incident Response or forensic authority.

Incident elevation may temporarily increase sampling, tracing, profiling, or logging under controlled authorization. The change shall be time-bounded, capacity-assessed, privacy-reviewed, and evidenced.
Telemetry shall preserve original source, time, transformation, sampling, and quality metadata. Investigators shall not treat a backend reconstruction as complete when collection gaps exist.
Evidence selected from telemetry shall enter the governed Evidence Chain with source and limitation recorded. Copying a dashboard image is not sufficient evidence by itself.

The Validation Pipeline shall independently verify observability requirements appropriate to the gate. Validation may test signal presence, resource identity, context propagation, semantic conventions, units, cardinality, redaction, tenant routing, sampling, pipeline loss, access, retention, and backend portability.
Positive and negative tests shall confirm both useful telemetry and absence of prohibited secrets or protected content. A successful exporter connection does not prove safe instrumentation.
The component producing telemetry, collector, or backend shall not be the sole validator of its own completeness. Known sampling and loss shall be represented honestly.

Material Observability Profile approvals, instrumentation changes, semantic convention changes, sampling changes, redaction changes, tenant-routing changes, export changes, retention changes, privileged query access, incident elevation, and major telemetry loss shall be recorded by the Audit Engine.

ilaten_requirement: Observability changes shall follow Section 5.7 and include purpose, affected signals, semantics, privacy, tenant, performance, cost, compatibility, storage, dashboards, monitoring, logging, audit, evidence, rollout, validation, and rollback.

An observability backend migration shall preserve required history, semantics, queries, access, retention, incident support, and evidence references. Dual-write periods shall identify duplicate, loss, and authority behavior.
Provider feature activation shall not silently expand telemetry collection or data use.

During a registered Single-Maintainer Bootstrap Profile, one authorized maintainer may temporarily perform multiple observability roles where independent personnel are unavailable. The absence of independent review shall be recorded and shall not be represented as Enterprise separation of duties.

The bootstrap profile shall maintain organizational ownership, least privilege, protected accounts and recovery factors, version-controlled configuration, mandatory Quality Gates, exact change attribution, privacy-safe defaults, bounded cost, protected Audit and Evidence integration, periodic access review, tested export and recovery, and a dated exit plan.

High-impact changes involving production payload collection, cross-tenant views, customer exports, global telemetry, profiling, redaction removal, retention expansion, or Audit/Evidence integration shall receive qualified external review before affecting a Stable release, production environment, or Enterprise operating profile; otherwise they shall remain blocked or constrained.

Bootstrap operation shall not waive protections where one-person compromise could expose multiple tenants, disable accountability, falsify official claims, or create unacceptable customer risk. Continued single-maintainer operation shall not become permanent through inaction.
Before an Observability Profile or material change becomes eligible, the applicable gates shall verify:
- explicit purpose, owner, service, environment, region, release, tenant, and support scope;
- defined metrics, traces, logs, events, profiles, health, topology, and correlation requirements;
- trusted resource and instrumentation identity;
- approved semantic conventions, units, attributes, names, and versions;
- safe context propagation and bounded baggage across trust boundaries;
- privacy, minimization, redaction, tenant isolation, residency, access, retention, and deletion;
- bounded metric cardinality, trace sampling, log volume, profile scope, and cost;
- collector identity, configuration, processing, routing, export, buffering, loss, and recovery;
- signal completeness, accuracy, timeliness, continuity, lineage, and known limitations;
- canonical-flow, Control Plane, intelligence, Model Gateway, Tool Gateway, Validation Pipeline, Audit Engine, Evidence Chain, and infrastructure coverage;
- customer-controlled, hybrid, isolated, and multi-region behavior;
- dashboards, queries, exports, incident elevation, and change correlation;
- positive and negative independent Validation Pipeline tests;
- required Audit Engine and Evidence Chain records; and
- exception ownership, scope, expiry, monitoring, and residual-risk acceptance.
No single dashboard, trace, metric, collector status, backend query, green health indicator, or telemetry completeness claim shall satisfy the complete gate.
The following practices are prohibited unless an explicitly defined canonical exception applies:
- treating telemetry, dashboards, anomalies, provider status, or observability tools as business authority;
- conflating Observability, Monitoring, Logging, Audit, Evidence, or Validation;
- using trace, request, span, or baggage identifiers as tenant authority, approval, or capability;
- trusting client-supplied resource, environment, release, tenant, or internal identity attributes;
- placing secrets, credentials, tokens, prompts, model outputs, documents, customer content, or unrestricted personal data in telemetry;
- using unbounded metric labels, span names, events, baggage, log fields, profiles, or debug collection;
- allowing external callers to force full sampling or suppress required visibility;
- representing sampled, aggregated, delayed, or transformed telemetry as complete truth;
- allowing collectors or backends universal production authority because they receive broad telemetry;
- permitting cross-tenant query, export, dashboard, cache, or routing without effective isolation;
- disabling redaction, encryption, authentication, or tenant controls for troubleshooting convenience;
- letting telemetry export block or exhaust business processing without bounded failure behavior;
- silently dropping telemetry without loss accounting;
- treating ordinary telemetry as the mandatory Audit Engine or Evidence Chain path;
- treating a green health check as release, validation, evidence, or business acceptance;
- retaining high-volume protected telemetry indefinitely by default;
- allowing incident-level verbosity or profiling to become permanent through inaction;
- treating automatic instrumentation or semantic mapping as accurate without validation;
- making unreviewed direct production observability changes;
- representing bootstrap self-review as independent Enterprise assurance; or
- giving any telemetry protocol, collector, backend, dashboard, provider, tool, customer preference, sales commitment, or engineering convenience architectural authority.
It does not claim that complete observability is technically achievable for every provider, customer environment, encrypted payload, or external system. Known limits shall be represented honestly.
- every production service is governed by an approved Observability Profile;
- Observability, Monitoring, Logging, Audit, Evidence, and Validation remain distinct;
- open and portable signal semantics are used where practical without granting protocol authority;
- resource, instrumentation, service, environment, region, release, and tenant-safe identities are explicit;
- metrics, traces, logs, events, profiles, health, and topology have governed purposes and contracts;
- context propagation and baggage are validated, minimized, bounded, and non-authoritative;
- signal correlation preserves canonical task, approval, capability, Tool Gateway, validation, audit, and evidence distinctions;
- semantic conventions, units, cardinality, sampling, aggregation, and transformations are versioned and validated;
- protected data, secrets, customer content, and personal data are minimized and access-controlled;
- tenant isolation covers collection, processing, buffering, export, storage, query, dashboard, and deletion;
- Telemetry Pipeline identity, security, capacity, loss, backpressure, availability, and recovery are controlled;
- canonical-flow, Control Plane, intelligence, Tool Gateway, validation, Trust Core, and infrastructure behavior are observable within defined limits;
- customer, hybrid, isolated, multi-region, residency, and export boundaries are explicit;
- observability changes, privileged access, incident elevation, and material data loss are audited and evidenced;
- the Validation Pipeline independently verifies observability controls without accepting business results;
- Audit Engine and Evidence Chain controls operate continuously and remain canonical;
- bootstrap limitations remain explicit, temporary, constrained, and subject to dated exit criteria; and
- architecture-significant observability decisions require an authorized ADR.
The following invariants are binding:
- observability reveals system behavior but does not create ILATEN business authority;
- telemetry is observation and not policy permission, approval, capability, validation, or acceptance;
- Observability, Monitoring, Logging, Audit, Evidence, and Validation remain separate capabilities;
- trace context and baggage are correlation data, not Immutable Context or authority;
- incoming telemetry context is untrusted at every boundary;
- signal semantics, units, resource identity, sampling, transformation, and quality are explicit;
- sampled or aggregated telemetry is not represented as complete truth;
- secrets, credentials, customer content, prompts, model outputs, and protected data are excluded by default;
- tenant isolation covers the complete Telemetry Pipeline and access lifecycle;
- the deterministic Policy Engine remains within the ILATEN Control Plane;
- the Approval Engine remains the accountable approval authority;
- every governed external action remains mediated by the Tool Gateway under constrained capability;
- the Validation Pipeline remains independent;
- Audit Engine and Evidence Chain controls operate continuously and are not replaced by metrics, traces, logs, events, profiles, dashboards, or provider telemetry;
- instrumentation, collectors, and backends receive no architectural authority;
- telemetry loss, quality limits, sampling, and collection gaps are represented honestly;
- observability cost and cardinality remain bounded;
- elevated debugging and profiling are authorized, time-bounded, and reviewed;
- bootstrap operation does not imply independent Enterprise assurance; and
- architecture-significant observability decisions require an authorized ADR.

An Observability implementation is non-conformant if it conflates telemetry with authority or acceptance; merges Observability, Monitoring, Logging, Audit, Evidence, and Validation into one ambiguous function; trusts propagated identifiers as tenant or capability authority; collects secrets, prompts, outputs, customer content, or protected data without exact governance; permits unbounded cardinality, baggage, sampling, profiling, or cost; hides telemetry loss, semantic drift, sampling, or quality limitations; allows cross-tenant access or routing; grants collectors or backends broad production authority; lets telemetry failure disable canonical controls; treats dashboards, health, traces, metrics, logs, events, profiles, or provider status as independent validation or canonical evidence; misrepresents customer-controlled or bootstrap limitations; or gives any protocol, collector, backend, dashboard, provider, customer preference, sales commitment, model output, or engineering convenience architectural authority.

A monitoring condition is an operational assessment, not a policy decision or independent validation result. An alert, alarm, anomaly, threshold breach, service-level objective violation, provider warning, dashboard state, or automated response shall not by itself grant tenant access, human approval, task capability, Tool Gateway authority, release acceptance, compliance, or architectural authority.
**Evidence** binds material records required to prove or examine what occurred.

Open and portable alert definitions, service objectives, labels, and notification contracts should be preferred where practical. Technology replacement shall preserve operational meaning, state, routing, history, and evidence.
A tool's default alert, severity, anomaly score, health state, or best-practice template shall not become an ILATEN standard without review and validation.
Monitoring shall:
**Inhibition.** Suppression of dependent alert notifications when a defined causal or higher-level alert is active. It shall not conceal unrelated failures.
Every production service and critical platform capability shall have an approved Monitoring Profile defining:
A service shall not be represented as production-ready when material failure modes lack an owner, detectable condition, safe response, or accepted documented limitation.
Indicators shall measure behavior that matters to users, customers, canonical control flow, security, and operations. Resource utilization alone is not a service outcome.
Every indicator shall define numerator, denominator, unit, source, aggregation, scope, successful and unsuccessful events, excluded events, missing-data behavior, window, freshness, and owner.

Availability indicators shall distinguish reachable, authenticated, authorized, accepted, processed, validated, and delivered outcomes where relevant. A successful transport response is not necessarily a successful ILATEN task.
Latency indicators shall define start and end boundaries, queue time, external dependency time, approval waiting, validation time, and percentiles. Averages shall not replace tail latency.
Correctness is rarely inferred from infrastructure telemetry alone. Where a correctness indicator uses validation outcome, its exact coverage and limitations shall be stated.
Objectives shall bind to a defined service, customer scope, Deployment Profile, release, region, measurement window, indicator, and data-quality standard.
Objectives shall be achievable, evidence-backed, and aligned to product maturity. Alpha, Beta, Release Candidate, Stable, and supported release profiles may use different objectives and claims.
An objective shall not be raised or lowered to match recent results without accountable product, reliability, architecture, and commercial review. Objective changes are governed decisions.
Unmeasured time, monitoring gaps, excluded maintenance, customer-caused conditions, and provider limitations shall be represented honestly rather than silently removed.
Budget consumption shall use the exact objective model and verified data. Missing or delayed telemetry shall not be treated automatically as successful service.

Exhaustion may trigger change restriction, reliability work, capacity adjustment, provider review, or product communication. It shall not automatically halt security remediation or mandatory compliance change.
Every condition shall define expression, input signals, units, labels, evaluation interval, pending duration, severity, recovery, missing-data behavior, owner, and change history.
Conditions shall be scoped narrowly enough to identify affected service, environment, region, release, tenant-safe boundary, dependency, and operation without creating unbounded alert cardinality.
Pending periods and hysteresis shall reduce transient noise without delaying material detection beyond the response objective.
Thresholds shall use the correct unit, aggregation, evaluation interval, and duration. A threshold copied across services without workload context is insufficient.
Warning and critical thresholds shall correspond to distinct response windows and actions rather than arbitrary colors.
Thresholds shall be reviewed after architecture, capacity, release, provider, or objective changes. Stale thresholds create false confidence or alert noise.
Training or baseline data shall be tenant-safe, representative, time-bounded, and protected. Attack or incident periods shall not silently become normal baseline.
Anomaly scores shall not directly grant or revoke business authority. High-impact automated response requires deterministic bounded policy and human accountability where applicable.
Model-generated monitoring recommendations shall be reviewed before they alter production alerting or response. The intelligence layer remains non-authoritative.
Monitoring shall distinguish healthy, unhealthy, unknown, not applicable, intentionally disabled, and data-unavailable states. Unknown shall not be represented as healthy.

Missing-data behavior shall reflect the signal. Absence of request errors may mean no traffic; absence of heartbeats may indicate telemetry or service failure; absence of audit events may be material.
Signal freshness, last successful evaluation, collection delay, sampling, and pipeline loss shall be visible. Alerts based on stale data shall carry that limitation.
Monitoring gaps shall create their own condition where the lost visibility is material. Critical controls shall not rely on one unmonitored collection path.

Monitoring may use inactive, pending, firing, acknowledged, mitigated, resolved, expired, or equivalent alert states. These are monitoring states and shall not create a competing Incident Response or Defect Lifecycle.

Resolution shall require the defined recovery condition and sufficient stability. Automatic disappearance caused by missing telemetry, rule deletion, label change, or backend restart shall not be represented as true recovery.
Alert history shall preserve start, transitions, acknowledgements, silences, routing, escalation, response, recovery, and closure references.
Alert identity shall remain stable across evaluations and shall include only bounded labels required for deduplication, routing, scope, and ownership.

Labels may include service, environment, region, release, severity, condition class, dependency, and privacy-safe tenant scope. Request IDs, raw URLs, user IDs, task IDs, error text, prompts, or unbounded provider fields shall not be alert labels.
Annotations may contain human guidance, summary, impact, dashboard, and runbook references but shall not contain secrets or protected customer data.
Severity shall be assigned from impact, urgency, scope, security, customer, data, evidence, recovery, and time sensitivity—not from one metric value alone.
The severity model shall define required acknowledgement, escalation, communication, and response targets. Severity names shall be consistent across services.
Downgrading severity shall be attributable and justified. It shall not suppress legal or customer obligations.
Every actionable alert shall route to a current accountable owner with an escalation path. Ownership shall survive team rename, service transfer, holiday, absence, and provider boundary.

Routing shall use service, severity, environment, region, tenant-safe scope, time, and support profile as appropriate. Customer-specific alerts shall not route protected details to unauthorized recipients.
Notification channels are delivery mechanisms, not authoritative alert stores. Channel failure shall not delete or resolve the alert.
Routing changes shall be version-controlled or equivalently governed, tested, and periodically reviewed.
Deduplication shall combine repeated notifications for the same alert identity without collapsing distinct tenants, regions, releases, dependencies, or root causes.
Grouping may reduce notification storms by combining related alerts, but the underlying instances and impact shall remain visible.
Deduplication keys shall not use unstable or unbounded values. Incorrect grouping can hide widespread impact or cross-tenant exposure.
Recovery notification shall correspond to the exact deduplicated or grouped condition and shall not imply resolution of unrelated instances.
Inhibition rules shall define source, target, equal-scope labels, duration, and safety. Missing labels shall not accidentally inhibit broad unrelated alerts.
Security, Audit Engine, Evidence Chain, tenant-isolation, and data-loss alerts shall not be inhibited merely because a general outage is active unless the risk treatment explicitly permits it.
Silences shall be exact, attributable, time-bounded, purpose-bound, and approved according to severity. Open-ended or all-alert silences are prohibited.
Silence matchers shall be reviewed to prevent broader scope than intended. Silence of one tenant, region, release, or maintenance activity shall not hide another.
Active and expired silences shall be periodically reviewed. Repeated silence of the same alert indicates a defect in the service, rule, objective, or operating model.
Planned maintenance shall define scope, owner, expected signals, allowed suppression, customer communication, start, end, rollback, validation, and evidence.
Maintenance windows shall not suppress unexpected security, tenant, data-integrity, Audit Engine, Evidence Chain, or broader dependency failures.
Expired maintenance suppression shall end automatically. A maintenance window shall not be extended indefinitely to conceal unresolved failure.
An actionable alert shall indicate what is wrong, affected scope, severity, start time, relevant evidence, likely impact, owner, runbook, and immediate safe action.

Alert quality shall be measured through precision, recall where assessable, actionability, duplicate rate, acknowledgement time, escalation, stale rate, false-positive rate, false-negative discoveries, and operator feedback.
Alerts that cannot lead to a meaningful decision should be removed, converted to dashboards, aggregated, or redesigned. Deleting noise shall not remove required coverage.
Post-incident review shall identify which alerts were early, late, missing, misleading, redundant, or unactionable.
Alert volume shall remain within the human and organizational capacity to respond. Excessive alerts reduce detection quality and encourage unsafe silencing.
Priority shall favor user impact, security, data, policy, validation, audit, evidence, and imminent saturation over low-value infrastructure variation.
Alert load shall be measured by owner, severity, service, time, and recurrence. Chronic alert burden shall enter Continuous Improvement and Defect Lifecycles.
Every material alert shall reference a versioned runbook or equivalent response guidance appropriate to the operating profile.

Runbooks shall define intent, scope, prerequisites, identity, data protection, diagnostic steps, safe containment, escalation, rollback, validation, customer communication, evidence, and stop conditions.
Commands and links shall be reviewed and safe against wrong environment, tenant, region, or broad target. Destructive steps shall require explicit confirmation and authority.
Runbooks shall not grant permission merely by being accessible. Every action remains subject to current identity, role, policy, approval, Tool Gateway, and change requirements.
Escalation shall define who is notified, when, through which independent channels, and what happens if acknowledgement or progress targets are missed.
High-severity conditions shall have paths to incident command, security, privacy, legal, customer, provider, architecture, and executive authority as applicable.
Escalation shall preserve accurate scope and uncertainty. An alert shall not be represented as confirmed breach or root cause before qualified assessment.
Escalation paths and contacts shall be tested and kept current. One unavailable individual shall not be a permanent Enterprise dependency.
Automated response shall be deterministic, least-privilege, idempotent or reconcilable, time-bounded, attributable, reversible where required, and constrained by an approved Response Profile.
Monitoring shall not directly approve business tasks, expand capabilities, bypass the Tool Gateway, accept results, alter Evidence Chain history, or make legal determinations.
The response shall validate preconditions, current state, target scope, release, tenant, and expected effect. Failure or ambiguous outcome shall escalate rather than repeat blindly.

Every automated or semi-automated response shall define trigger, authority, actor identity, scope, preconditions, action, maximum impact, timeout, retry, rollback, evidence, human oversight, and exit conditions.
Response profiles shall distinguish advisory, approval-required, automatic reversible, automatic protective, and prohibited actions.
Anomaly or model-generated recommendations may propose a response but shall not execute it without deterministic evaluation and required approval.
Response automation shall enter a safe mode when monitoring input is stale, contradictory, incomplete, or unavailable.

Synthetic identities, tenants, data, and credentials shall be clearly segregated and least-privilege. Synthetic checks shall not perform irreversible customer or Tool Gateway actions unless a dedicated safe target and reconciliation exist.
Internal indicators provide diagnostic depth but can remain green while the customer journey fails. They shall complement, not replace, outcome-oriented monitoring.
White-box access shall be least-privilege and protect topology, secrets, tenant data, and security controls.
Monitoring queries shall be efficient and shall not create load that causes the condition being monitored.

Synthetic transactions shall use controlled test accounts, data, destinations, schedules, rate, and cleanup. They shall be distinguishable from customer traffic and excluded or included in objectives according to explicit policy.

End-to-end synthetics may test canonical flow through identity, policy, approval simulation where safe, Tool Gateway test connectors, validation, and delivery. They shall not use production approval authority or irreversible external systems without exact control.
Synthetic failures shall be correlated with internal telemetry before severity is assigned. A test harness defect shall not be represented as customer outage.
Synthetic data and credentials shall follow secrets, retention, and tenant-isolation controls.
Critical product journeys shall have defined entry, successful outcome, failure categories, dependencies, latency, and validation requirements.
Monitoring shall distinguish user waiting from processing, provider latency, approval delay, queueing, validation, and delivery.
Journey completion shall not be inferred solely from a final HTTP response if authoritative state or validation is pending.
Monitoring shall evaluate the twelve canonical operational stages and their waiting, failure, retry, rejection, and completion states without collapsing authority boundaries.
Audit Engine and Evidence Chain health apply continuously across all stages. Evidence backlog or append failure shall not be monitored only after execution.
Stage monitoring shall use canonical state rather than inferred trace order where the two differ.

Monitoring shall detect authentication failure patterns, privileged access, unusual elevation, dormant-account use, recovery-factor use, impossible or anomalous access where reliable, credential expiry, certificate expiry, token-validation failure, and authorization-denial changes.
An anomaly is not proof of compromise. Response shall consider identity assurance, device, service, tenant, environment, time, and supporting evidence.
Monitoring shall not expose authentication secrets or personal behavior beyond the approved purpose. Security monitoring access shall be restricted.
Privileged access monitoring shall integrate with the Audit Engine and Incident Response while preserving legal and human-review requirements.

Policy Engine monitoring shall include availability, latency, evaluation volume, outcome categories, rule and bundle version, error, timeout, cache freshness, dependency state, and deny/allow distribution within privacy-safe bounds.
Monitoring shall not expose sensitive policy logic or allow telemetry to modify policy. A monitoring rule cannot override a deterministic Policy Engine decision.
Policy Engine error or unavailable state shall trigger the defined fail-safe behavior rather than default allow.
Approval monitoring shall cover queue size and age, expiry, assignment, escalation, duplicate requests, decision latency, unavailable approvers, high-risk backlog, and integrity failures.
Human productivity metrics shall be minimized and shall not become intrusive personnel surveillance. The purpose is process safety and service reliability.
Monitoring shall distinguish waiting for required approval from system latency. Approval timeout shall not become implicit approval.
Operational alerts shall reference canonical approval records without duplicating protected identity unnecessarily.

Model monitoring shall cover approved provider and model availability, latency, token or compute use, cost, error categories, routing, fallback, rate limits, safety outcomes, response truncation, configuration, and supported-region state.
Model output quality, confidence, drift, and validation outcomes shall use Section 6 semantics. Provider success and low latency do not establish correctness.
Fallback alerts shall verify that selection remained within approved privacy, residency, customer, release, and model boundaries.
Raw prompts, responses, reasoning content, embeddings, or customer documents shall not be copied into alerts by default.

Tool Gateway monitoring shall cover connector availability, destination health, credential expiry, capability denial, rate limit, queue age, timeout, ambiguous outcome, retry, reconciliation, tenant fairness, and external side-effect failures.
Direct governed action outside the Tool Gateway shall generate a high-priority security condition where detectable.
An external success code is not proof of intended effect. Alerts shall distinguish confirmed failure, rejected action, ambiguous result, duplicate protection, and validation rejection.
Monitoring-triggered connector control shall remain within an approved Response Profile and current policy.

Validation monitoring shall cover throughput, backlog, oldest age, outcome categories, rule version, dependency health, evidence availability, timeout, incomplete state, and independent-service availability.
Unavailable or saturated validation shall not cause results to be accepted by default. Pending or constrained outcomes shall remain visible.
A high rejection rate may indicate source defects, provider change, attack, policy change, or validator defect. Monitoring shall not assume the cause.
Monitoring shall cover Audit Engine ingestion, buffer depth, durable append latency, ordering, duplication, storage, export, access anomalies, and retention operations.

Inventory linkage shall identify affected releases, environments, tenants, images, nodes, artifacts, and support lines.
Scanner severity is an input. Risk disposition shall consider reachability, privilege, data, tenant impact, compensating controls, and current threat intelligence.

Monitoring shall cover backup completion, age, scope, immutability, replication, key availability, capacity, retention, restore-test status, RPO, RTO, and failed recovery dependencies.

Dormant recovery paths shall not be considered healthy solely because no failure has been reported.
Deployments, configuration, policy, model, provider, schema, network, storage, autoscaling, observability, monitoring, and logging changes shall produce attributable change markers.
Monitoring shall compare relevant indicators before, during, and after rollout. Canary, progressive, and full release stages shall remain distinguishable.
Automatic rollback conditions shall be bounded and validated. Rollback shall not restore revoked authority, vulnerable artifacts, incompatible schemas, or ineligible provider configuration.
Change correlation suggests association but does not prove root cause. Investigation remains required.
Monitoring shall cover compute, accelerator, model, storage, network transfer, observability, backup, validation, evidence, provider, and support costs within approved budgets.

Alerts, notifications, tickets, status pages, runbooks, dashboards, and exports shall minimize personal, customer, model, repository, security, and infrastructure data.

Administrative access shall use strong authentication, least privilege, attributable elevation, logging, review, and protected recovery.

During a registered Single-Maintainer Bootstrap Profile, one authorized maintainer may temporarily own multiple monitoring roles where independent personnel are unavailable. High-impact changes to security monitoring, tenant alerts, customer status, Tool Gateway response, Audit Engine or Evidence Chain monitoring, public service objectives, and automated production containment shall receive qualified external review before affecting a Stable release, production environment, or Enterprise operating profile; otherwise they shall remain constrained.

Before a Monitoring Profile or material change becomes eligible, the applicable gates shall verify:
- owner, service, criticality, Deployment Profile, environment, region, release, tenant, and support scope;
- critical journeys, canonical stages, dependencies, failure modes, and protected controls;
- service-level indicators with exact numerator, denominator, unit, scope, source, window, and quality;
- evidence-backed objectives, error-budget semantics, exclusions, and customer-commitment boundaries;
- conditions, thresholds, anomalies, evaluation, pending, recovery, and missing-data behavior;
- stable alert identity, bounded labels, severity, routing, ownership, escalation, and runbooks;
- safe deduplication, grouping, inhibition, silences, maintenance, and acknowledgement;
- deterministic bounded automated response with Tool Gateway and human-approval controls;
- black-box, white-box, synthetic, user-journey, security, capacity, backup, recovery, and monitoring-system coverage;
- privacy, tenant isolation, security, residency, retention, and access;
- controlled rule, objective, route, response, and customer-status change;
- positive and negative independent Validation Pipeline tests;
- required Audit Engine and Evidence Chain records; and
- exception ownership, scope, expiry, monitoring, and residual-risk acceptance.
No single green dashboard, active alert, successful notification, rule test, objective report, provider status, or monitoring-platform health state shall satisfy the complete gate.
The following practices are prohibited unless an explicitly defined canonical exception applies:
- treating alerts, anomalies, objectives, dashboards, or monitoring systems as business authority or independent validation;
- conflating Monitoring with Observability, Logging, Audit, Evidence, Validation, Incident Response, or the Defect Lifecycle;
- defining objectives without exact indicators, scope, windows, data quality, and ownership;
- using error budget as permission to violate security, privacy, policy, approval, validation, evidence, safety, or law;
- treating missing or stale monitoring data as healthy by default;
- using unbounded alert labels, customer data, prompts, model outputs, secrets, or personal data in alerts;
- routing protected alert content to unauthorized recipients or channels;
- creating alerts without owners, escalation, or actionable response;
- using broad, indefinite, or unaudited silences and inhibition;
- allowing maintenance suppression to hide unrelated security, tenant, data, audit, or evidence failures;
- allowing anomaly systems or model recommendations to execute high-impact actions without deterministic policy and required approval;
- permitting monitoring-triggered governed external action outside the Tool Gateway;
- accepting results, approvals, or capabilities based on alert state;
- treating provider alarms or Kubernetes metrics as complete service monitoring;
- allowing monitoring failure to be represented as normal service;
- publishing customer status directly from unverified raw alerts where accountable review is required;
- making unreviewed direct production rule, route, severity, or response changes;
- allowing emergency rules, silences, or elevated response to become permanent through inaction;
- representing bootstrap self-review and single-person coverage as independent Enterprise assurance; or
- giving any alert engine, anomaly service, provider, dashboard, notification system, customer preference, sales commitment, or engineering convenience architectural authority.
It does not promise that every failure, attack, customer impact, model-quality problem, or provider defect can be detected before consequence. Coverage and limitations shall be represented honestly.
- every production service and critical control is governed by an approved Monitoring Profile;
- Monitoring remains distinct from Observability, Logging, Audit, Evidence, Validation, Incident Response, and Defect Lifecycle;
- indicators, objectives, error budgets, conditions, thresholds, anomalies, and missing-data behavior are exact and governed;
- alerts have stable identity, bounded labels, severity, ownership, routing, escalation, runbooks, and history;
- deduplication, grouping, inhibition, silences, maintenance, and acknowledgement preserve truth and scope;
- automated response is deterministic, least-privilege, bounded, attributable, and subject to Tool Gateway and approval controls;
- black-box, white-box, synthetic, user-journey, canonical-flow, security, capacity, infrastructure, backup, recovery, and cost monitoring are applied according to risk;
- Policy Engine, Approval Engine, Model Gateway, Tool Gateway, Validation Pipeline, Audit Engine, and Evidence Chain health are monitored without transferring authority;
- monitoring coverage, signal quality, alert quality, monitoring-system health, and known gaps are assessed continuously;
- privacy, tenant isolation, residency, access, retention, and notification-channel security are effective;
- change, release, customer impact, customer status, incident handoff, and recovery are governed;
- the Validation Pipeline independently verifies monitoring controls and does not accept business results through alert state;
- Audit Engine and Evidence Chain controls operate continuously and remain canonical;
- bootstrap limitations remain explicit, constrained, temporary, and subject to dated exit criteria; and
- architecture-significant monitoring decisions require an authorized ADR.
The following invariants are binding:
- monitoring evaluates signals but does not create ILATEN business authority;
- an alert is an operational condition, not policy permission, approval, capability, validation, incident cause, or legal conclusion;
- Monitoring, Observability, Logging, Audit, Evidence, Validation, Incident Response, and Defect Lifecycle remain distinct;
- unknown, stale, sampled, partial, and missing monitoring data are not represented as healthy certainty;
- every actionable alert has bounded identity, owner, severity, routing, escalation, and response guidance;
- error budgets never waive non-waivable security, privacy, tenant, policy, approval, validation, audit, evidence, safety, or legal controls;
- silences and inhibition suppress notification, not truth, collection, evidence, or obligation;
- automated response remains deterministic, bounded, attributable, and separately authorized;
- the deterministic Policy Engine remains within the ILATEN Control Plane;
- the Approval Engine remains the accountable approval authority;
- every governed external action remains mediated by the Tool Gateway under constrained capability;
- the Validation Pipeline remains independent and alert state does not become acceptance;
- Audit Engine and Evidence Chain controls operate continuously and are not replaced by alerts, objectives, dashboards, status pages, or provider alarms;
- monitoring systems monitor their own health, rules, data, routes, and notification paths;
- tenant isolation covers evaluation, labels, grouping, routing, notification, dashboards, status, and history;
- customer status and contractual claims use accountable approved processes;
- monitoring limitations and coverage gaps are represented honestly;
- bootstrap operation does not imply independent Enterprise continuity or assurance; and
- architecture-significant monitoring decisions require an authorized ADR.

A Monitoring implementation is non-conformant if it treats alerts, objectives, anomalies, dashboards, provider status, or monitoring tools as authority or validation; merges Monitoring with Observability, Logging, Audit, Evidence, Incident Response, or Defect Lifecycle; defines ambiguous indicators or unsupported objectives; treats missing data as healthy; uses unowned, unrouteable, unbounded, or privacy-unsafe alerts; hides conditions through broad silence, inhibition, maintenance, or rule deletion; permits automated response to bypass deterministic policy, required approval, or Tool Gateway; accepts results based on alert state; fails to monitor Validation, Audit, Evidence, monitoring infrastructure, or critical dependencies; misrepresents customer impact, status, coverage, or bootstrap continuity; or gives any rule engine, alert manager, anomaly detector, status page, notification provider, model output, customer preference, sales commitment, or engineering convenience architectural authority.

Audit Engine and Evidence Chain controls operate continuously across material lifecycle events. A logging failure shall be visible and treated according to risk, but ordinary logging availability shall not be represented as proof that audit or evidence obligations were satisfied.
**Evidence** binds material artifacts and events required to prove, verify, or examine a governed outcome.

A log query result shall not grant permission, approve a change, accept a task, close a defect, declare compliance, establish legal fact, or modify architecture. Any action arising from log analysis must pass through the applicable policy, approval, capability, Tool Gateway, validation, audit, and evidence controls.

ILATEN shall define portable event semantics independently of a specific vendor. Implementations may map canonical fields to an approved open telemetry model or another documented representation when meaning, type, scope, ordering limitations, security, and lifecycle controls remain intact.

New systems should prefer structured event emission and portable schemas. Existing text logs may be collected through controlled parsing, but parsing assumptions, ambiguity, loss, multiline behavior, timestamp behavior, and schema coverage shall be documented and validated.

Provider replacement shall preserve required event classes, correlation, access, retention, export, deletion, integrity, and investigation capability. Proprietary enrichment or detection may supplement canonical records but shall not become the only representation of a material event without an approved portability and continuity treatment.
Logging shall:
**Logging Coverage Gap.** A known or detected absence, degradation, ambiguity, delay, or loss in required event visibility.
These terms shall not be collapsed. A Log Record is not an Alert Instance, Audit Record, Evidence Object, Validation Result, Incident, or Defect merely because a system links them.
Every production service, security-relevant component, and critical platform dependency shall have an approved Logging Profile proportionate to its risk and Deployment Profile.
The profile shall define:
- required Event Classes, Event Codes, levels, field schemas, versioning, and compatibility rules;
- fields prohibited by default and any narrowly approved sensitive-field exceptions;
- sampling, suppression, deduplication, and rate-limiting rules, including protected event classes that shall not be discarded;

A service shall not enter an unrestricted production profile without an accepted Logging Profile or an approved, time-bounded exception that identifies the missing coverage and constrains the affected capability.

Profiles shall be versioned. A change to an Event Code meaning, sensitive-data treatment, tenant scope, retention class, mandatory field, routing rule, or protected event class is a governed change and shall not be introduced as an undocumented configuration adjustment.
The canonical event taxonomy shall support at least the following classes where applicable:
- tenant-context creation, binding, validation, routing, isolation, and rejection;

Event taxonomies shall describe stable semantic meaning, not product-specific screen labels. One event may belong to more than one approved class, but it shall retain one unambiguous primary Event Code and source identity.

Routine successful events and exceptional failures shall remain distinguishable. A generic message such as “operation failed” is insufficient for a material control path when a stable reason code and bounded state can be emitted safely.
Machine-generated records shall be structured by default. Human-readable text may accompany structured fields but shall not be the sole source of material meaning.
Each applicable record shall include:
- actor class and pseudonymous or approved subject reference where attribution is required;
- data classification, retention class, redaction status, and source trust classification where required;
Field names, types, permitted values, null semantics, units, maximum lengths, normalization rules, and privacy classifications shall be defined in a versioned schema.

Raw request bodies, response bodies, prompts, model outputs, files, database rows, authorization tokens, secrets, cryptographic key material, cookies, session identifiers, and customer content shall not be included by default. A business identifier shall be logged only when necessary for an approved purpose and protected according to classification.
Logging schemas are governed interfaces. They shall have accountable ownership, machine-readable definitions where practical, compatibility tests, lifecycle status, and change history.

Additive optional fields may be introduced compatibly when consumers tolerate absence and unknown fields. Removal, rename, type change, semantic change, required-field introduction, enum narrowing, identifier format change, or retention-class change requires explicit compatibility treatment.

Event Codes shall not be silently reused for different semantics. Deprecated codes shall have a transition plan and an approved retention period sufficient for dependent detection, search, audit-support, and customer integration rules to migrate.

Collectors may normalize heterogeneous sources into a canonical envelope. The original source identity and transformation history shall remain attributable. Normalization shall not invent precision, identity, tenant, outcome, or completeness that the source did not provide.

Schema registries, semantic-convention catalogs, or code generation may support consistency but do not replace review. Vendor-defined fields shall be mapped explicitly and shall not override canonical meanings.
Event identifiers shall support detection of duplicates without creating a false claim of global uniqueness. The identity scope and generation method shall be documented.

Collectors and sinks may retry delivery. At-least-once transport may create duplicates; at-most-once transport may lose records. The Logging Profile shall declare delivery semantics and how consumers detect or tolerate duplication and loss.

Deduplication shall preserve a count, first-seen time, last-seen time, source set, and rule identity where removal of duplicates could affect investigation. It shall not erase evidence of repeated security attempts or independent occurrences that merely share message text.
An idempotency key used for business execution shall not automatically become a public log identifier. Correlation must preserve security and privacy boundaries.
**Fatal** records an unrecoverable condition that causes the emitting process or critical service boundary to terminate or become unavailable. It shall not be used merely to increase alert urgency.

Severity shall describe the emitted event, not automatically determine alert severity, incident severity, defect priority, customer communication, or regulatory significance. Monitoring rules may derive operational conditions from records under Section 7.9.

Routine denials produced by correct policy enforcement are not necessarily errors. A denial may be informational, warning, or security-relevant depending on context, frequency, source, and risk. Conversely, a nominally successful operation that bypassed a required control is a critical security event.

Dynamic level changes require authorization, exact scope, start time, expiry, purpose, owner, rollback, and monitoring. Production Trace or Debug shall expire automatically where feasible. It shall not be used to capture prohibited data.
Emitters shall use synchronized time sources appropriate to the Deployment Profile. Timestamp precision and source shall be documented.
Records shall distinguish event time from collection or ingestion time. A late-arriving event shall retain its original event time and an observable arrival delay.

Distributed systems do not guarantee total order merely because timestamps exist. Clock skew, batching, buffering, retries, offline operation, region boundaries, provider queues, and restoration can reorder records. Investigations shall use correlation, sequence numbers, causal references, and source state where available.

Components on a material control path should emit bounded sequence or transition references when order matters. A sequence gap shall be detectable and shall not be silently closed by downstream sorting.

Clock synchronization failure, excessive skew, timestamp regression, unknown timezone, invalid timestamp, and timestamp precision loss shall be monitored and logged. Systems shall use a standard unambiguous time representation and preserve source offset only where needed.
Time corrections shall not rewrite historical records silently. Any normalization or correction applied downstream shall preserve the original value and transformation metadata.

Correlation identifiers shall connect the canonical operational flow from request intake through identity, tenant binding, context creation, recommendation, policy, risk, approval, capability issuance, Tool Gateway execution, validation, acceptance or rejection, delivery, closure, audit, and evidence.

Correlation shall be scoped to prevent cross-tenant discovery. Identifiers exposed to customers, providers, or untrusted clients shall not reveal internal topology, sequence, volume, account data, or reusable authority.

Propagation shall be allowlisted across trust boundaries. Untrusted callers shall not be permitted to forge internal source identity, privileged actor identity, approval identity, policy result, audit identity, or evidence reference through arbitrary headers or payload fields.

Where an external provider supplies a request identifier, ILATEN shall preserve it as provider-scoped metadata and bind it to an internally generated reference. It shall not replace internal identity.

Errors shall be recorded with stable failure class, reason code, affected operation, bounded context, retryability, external-effect state, and correlation references. Human-readable messages should state the condition without exposing protected data.

Stack traces, query fragments, provider messages, serialized objects, environment variables, paths, and command output can contain secrets or customer information. They shall be filtered, truncated, classified, and access-controlled before leaving the trusted diagnostic boundary.

An exception handler shall not log the same failure repeatedly at every layer without added semantic value. The profile shall define the accountable recording boundary and preserve causal relationships without creating unbounded duplication.

Catch-and-ignore behavior shall not conceal a material error. If a failure is intentionally suppressed, the system shall record the governing reason, bounded impact, and responsible control where required.

Tool Gateway records shall distinguish not dispatched, dispatched, acknowledged, partially completed, completed, rejected, timed out, and outcome unknown. A transport timeout after dispatch shall not be logged as a definite execution failure when an external effect may have occurred.

Validation rejection shall remain distinct from technical execution failure. Model refusal, provider failure, policy denial, approval denial, capability expiry, tool failure, validation rejection, and delivery failure shall have different Event Codes.
Untrusted values shall be recorded as typed fields rather than concatenated into free-form messages where practical.

Each function shall have a charter, accountable owner, delegated decision scope, required competence, escalation path, meeting or review cadence, durable decision record, and succession or continuity arrangement. Decisions affecting non-waivable controls, cross-tenant access, cryptographic custody, evidence integrity, release promotion, or irreversible customer impact shall require the exact independent participation defined by policy.

Machine roles shall be separate identities with bounded capabilities and shall never inherit human accountability.

Every machine agent manifest shall include a stable machine identifier, human-readable alias, role, team, capabilities, permissions, accepted inputs, produced outputs, dependencies, allowed callers, allowed targets, escalation path, verifier, version, and lifecycle status. Aliases may change without changing machine identity. A missing or ambiguous manifest field shall fail closed for governed execution.

The proposer, approver, executor, verifier, and evidence custodian shall be separated when risk policy requires. A generator shall not independently verify its own material output. A model or agent shall not approve its own authority, budget, exception, release, or evidence. Privileged administration shall be separate from ordinary access and shall use separately authorized identities and sessions.

Delegation shall be explicit, scoped, time-bounded, revocable, attributable, and no broader than the delegator's authority. Delegation shall not transfer accountability or bypass required independence. Acting assignments, emergency substitutions, and succession shall be recorded and reviewed.

Role assignments, service identities, machine agents, privileged groups, provider access, break-glass access, and delegated authority shall undergo periodic and event-driven review. Termination, role change, compromise, inactivity, or control failure shall trigger timely revocation.

Audit governance shall define the independent assessment scope, cadence, competence, access, evidence sources, sampling limitations, issue classification, remediation ownership, and reporting route. Operational logging, dashboards, provider attestations, and self-authored evidence may inform audit but shall not replace independent validation or canonical evidence.

Auditors shall have read-only, least-privilege access to the evidence required for their approved scope. Audit access itself shall be attributable, monitored, and subject to tenant, privacy, retention, and legal restrictions.

Audit findings shall have stable identifiers, severity, affected controls and tenants, evidence references, accountable owner, remediation plan, due date, residual risk, verification requirement, and closure decision. Management acceptance shall not erase a finding or alter historical evidence. Overdue or repeated findings shall escalate according to risk.

ILAIOS shall not claim certification, regulatory compliance, control effectiveness, non-repudiation, or independent assurance without the exact external or independent evidence required for that claim. Scope, date, exclusions, dependencies, and expiration shall accompany any assurance statement.

Risk governance shall maintain a versioned taxonomy for security, privacy, AI/model, operational, availability, financial, legal, compliance, vendor, data, safety, and strategic risk. Risk records shall identify assets, threats or failure modes, likelihood, impact, affected tenants and data, existing controls, residual risk, owner, treatment, target date, monitoring, and evidence.

Risk classification shall drive approval, verification V0-V4, authority scope, sandboxing, DLP, budget, rollout, observability, recovery, and human-in-the-loop requirements. Models may recommend classifications but cannot determine or waive binding treatment.

Accepted treatments are avoid, reduce, transfer where real and evidenced, or explicitly accept within authorized appetite. Risk acceptance shall be time-bounded and cannot waive law, tenant isolation, evidence integrity, authorization, required human accountability, or other non-waivable controls. Material residual risk shall be visible to the accountable decision maker before approval.

AI risk assessment shall include prompt injection, indirect prompt injection, tool manipulation, data exfiltration, training-data or provider leakage, hallucination, insecure output handling, model substitution, provider compromise, excessive agency, runaway retries, context poisoning, memory poisoning, identity confusion, and verifier collusion. Mitigation shall use deterministic policy, permission firewalls, content and DLP controls, bounded tools, independent verification, rate and budget limits, circuit breakers, and escalation.

Changes shall be classified as standard, normal, emergency, security-critical, architecture-significant, data-affecting, model/provider, policy, or release/promotion changes. Each class shall define required review, tests, approvals, evidence, rollback, scheduling, communication, and post-change verification.

Architecture-significant changes require an ADR. Security, policy, grant, approval, verifier, audit, evidence, tenant-isolation, DLP, secrets, cryptographic, billing, or release controls shall not be silently weakened through ordinary change workflows.

Capability maturity and ReleaseState remain independent. Test success or `VERIFIED` maturity shall not imply deployment. RELEASE.R01, RELEASE.R02, and RELEASE.R03 require explicit authorized human promotion decisions, bounded exposure, health gates, evidence, and tested rollback. No automation may infer promotion permission.

Emergency changes shall use the smallest safe scope, separately authenticated privileged access, recorded rationale, real-time or retrospective independent review according to urgency, continuous evidence, rollback or containment, expiry, and mandatory follow-up. Emergency status shall not create permanent bypasses.

Compliance controls shall be implemented as modular, versioned profiles bound to applicable tenants, regions, data classes, contracts, and services. A profile shall state its authority, scope, exclusions, evidence requirements, control owners, assessment method, review cadence, and retirement conditions.

Enabling a profile shall not constitute certification. ILAIOS shall report capability, implementation, assessment, and certification states separately. Unknown applicability shall escalate rather than default to a compliance claim.

Canonical requirements may map to multiple external frameworks, but external framework language shall not override stricter ILAIOS controls. Mappings shall retain source version, interpretation, evidence, assessor, gaps, and review date. One test or artifact shall not be treated as universal compliance proof.

Compliance operations shall support governed access, export, correction where applicable, deletion, restriction, objection, retention, and legal-hold workflows. Requests shall verify identity and authority, preserve tenant scope, minimize disclosure, record approvals and exceptions, and produce auditable disposition evidence.

Each critical service and dependency shall have an owned Business Continuity Plan identifying critical outcomes, maximum tolerable disruption inputs, dependency alternatives, staffing and communication plans, data and evidence requirements, recovery strategy, exercise cadence, and improvement actions. Concrete RPO, RTO, SLO, and contractual values shall remain deployment-profile configuration until approved for a business tier.

Backups shall be encrypted, tenant- and region-aware, access-controlled, inventoried, retention-governed, integrity-checked, and isolated from ordinary compromise paths. Backup creation alone does not prove recoverability. Restore tests shall verify data, authorization, tenant isolation, keys, evidence continuity, version compatibility, and application behavior.

Disaster recovery shall define declaration authority, incident command, recovery order, eligible regions and providers, data-consistency treatment, failover and failback, credential and key access, communications, evidence collection, and return-to-normal criteria. Failover shall not select an ineligible tenant, region, provider, release, data authority, or security posture.

Exercises shall record scenario, participants, actual timings, achieved data point, failures, manual actions, evidence, corrective work, and independent review. Unexercised assumptions shall remain explicit gaps.

Every production service shall define measurable SLIs, configurable SLOs, measurement windows, data-quality rules, error budgets, owners, and escalation policy. Numerical targets shall be selected by approved deployment profile and business tier and shall not be invented as contractual guarantees.
